## 10. Avakujja Sutta

30. Bhikkhus, these three types of persons are found existing in the world. Which three? The person with overturned-pot-like wisdom, the person with lap-like wisdom, and the person with wide wisdom.

And what, bhikkhus, is the person with overturned-pot-like wisdom? Here, bhikkhus, a certain person frequently goes to the monastery to hear the Dhamma from the bhikkhus. The bhikkhus teach him the Dhamma that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with the right meaning and phrasing; they reveal the perfectly complete and pure holy life. While sitting in that place of hearing the Dhamma, he does not attend to the beginning of that talk, does not attend to the middle, and does not attend to the end. Even after rising from that seat, he does not attend to the beginning, middle, or end of that talk.

Bhikkhus, just as water poured onto an overturned pot spills away and does not stay, even so, bhikkhus, a certain person here frequently goes to the monastery to hear the Dhamma from the bhikkhus. The bhikkhus teach him the Dhamma that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with the right meaning and phrasing; they reveal the perfectly complete and pure holy life. While sitting in that place, he does not attend to the beginning, middle, or end of that talk. Even after rising from that seat, he does not attend to the beginning, middle, or end of that talk. This, bhikkhus, is called the person with overturned-pot-like wisdom.

And what, bhikkhus, is the person with lap-like wisdom? Here, bhikkhus, a certain person frequently goes to the monastery to hear the Dhamma from the bhikkhus. The bhikkhus teach him the Dhamma that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with the right meaning and phrasing; they reveal the perfectly complete and pure holy life. While sitting in that place, he attends to the beginning of that talk, attends to the middle, and attends to the end. But when he rises from that seat, he does not attend to the beginning, middle, or end of that talk.

Bhikkhus, suppose a man has various kinds of food scattered in his lap—sesame, rice, cakes, and jujubes...
129:
Just as if that person, upon rising from that seat, were to scatter them all about through forgetfulness; in the same way, bhikkhus, here a certain person frequently goes to the monastery to hear the Dhamma in the presence of the bhikkhus. To him, the bhikkhus teach the Dhamma that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with the meaning and the phrasing; they proclaim the holy life, entirely complete and pure. While sitting in that seat, he attends to the beginning of the talk, attends to the middle, and attends to the end. However, upon rising from that seat, he does not attend to the beginning, the middle, or the end of that talk. This, bhikkhus, is called the person with lap-like wisdom.

And what, bhikkhus, is the person of broad wisdom? Here, bhikkhus, a certain person frequently goes to the monastery to hear the Dhamma in the presence of the bhikkhus. To him, the bhikkhus teach the Dhamma that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with the meaning and the phrasing; they proclaim the holy life, entirely complete and pure. While sitting in that seat, he attends to the beginning of the talk, attends to the middle, and attends to the end. Even after rising from that seat, he attends to the beginning, the middle, and the end of that talk. Just as, bhikkhus, when water is poured into an upright pot, it stays there and does not leak out; in the same way, bhikkhus, here a certain person frequently goes to the monastery to hear the Dhamma in the presence of the bhikkhus. To him, the bhikkhus teach the Dhamma that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with the meaning and the phrasing; they proclaim the holy life, entirely complete and pure. While sitting in that seat, he attends to the beginning of the talk, attends to the middle, and attends to the end. Even after rising from that seat, he attends to the beginning, the middle, and the end of that talk. This, bhikkhus, is called the person of broad wisdom. These three types of persons, bhikkhus, are found existing in the world.

A man of upside-down wisdom, unintelligent and undiscerning,
Even if he frequently goes to the presence of the bhikkhus,
Such a person is unable to grasp the beginning,
The middle, or the end of the talk,
130:
For he simply lacks wisdom. The person with lap-like wisdom is said to be better than the person with upside-down wisdom. Even if he frequently goes to the presence of the bhikkhus, while sitting in that seat, though he grasps the beginning, the middle, and the end of the talk and its phrasing, upon rising, he does not understand it; what he has grasped is forgotten. The person of broad wisdom is said to be better than those previously mentioned. If such an excellent person frequently goes to the presence of the bhikkhus, while sitting in that seat, he grasps the beginning, the middle, and the end of the talk, and upon rising, he retains the phrasing. That person, with noble intentions and an undistracted mind, practicing in accordance with the Dhamma, would make an end of suffering.

Tenth Sutta.
The third, Puggala Vagga, is finished.

## 4. Devadūta Vagga
## 1. Sabrahmaka Sutta

31. Bhikkhus, those families where the parents are honored in the home by their children are said to live with Brahmā. Bhikkhus, those families where the parents are honored in the home by their children are said to live with the first teachers. Bhikkhus, those families where the parents are honored in the home by their children are said to live with those worthy of offerings brought from afar. Bhikkhus, 'Brahmā' is a designation for parents. Bhikkhus, 'first teachers' is a designation for parents. Bhikkhus, 'those worthy of offerings brought from afar' is a designation for parents.
131:
For what reason is that so? Monks, parents are of great help to their children; they are the providers of life, the nourishers, and those who show this world (to their children).

Parents are called "Brahmā," they are called "First Teachers," and they are "Worthy of Offerings" from their children, for they are compassionate toward their progeny.

Therefore, a wise person should revere and honor those parents with food and drink, with clothing and bedding, by massaging and bathing them, and by washing their feet. Because of such service to their parents, the wise praise that person in this very life, and after passing away, that person rejoices in heaven.

First Sutta.

## 2. Ānanda Sutta

32. Then the Venerable Ānanda approached the Blessed One, paid homage, and sat down to one side. Sitting there, the Venerable Ānanda said to the Blessed One: "Venerable Sir, could a bhikkhu attain such a state of concentration that in this conscious body, there would be no I-making (ahaṅkāra), no mine-making (mamaṅkāra), and no underlying tendency to conceit (mānānusaya); and regarding all external signs, there would be no I-making, no mine-making, and no underlying tendency to conceit; and that he would enter and dwell in that liberation of mind (cetovimutti) and liberation by wisdom (paññāvimutti) where I-making, mine-making, and the underlying tendency to conceit no longer exist?"

"Ānanda, a bhikkhu could attain such a state of concentration that in this conscious body, there would be no I-making, no mine-making, and no underlying tendency to conceit; and regarding all external signs, there would be no I-making, no mine-making, and no underlying tendency to conceit; and that he would enter and dwell in that liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom where I-making, mine-making, and the underlying tendency to conceit no longer exist."

"Venerable Sir, in what way could a bhikkhu attain such a state of concentration that in this conscious body, there would be no I-making, no mine-making, and no underlying tendency to conceit; and regarding all external signs, there would be no I-making..."
132:
...no mine-making, and no underlying tendency to conceit; and that he would enter and dwell in that liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom where I-making, mine-making, and the underlying tendency to conceit no longer exist; in what way could a bhikkhu attain such a state of concentration?"

"Ānanda, in this Teaching, a bhikkhu has this thought: 'This is peaceful, this is sublime, namely, the stillness of all formations (saṅkhāra), the relinquishment of all acquisitions (upadhi), the destruction of craving, dispassion, cessation, Nibbāna.' In this way, Ānanda, a bhikkhu could attain such a state of concentration that in this conscious body, there would be no I-making, no mine-making, and no underlying tendency to conceit; and regarding all external signs, there would be no I-making, no mine-making, and no underlying tendency to conceit; and that he would enter and dwell in that liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom where I-making, mine-making, and the underlying tendency to conceit no longer exist. Ānanda, with reference to this Nibbāna, I have spoken thus in the Pārāyana Vagga, in the Question of the Youth Punnaka:

'Having discerned the high and low in the world,
He for whom there is no perturbation anywhere in the world,
Peaceful, free from the smoke (of defilements), untroubled, and desireless,
He has crossed over birth and aging, I say.'"

Second Sutta.

## 3. Sāriputta Sutta

33. Then the Venerable Sāriputta approached the Blessed One, paid homage, and sat down to one side. As the Venerable Sāriputta was sitting there, the Blessed One said to him: "Sāriputta, I could teach the Dhamma in brief; I could teach the Dhamma in detail; I could teach the Dhamma both in brief and in detail. But those who understand are rare."

"Blessed One, it is the time for this! Sublime One, it is the time for this! That the Blessed One should teach the Dhamma in brief, teach it in detail, and teach it both in brief and in detail. There will be those who understand the Dhamma."

"Therefore, Sāriputta, you should train yourselves thus: 'In this conscious body, there shall be no I-making, no mine-making, and no underlying tendency to conceit; and regarding all external signs, there shall be no I-making, no mine-making, and no underlying tendency to conceit...'
133:
"For one who dwells having attained the liberation of mind (Arahatta-phala Samādhi) and the liberation by wisdom (Arahatta-phala Paññā), there are no 'I-making' (ahaṅkāra), 'mine-making' (mamaṅkāra), and the underlying tendency of conceit (mānānusaya). One should train thus: 'We will dwell having attained that liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom.' Sāriputta, this is how you should train."

"Sāriputta, when for a bhikkhu, there are no 'I-making', 'mine-making', and the underlying tendency of conceit in this body with consciousness; and there are no 'I-making', 'mine-making', and the underlying tendency of conceit in all external signs (nimitta); and when he dwells having attained that liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom where 'I-making', 'mine-making', and the underlying tendency of conceit do not occur—then, Sāriputta, this bhikkhu is called one who has cut off craving, overturned the fetters, and by the right breakthrough of conceit, has made an end of the suffering of the round (vaṭṭa). Sāriputta, it was with reference to this that I said in the Pārāyana Vagga, in the Questions of Udaya:

'The abandoning of both sensual perceptions and grief,
The dispelling of sloth, and the warding off of remorse.
Purified by equanimity and mindfulness, preceded by right thought,
I speak of liberation through final knowledge (aññāvimokkha), the shattering of ignorance.'"

The third sutta.

## 4. Nidāna Sutta

34. "Bhikkhus, there are these three causes for the origination of kamma (that lead to the round of suffering). Which three? Greed is a cause for the origination of kamma, hatred is a cause for the origination of kamma, and delusion is a cause for the origination of kamma. Bhikkhus, whatever kamma is performed with greed, born of greed, caused by greed, originated from greed: in whatever realm that person's individual existence (attabhāva) is produced, there that kamma ripens. Wherever that kamma ripens, there he experiences the result of that kamma, whether in the present life, in the next life, or in some subsequent existence. Bhikkhus, whatever kamma is performed with hatred, born of hatred, caused by hatred, originated from hatred: in whatever realm that person's individual existence is produced, there that kamma ripens."
134:
"Wherever that kamma ripens, there he experiences the result of that kamma, whether in the present life, in the next life, or in some subsequent existence. Bhikkhus, whatever kamma is performed with delusion, born of delusion, caused by delusion, originated from delusion: in whatever realm that person's individual existence is produced, there that kamma ripens. Wherever that kamma ripens, there he experiences the result of that kamma, whether in the present life, in the next life, or in some subsequent existence."

"Bhikkhus, it is just as if seeds that are unfragmented, unrotten, undamaged by wind and sun, capable of sprouting, and well-preserved, were sown in a good field, in well-prepared soil. And if the rain-god were to provide a good rainfall. In such a case, those seeds would reach growth, increase, and abundance. In the same way, bhikkhus, whatever kamma is performed with greed, born of greed, caused by greed, originated from greed: in whatever realm that person's individual existence is produced, there that kamma ripens. Wherever that kamma ripens, there he experiences the result of that kamma, whether in the present life, in the next life, or in some subsequent existence. Whatever kamma is performed with hatred, born of hatred... [etc.] ...Whatever kamma is performed with delusion, born of delusion, caused by delusion, originated from delusion: in whatever realm that person's individual existence is produced, there that kamma ripens. Wherever that kamma ripens, there he experiences the result of that kamma."

"Whether in the present life, in the next life, or in some subsequent existence, he experiences the result of that kamma. Bhikkhus, these are the three causes for the origination of kamma (that lead to the round of suffering)."

"Bhikkhus, there are these three causes for the origination of kamma (that lead to Nibbāna, the cessation of the round of suffering). Which three? Non-greed is a cause for the origination of kamma, non-hatred is a cause for the origination of kamma, and non-delusion is a cause for the origination of kamma. Bhikkhus, whatever kamma is performed with non-greed, born of non-greed, caused by non-greed, originated from non-greed: when greed has vanished, that kamma is thus abandoned, cut off at the root, made like a palm-tree stump (tālāvatthukata), obliterated, and not subject to future arising. Bhikkhus, whatever kamma is performed with non-hatred, born of non-hatred, caused by non-hatred, originated from non-hatred: when hatred has vanished, that kamma is thus abandoned, cut off at the root, made like a palm-tree stump, obliterated, and not subject to future arising. Bhikkhus, whatever kamma is performed with non-delusion, born of non-delusion, caused by non-delusion, originated from non-delusion: when delusion has vanished, that kamma is thus abandoned,"
135:
...its roots are utterly cut off, made like a palm stump, done away with, so that it is no longer subject to future arising.

Monks, suppose there were seeds that are unbroken, not rotten, not damaged by wind and sun, fertile, and well-preserved. If a man were to burn them with fire, and having burned them, make them into ashes, and having made them into ashes, winnow them in a strong wind or let them be carried away by a swift-flowing river. Monks, if this were done, those seeds would have their roots cut off, be made like a palm stump, done away with, so that they are no longer subject to future arising. In the same way, monks, whatever kamma is performed without greed (alobha), born of non-greed, caused by non-greed, originating from non-greed; when greed has vanished, that kamma is abandoned, its roots cut off, made like a palm stump, done away with, so that it is no longer subject to future arising. Whatever kamma is performed without hatred (adosa)... [as above] ...Whatever kamma is performed without delusion (amoha), born of non-delusion, caused by non-delusion, originating from non-delusion; when delusion has vanished, that kamma is abandoned... [as above] ...no longer subject to future arising. Monks, these are the three origins for the arising of kamma (that leads to the cessation of the round of suffering).

Whether a little or a lot, the ignorant one performs kamma born of greed, kamma born of hatred, and kamma born of delusion. That ignorant one must experience that kamma right here in this very self; no other basis for it exists. Therefore, a wise monk, having understood greed, hatred, and kamma born of delusion, and giving rise to knowledge (vijjā), should abandon all miserable states (duggati).

Fourth Sutta.

## 5. Hatthaka Sutta

35. Thus have I heard: At one time the Blessed One was staying at Āḷavī on a bed of leaves in the Siṃsapā forest on the cattle path (Gomagga). Then Hatthaka of Āḷavī, while wandering and walking for exercise, saw the Blessed One sitting on a bed of leaves in the Siṃsapā forest on the cattle path. Having seen him, he approached the Blessed One, paid homage, and sat down to one side. Sitting there, Hatthaka of Āḷavī said to the Blessed One: "Venerable Sir, did the Blessed One sleep well?"

"Prince, I slept well. Among those in the world who sleep well, I am one of them," the Blessed One replied.
136:
"Venerable Sir, the winter night is cold; it is the time of the 'eight-day interval' (antarāṭṭhaka) between the months of Tabodwe and Tabaung when snow falls. The ground is rough, trampled by cattle hooves. The bed of leaves is thin. The leaves of the trees are sparse. The saffron robes are thin. And a cold wind blows from all four directions. Yet, despite this, the Blessed One says: 'Prince, I slept well. Among those in the world who sleep well, I am one of them.'"

"In that case, Prince, I will question you in return. Answer as you see fit. What do you think, Prince? Suppose there were a householder or a householder's son in a gabled house, plastered inside and out, draft-free, with bolted doors and well-fitted windows. Therein was a couch spread with a long-fleeced woolen rug, a white woolen coverlet, a multi-colored patchwork quilt, a choice rug of antelope hide, with a canopy above and red pillows at both ends. A lamp would be burning there, and four wives would attend to him with all kinds of pleasantries. What do you think, Prince? Would that householder sleep well or not? What is your opinion on this?"

"Venerable Sir, he would sleep well. Among those in the world who sleep well, he would be one of them."

"What do you think, Prince? Might there arise in that householder or householder's son fevers of the body or mind born of lust (rāga), burning with which he would sleep poorly?"

"Yes, Venerable Sir, he would sleep poorly."

"Prince, those fevers born of lust, burning with which that householder or householder's son would sleep poorly—that lust has been abandoned by the Tathāgata, its roots cut off, made like a palm stump, done away with, so that it is no longer subject to future arising. Therefore, I sleep well. What do you think, Prince? Might there arise in that householder or householder's son fevers of the body or mind born of hatred (dosa)... [as above] ...or born of delusion (moha), burning with which he would sleep poorly?"
137:
"It is true, Bhante, that one sleeps in suffering," he said.

"Prince, whatever householder or householder's son burns with the fevers born of delusion, he sleeps in suffering. That delusion has been abandoned by the Tathāgata, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, done away with, so that it is no longer subject to future arising. Therefore, I sleep happily."

"Always indeed he sleeps happily, the Brahmin who is fully extinguished, who does not cling to sensual pleasures, who has become cool and is without acquisitions. Having cut all attachments, having removed the distress in the heart, the peaceful one sleeps happily, having attained peace of mind."

The fifth discourse.

## 6. Devadūta Sutta

36. "Monks, there are these three divine messengers. Which three? Here, monks, a certain person conducts himself wrongly in body, wrongly in speech, and wrongly in mind. Because he has conducted himself wrongly in body, speech, and mind, after the breakup of the body, after death, he is reborn in a state of misery, a bad destination, a state of ruin, in hell. Monks, the wardens of hell, seizing him by both arms, present him to King Yama, saying: 'Sire, this man was undutiful to his mother, undutiful to his father, undutiful to ascetics, undutiful to brahmins, and did not respect the elders in his family. May Your Majesty decree a punishment for him.'

"Then, monks, King Yama questions, cross-examines, and speaks to him regarding the first divine messenger: 'My good man, did you not see the first divine messenger who appeared among human beings?' He says: 'I did not see him, Bhante.'

"Then, monks, King Yama says to him: 'My good man, did you not see among human beings a woman or a man, eighty, ninety, or a hundred years old, aged, as crooked as a roof-rafter, bent, leaning on a staff, trembling as they go, ailing, past their prime, with broken teeth, grey hair, scanty hair, bald, with wrinkled skin and limbs covered with blotches?' He says: 'I saw them, Bhante.'"
138:
"...ninety, or a hundred years old, an old woman or an old man?" He says: "I saw them, Bhante."

Then, monks, King Yama says to him: "My good man, being a wise and mature person, did it not occur to you: 'I too am subject to old age, I have not gone beyond old age. Let me now do what is good in body, speech, and mind'?" He says: "I was unable, Bhante. I was negligent, Bhante."

Then, monks, King Yama says to him: "My good man, through negligence you did not do what is good in body, speech, and mind. Surely, my good man, they will deal with you in accordance with your negligence. For this evil deed of yours was not done by your mother, nor by your father, nor by your brother, nor by your sister, nor by your friends and colleagues, nor by your kinsmen and relatives, nor by the deities, nor by ascetics and brahmins. Rather, this evil deed was done by you yourself, and you alone will experience its result."

Then, monks, King Yama, having questioned, cross-examined, and spoken to him regarding the first divine messenger, questions, cross-examines, and speaks to him regarding the second divine messenger: "My good man, did you not see the second divine messenger who appeared among human beings?" He says: "I did not see him, Bhante."

Then, monks, King Yama says to him: "My good man, did you not see among human beings a woman or a man, afflicted, suffering, gravely ill, lying fouled in their own excrement and urine, lifted up by others and put to bed by others?" He says: "I saw them, Bhante."

Then, monks, King Yama says to him: "My good man, being a wise and mature person, did it not occur to you: 'I too am subject to illness, I have not gone beyond illness...'
139:
Did it not occur to you—being wise and mature—'Now I will do good deeds by body, speech, and mind'?" (He asks). "Venerable sir, I was unable to do so; I was negligent," that man replies. Bhikkhus, King Yama says to him: "Friend, because of negligence you did not do good deeds by body, speech, and mind. Surely, friend, they will deal with you in accordance with your negligence. This evil deed of yours was not done by your mother, nor by your father, nor by your brother, nor by your sister, nor by your friends and colleagues, nor by your kinsmen and relatives, nor by the deities, nor by recluses and brahmins. Instead, this evil deed was done by you yourself, and you alone shall experience its result." (2)

Bhikkhus, after King Yama has questioned, cross-examined, and addressed him concerning the second divine messenger, he questions, cross-examines, and addresses him concerning the third divine messenger: "Friend, did you not see the third divine messenger who appeared among men?" He says: "I did not see him, venerable sir." Bhikkhus, King Yama asks him again: "Friend, did you not see among men a woman or a man, dead for one day, or two days, or three days, swollen, blue-black, and festering like a disgusting, putrid corpse?" He says: "I saw him, venerable sir." Bhikkhus, King Yama asks that man again: "Friend, did it not occur to you—being wise and mature—'I too am subject to death, I have not gone beyond death; now I will do good deeds by body, speech, and mind'?" (He asks again). "Venerable sir, I was unable to do so; I was negligent," that man replies. Bhikkhus, King Yama says to that man again: "Friend, because of negligence you did not do good deeds by body, speech, and mind...
140:
...by body, speech, and mind. Surely, friend, they will deal with you in accordance with your negligence. This evil deed of yours was not done by your mother, nor by your father, nor by your brother, nor by your sister, nor by your friends and colleagues, nor by your kinsmen and relatives, nor by the deities, nor by recluses and brahmins. Instead, this evil deed was done by you yourself, and you alone shall experience its result." (3)

Bhikkhus, after King Yama has questioned, cross-examined, and addressed him concerning the third divine messenger, he remains silent. Bhikkhus, the hell-wardens then subject that man to the punishment called the fivefold binding. They drive a red-hot iron stake through one hand, they drive a red-hot iron stake through the second hand, they drive a red-hot iron stake through one foot, they drive a red-hot iron stake through the second foot, and they drive a red-hot iron stake through the middle of his chest. There he feels painful, racking, piercing, and bitter sensations of suffering, yet he does not die as long as that evil deed is not exhausted. Bhikkhus, the hell-wardens then drag him away and chop him with axes. There he feels painful, racking, piercing, and bitter sensations of suffering, yet he does not die as long as that evil deed is not exhausted. Bhikkhus, the hell-wardens then take him feet up and head down and plane him with adzes. ... [Pe] ... Bhikkhus, the hell-wardens harness him to a chariot and drive him back and forth across ground that is burning, blazing, and glowing with fire. ... [Pe] ... Bhikkhus, the hell-wardens make him climb up and down a great mountain of coals that is burning, blazing, and glowing with fire. ... [Pe] ... Bhikkhus, the hell-wardens take him feet up and head down and throw him into a red-hot copper cauldron that is burning, blazing, and glowing with fire. There he is cooked, rising up in a foam, and he goes up once,

[The Great Hell description in verse:]
"It has four corners and four gates, divided into equal parts, surrounded by an iron wall, and covered with an iron roof. Its floor is made of iron, heated and glowing with fire; it stands always pervading a hundred yojanas all around."

"In the past, bhikkhus, this thought occurred to King Yama: 'Those who do evil deeds in the world are subjected to such various punishments. Oh, that I might attain the human state, and that a Tathāgata, an Arahant, a Perfectly Enlightened One, might arise in the world! May I attend upon that Blessed One, may that Blessed One teach me the Dhamma, and may I understand the Dhamma of that Blessed One!' Now, bhikkhus, I do not say this having heard it from another recluse or brahmin; rather, I say it because I have known it, seen it, and understood it for myself."
141:
He sinks down once, and he floats across once. There he experiences feelings that are painful, racking, and piercing, as long as that evil kamma is not exhausted, he does not die. Monks, the hell-wardens throw him into the Great Hell (Avīci). Monks, that Great Hell has four corners and four gates; it is divided into equal portions, surrounded by an iron wall, and covered with an iron roof. The floor of that hell is made of iron, glowing with heat, and joined with flames. It stands always spreading for a hundred yojanas all around.

The Sixth Sutta.

## 7. Yamarāja Sutta

37. Monks, in the past, this thought occurred to King Yama: 'Friends, those who perform low deeds in the world are subjected to such various and diverse tortures. If only I could attain the human state, and if a Tathāgata, an Arahant, a Perfectly Enlightened One were to appear in the world, and if I could attend upon that Blessed One, and if that Blessed One were to teach me the Dhamma, and if I were to understand that Dhamma of the Blessed One, that would be wonderful for me!' Monks, I do not say this having heard it from another ascetic or brahmin.
142:
Monks, what I have known for myself, seen for myself, and understood for myself, that I speak of just as I have known and seen it.

Those mortals who, urged by the divine messengers, are negligent,
They sorrow for a long time, having gone to a low body.
But those good people here, who are urged by the divine messengers,
Are never negligent in the Noble Dhamma.

Having seen fear in clinging, which is the source of birth and death,
They are liberated through non-clinging, in the destruction of birth and death.
They are diligent, happy, cooled in this very life,
143:
Those virtuous ones who have transcended all dangers have transcended all suffering.

The Seventh Discourse.

## 8. Dutiya Caturmahārāja Sutta

38. "Bhikkhus, on the eighth day of the fortnight, the ministers of the Four Great Kings wander through this world to see: 'Are many people in the world dutiful towards their mothers? Are they dutiful towards their fathers? Are they dutiful towards recluses? Are they dutiful towards brahmins? Do they respect the elders in the family? Do they observe the Uposatha? Do they observe the extraordinary Uposatha? Do they perform meritorious deeds?'

Bhikkhus, on the fourteenth day of the fortnight, the sons of the Four Great Kings wander through this world to see: 'Are many people in the world dutiful towards their mothers? Are they dutiful towards their fathers? Are they dutiful towards recluses? Are they dutiful towards brahmins? Do they respect the elders in the family? Do they observe the Uposatha? Do they observe the extraordinary Uposatha? Do they perform meritorious deeds?'

Bhikkhus, on the fifteenth day, the Uposatha day, the Four Great Kings themselves wander through this world to see: 'Are many people in the world dutiful towards their mothers? Are they dutiful towards their fathers? Are they dutiful towards recluses? Are they dutiful towards brahmins? Do they respect the elders in the family? Do they observe the Uposatha? Do they observe the extraordinary Uposatha? Do they perform meritorious deeds?'

Bhikkhus, if only a few people in the world are dutiful towards their mothers, dutiful towards their fathers, dutiful towards recluses, dutiful towards brahmins, respect the elders in the family, observe the extraordinary Uposatha, and perform meritorious deeds, then the Four Great Kings report this matter to the Tāvatiṃsa gods who are assembled and seated in the Sudhamma assembly hall, saying: 'O lords, only a few people in the world are dutiful towards their mothers... [as above]... and perform meritorious deeds.' Bhikkhus, at that time, the Tāvatiṃsa gods are displeased, thinking: 'Alas, the heavenly realms will diminish, and the four lower realms will be filled.'

Bhikkhus, if many people in the world are dutiful towards their mothers... [as above]... and perform meritorious deeds, then the Four Great Kings report this matter to the Tāvatiṃsa gods... saying: 'O lords, many people in the world are dutiful towards their mothers... [as above]... and perform meritorious deeds.' Bhikkhus, at that time, the Tāvatiṃsa gods are delighted, thinking: 'The heavenly realms will be filled, and the four lower realms will diminish.'

Bhikkhus, in the past, Sakka, Lord of the Gods, wishing to instruct the Tāvatiṃsa gods, recited this verse at that time:

'On the fourteenth, the fifteenth,
And the eighth day of the fortnight,
And on the extraordinary fortnight,
One should observe the Uposatha
Endowed with the eight factors,
A man such as I.'

Bhikkhus, that verse was poorly sung by Sakka, Lord of the Gods, not well sung; poorly spoken, not well spoken. Why is that? Because Sakka, Lord of the Gods, is not yet free from lust, hate, and delusion.

Bhikkhus, for a bhikkhu who is an Arahant, one whose taints are destroyed, who has lived the holy life, done what had to be done, laid down the burden, reached his own goal, utterly destroyed the fetters of existence, and is completely liberated through final knowledge—for such a bhikkhu, it is fitting to say:

'On the fourteenth, the fifteenth,
And the eighth day of the fortnight,
And on the extraordinary fortnight,
One should observe the Uposatha
Endowed with the eight factors,
A man such as I.'

Why is it fitting? Because that bhikkhu is free from lust, hate, and delusion. Bhikkhus, in the past, Sakka, Lord of the Gods, wishing to instruct the Tāvatiṃsa gods, recited this verse at that time:

'On the fourteenth, the fifteenth,
And the eighth day of the fortnight,
And on the extraordinary fortnight,
One should observe the Uposatha
Endowed with the eight factors,
A man such as I.'

Bhikkhus, that verse was poorly sung by Sakka, Lord of the Gods, not well sung; poorly spoken, not well spoken. Why is that? Because Sakka, Lord of the Gods, is not yet free from birth, aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair; he is not free from suffering, I say.

Bhikkhus, for a bhikkhu who is an Arahant... [as above]... and is completely liberated through final knowledge—for such a bhikkhu, it is fitting to say:

'On the fourteenth, the fifteenth,
And the eighth day of the fortnight,
And on the extraordinary fortnight,
One should observe the Uposatha
Endowed with the eight factors,
A man such as I.'

Why is it fitting? Because that bhikkhu is free from birth, aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair; he is free from suffering, I say.

The Eighth Discourse.

## 9. Sukhumāla Sutta

39. "Bhikkhus, I was delicate, extremely delicate, exceedingly delicate. In my father's residence, lotus ponds were made for me: in one pond blue lotuses, in another red lotuses, in another white lotuses were planted solely for my sake. Bhikkhus, I did not use sandalwood that was not from Kāsi. Bhikkhus, my turban was made of Kāsi cloth, my jacket was of Kāsi cloth, my lower garment was of Kāsi cloth, and my upper garment was of Kāsi cloth."
144:
Monks, a white umbrella was held over me day and night [with the thought]: 'Let not cold, heat, grass, dust, or dew touch him.'

Monks, I had three palaces: one for the winter, one for the summer, and one for the rainy season. Monks, in the rainy season palace, for the four months of the rains, I was entertained by musicians who were solely women, and I did not descend from the palace. Monks, just as in other people's homes, servants, workers, and laborers are given broken rice with sour gruel as their food, even so, in my father's palace, servants, workers, and laborers were given choice rice with meat.

Monks, to me, who was endowed with such fortune and such extreme delicacy, this thought occurred: 'An uninstructed worldling, though himself subject to aging and not beyond aging, when seeing another who is aged, is troubled, ashamed, and disgusted, forgetting his own condition. I too am subject to aging and not beyond aging. If I, being subject to aging and not beyond aging, were to be troubled, ashamed, and disgusted upon seeing another who is aged, that would not be fitting for me.' As I reflected thus, monks, all pride in youth (yobbana-mada) entirely vanished.

'An uninstructed worldling, though himself subject to sickness and not beyond sickness, when seeing another who is sick, is troubled, ashamed, and disgusted, forgetting his own condition. I too am subject to sickness and not beyond sickness. If I, being subject to sickness and not beyond sickness, were to be troubled, ashamed, and disgusted upon seeing another who is sick, that would not be fitting for me.' As I reflected thus, monks, all pride in health (ārogya-mada) entirely vanished.

'An uninstructed worldling, though himself subject to death and not beyond death, when seeing another who is dead, is troubled, ashamed, and disgusted, forgetting his own condition. I too am subject to death and not beyond death. If I, being subject to death and not beyond death...'
145:
...were to be troubled, ashamed, and disgusted upon seeing another who is dead, that would not be fitting for me.' As I reflected thus, monks, all pride in life (jīvita-mada) entirely vanished.

Monks, there are these three intoxications. Which three? Intoxication with youth, intoxication with health, and intoxication with life. Monks, an uninstructed worldling, intoxicated with youth, conducts himself badly in body, speech, and mind. Having conducted himself badly in body, speech, and mind, after the breakup of the body, after death, he is reborn in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, the downfall, hell. Monks, an uninstructed worldling, intoxicated with health... (as above)... Monks, an uninstructed worldling, intoxicated with life, conducts himself badly in body, speech, and mind. Having conducted himself badly in body, speech, and mind, after the breakup of the body, after death, he is reborn in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, the downfall, hell.

Monks, a monk who is intoxicated with youth gives up the training and returns to the lower life. Monks, a monk who is intoxicated with health gives up the training and returns to the lower life. Monks, a monk who is intoxicated with life gives up the training and returns to the lower life.

Subject to sickness, subject to aging,
And also subject to death,
Worldlings are disgusted [by others],
Though they themselves are of that same nature.

If I were to be disgusted
With beings of such a nature,
It would not be fitting for me,
Living as I do.

While living thus,
Knowing the state free from acquisitions,
I overcame all intoxications—
Of health, of youth, and of life.

Seeing safety in renunciation,
Zeal arose in me
As I looked toward Nibbāna.

Now I am incapable
Of indulging in sensual pleasures;
I shall be one who does not turn back,
Intent on the holy life.
146:
Ninth Sutta.
## 10. Ādhipateyya Sutta
40. "Monks, there are these three kinds of supremacy. Which three? Self-supremacy (attādhipateyya), world-supremacy (lokādhipateyya), and Dhamma-supremacy (dhammādhipateyya).

And what, monks, is self-supremacy? Here, monks, a monk who has gone to the forest, to the root of a tree, or to an empty hut, reflects thus: 'I did not go forth from the home life into homelessness for the sake of robes, almsfood, or lodgings, nor for the sake of this or that state of becoming. Rather, I am overwhelmed by birth, aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair; I am overwhelmed by suffering, beset by suffering. Perhaps an end to this entire mass of suffering might be known.' [With this thought,] he went forth from the home life into homelessness. [He then reflects:] 'If I, having abandoned such sensual pleasures to go forth from the home life into homelessness, were to seek those same sensual pleasures or even worse ones, that would not be proper for me.'

That monk reflects again: 'When I have fully exerted myself, my energy shall be aroused and unsluggish, my mindfulness shall be established and unconfused through the power of the four foundations of mindfulness, my physical and mental bodies shall be tranquil and free from distress, and my mind shall be concentrated and one-pointed upon its object.' Having made himself the governing principle, he abandons the unwholesome and develops the wholesome; he abandons the blameworthy and develops the blameless; he maintains himself in purity. This, monks, is called self-supremacy.

And what, monks, is world-supremacy? Here, monks, a monk who has gone to the forest, to the root of a tree, or to an empty hut, reflects thus: 'I did not go forth from the home life into homelessness for the sake of robes, almsfood, or lodgings, nor for the sake of this or that state of becoming. Rather, I am overwhelmed by birth, aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair; I am overwhelmed by suffering, beset by suffering. Perhaps an end to this entire mass of suffering might be known.' [With this thought,] he went forth from the home life into homelessness. [He then reflects:] 'If I, having gone forth in this way, were to think thoughts of sensuality (kāmavitakka), thoughts of ill-will (byāpādavitakka), or thoughts of cruelty (vihiṃsāvitakka)—this world-system, the abode of beings, is indeed vast. In this vast world-system, there are ascetics and brahmins who possess psychic powers, the divine eye, and knowledge of others' minds. They see from afar, they are not seen even when near, and they know the minds of others with their own minds. They would know me thus: "Look, sirs, at this clansman..."'
147:
‘This clansman, having gone forth from the home life into homelessness out of faith, lives entangled with evil, unwholesome states.’

There are deities who possess psychic powers, the divine eye, and the ability to know the minds of others. They see from afar, and though near, they are not seen; they know the minds of others with their own minds. They would know me thus: ‘Look, sirs, at this clansman who, having gone forth from the home life into homelessness out of faith, lives entangled with evil, unwholesome states.’ That bhikkhu reflects thus: ‘My energy shall be aroused and unflagging, my mindfulness shall be established and unconfused by the power of the four foundations of mindfulness, my physical and mental body shall be tranquil and untroubled, and my mind shall be well-concentrated and one-pointed.’ Having made the world his supreme authority, he abandons the unwholesome, develops the wholesome, abandons what is blameworthy, develops what is blameless, and maintains himself in purity. This, bhikkhus, is called the supremacy of the world (lokādhipateyya).

And what, bhikkhus, is the supremacy of the Dhamma (dhammādhipateyya)? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu who has gone to a forest, to the foot of a tree, or to an empty hut reflects thus: ‘I did not go forth from the home life into homelessness for the sake of robes, almsfood, or lodgings, nor for the sake of becoming this or that. Rather, I am beset by birth, aging, and death, by sorrow, lamentation, pain, dejection, and despair; I am beset by suffering, overcome by suffering. Perhaps an end to this entire mass of suffering might be known.’ The Dhamma is well-expounded by the Blessed One, directly visible, immediate, inviting one to come and see, applicable, to be personally experienced by the wise. There are my fellow practitioners who live knowing and seeing. If I, having gone forth in such a well-expounded Dhamma and Vinaya, were to live lazy and negligent, it would not be proper for me. That bhikkhu reflects thus: ‘My energy shall be aroused and unflagging, my mindfulness shall be established and unconfused by the power of the four foundations of mindfulness, my mind shall be well-concentrated, my physical and mental body shall be tranquil and untroubled, and my mind shall be well-concentrated and one-pointed.’ Having made the Dhamma his supreme authority, he abandons the unwholesome, develops the wholesome, abandons what is blameworthy, develops what is blameless, and maintains himself in purity. This, bhikkhus, is called the supremacy of the Dhamma. These, bhikkhus, are the three types of supremacy.

O man, there is no secret place in the world for one who does evil.
148:
Whether it be true or false, you know the deed you have done. Indeed, sirs, you disregard your own self, which is a witness to the good, when you hide the evil that exists within yourself. Deities and the Tathāgatas see the fool who lives dishonestly in the world. Therefore, the bhikkhu who makes himself his supreme authority, and the wise one who makes the world his supreme authority, being a meditator who burns away defilements, and the bhikkhu who makes the Dhamma his supreme authority, practicing in accordance with the Dhamma, a sage of true striving, does not decline. Having conquered Māra the defiler, having overcome the Ender (Death), that one who has reached the destruction of birth through striving, such a one is a knower of the world, a man of great wisdom, a sage unattached to all things, endowed with wisdom; such an Arahant never declines.

The tenth sutta is finished.
The fourth, Devadūta Vagga, is finished.

## 1-Sammukhībhāva Sutta

41. Bhikkhus, through the presence of three things, a faithful clansman generates much merit. What three? Bhikkhus, through the presence of faith, a faithful clansman generates much merit. Bhikkhus, through the presence of a gift (deyyadhamma), a faithful clansman generates much merit. Bhikkhus, through the presence of those worthy of offerings (dakkhiṇeyyāna), a faithful clansman generates much merit. Bhikkhus, through the presence of these three things, a faithful clansman generates much merit.
149:
The First Sutta.

## 2. Tiṭṭhāna Sutta
42. "Monks, a person who is devoted should be known as one endowed with faith through three grounds. What three? He desires to see those possessed of virtue; he desires to hear the true Dhamma; and he dwells at home with a mind free from the stain of stinginess, open-handed, delighting in relinquishment, devoted to charity, and delighting in the distribution of gifts. Monks, through these three grounds, a person who is devoted should be known as one endowed with faith."

"Desiring to see the virtuous, 
He wishes to hear the true Dhamma, 
And removes the stain of stinginess in the discipline—
He is indeed called one endowed with faith."

The Second Sutta.

## 3. Atthavasa Sutta
43. "Monks, seeing three reasons, it is indeed proper to teach the Dhamma to others. What three? The one who teaches the Dhamma understands the meaning and understands the text. The one who hears the Dhamma understands the meaning and understands the text. Both the one who teaches the Dhamma and the one who hears it understand the meaning and understand the text. Monks, seeing these three reasons, it is indeed proper to teach the Dhamma to others."

The Third Sutta.

## 4. Kathāpavattī Sutta
44. "Monks, the occurrence of talk is due to three grounds. What three? The one who teaches the Dhamma understands the meaning and understands the text. The one who hears the Dhamma understands the meaning and understands the text. Both the one who teaches the Dhamma and the one who hears it understand the meaning and understand the text. Monks, these are the three grounds for the occurrence of talk."

The Fourth Sutta.

## 5. Paṇḍita Sutta
45. "Monks, these three things are prescribed by the wise and the good. What three? Monks, giving (dāna) is prescribed by the wise and the good. Monks, going forth (pabbajjā) is prescribed by the wise and the good."
150:
Monks, serving one's parents is prescribed by the wise and the good. Monks, these are the three things prescribed by the wise and the good."

"Giving, non-violence, 
Restraint, and self-control are prescribed by the good; 
As is serving one's parents, 
By the peaceful who lead the holy life."

"These are the grounds of the good, 
Which the wise should cultivate; 
That noble one, endowed with vision, 
Reaches the peaceful heavenly world."

The Fifth Sutta.

## 6. Sīlavanta Sutta
46. "Monks, when virtuous monks live in dependence on a village or town, the people there generate much merit through three grounds. What three? Through the body, through speech, and through the mind. Monks, when virtuous monks live in dependence on a village or town, the people there generate much merit through these three grounds."

The Sixth Sutta.

## 7. Saṅkhatalakkhaṇa Sutta
47. "Monks, there are these three conditioned characteristics of the conditioned.1 What three? Arising (uppāda) is evident; vanishing (vaya) is evident; and alteration of what is present (ṭhitassa aññathatta) is evident. Monks, these are the three conditioned characteristics of the conditioned."

The Seventh Sutta.

1. Saṅkhata: that which is produced by a combination of causes.
2. Lakkhaṇa: the signs or marks by which one knows a thing is conditioned.

## 8. Asaṅkhatalakkhaṇa Sutta
48. "Monks, there are these three unconditioned characteristics of the unconditioned. What three? No arising is evident; no vanishing is evident; and no alteration of what is present is evident. Monks, these are the three unconditioned characteristics of the unconditioned."

The Eighth Sutta.

## 9. Pabbatarāja Sutta
49. "Monks, in dependence on Himavanta, the king of mountains, the great trees grow in three ways. What three? They grow in branches, leaves, and foliage; they grow in bark and shoots; they grow in softwood and heartwood."
151:
Monks, depending on Himavant, the king of mountains, the great trees grow with three types of growth. Monks, in the same way, depending on a faithful head of the family, the members of the household grow with three types of growth. What are the three? They grow in faith (saddhā), they grow in virtue (sīla), and they grow in wisdom (paññā). Monks, depending on a faithful head of the family, the members of the household grow with these three types of growth.

Just as the rocky mountain stands in the vast forest,
And depending on it, the trees, the lords of the forest, grow;

Even so, in this world, depending on a faithful head of the family
Who is accomplished in virtue, the wife and children,
Friends, companions, and relatives,
And those who depend on him for their livelihood, all grow.

Seeing the virtue, the generosity, and the good conduct
Of that virtuous one, those who are wise and see their own benefit
Follow his example.

Having practiced the Dhamma in this world,
The path leading to a happy destination,
They rejoice in the deva world, enjoying the pleasures they desire.

The Ninth Sutta.

## 10. Ātappakaraṇီya Sutta
50. Monks, exertion (ātappa) should be made in three instances. What are the three? Exertion should be made to prevent the arising of unarisen evil, unwholesome states; exertion should be made for the arising of unarisen wholesome states; and exertion should be made to endure bodily feelings that have arisen—painful, racking, sharp, piercing, unpleasant, disagreeable, and life-threatening. Monks, exertion should be made in these three instances.

Monks, when a monk makes an exertion to prevent the arising of unarisen evil, unwholesome states; makes an exertion for the arising of unarisen wholesome states; and makes an exertion to endure bodily feelings that have arisen—painful, racking, sharp, piercing, unpleasant, disagreeable, and life-threatening—
152:
Monks, at that time, this monk is called one who is ardent, prudent, and mindful, for the sake of making a complete end of suffering.

The Tenth Sutta.

## 11. Mahācora Sutta
51. Monks, possessing three factors, a great thief breaks into houses, plunders villages, commits robbery in a single house, and waits in ambush on the highway. What are the three? Here, monks, a great thief relies on uneven ground, relies on thickets, and relies on the powerful. And how, monks, does a great thief rely on uneven ground? Here, monks, a great thief relies on a river difficult to cross or an uneven mountain. This is how a great thief relies on uneven ground.

And how, monks, does a great thief rely on thickets? Here, monks, a great thief relies on a thicket of grass, a thicket of trees, a dense grove, or a great forest. This is how a great thief relies on thickets.

And how, monks, does a great thief rely on the powerful? Here, monks, a great thief relies on kings or royal ministers. He thinks: 'If anyone says anything to me, these kings or royal ministers will defend me and speak on my behalf.' If anyone says anything to him, those kings or royal ministers defend him and speak on his behalf. This is how a great thief relies on the powerful. Monks, possessing these three factors, a great thief breaks into houses, plunders villages, commits robbery in a single house, and waits in ambush on the highway.

In the same way, monks, possessing three factors, a bad monk carries himself about as one who is uprooted and destroyed; he is blameworthy, he is censured by the wise, and he generates much demerit. What are the three? Here, monks, a bad monk relies on uneven ground, relies on thickets, and relies on the powerful.

And how, monks, does a bad monk rely on uneven ground? Here, monks, a bad monk is possessed of uneven bodily action, possessed of uneven—
153:
verbal action, and possessed of uneven mental action. This is how a bad monk relies on uneven ground.

And how, monks, does a bad monk rely on thickets? Here, monks, a bad monk has wrong view; he is possessed of extremist views (antaggāhikadiṭṭhi) such as eternalism and so forth. This is how a bad monk relies on thickets.

And how, monks, does a bad monk rely on the powerful? Here, monks, a bad monk relies on kings or royal ministers. He thinks: 'If anyone says anything to me, these kings or royal ministers will defend me and speak on my behalf.' If anyone says anything to him, those kings or royal ministers defend him and speak on behalf of that bad monk. This is how a bad monk relies on the powerful. Monks, possessing these three factors, a bad monk carries himself about as one who is uprooted and destroyed; he is blameworthy, he is censured by the wise, and he generates much demerit.

The Eleventh Sutta.

The Minor Chapter (Cūḷavagga), the Fifth.

The summary of it:
Sammukhī, Ṭhāna, Atthavasa, Pavatti, Paṇḍita, Sīlavant,
Saṅkhata, Pabbata, Ātappa, and Mahācora—these are the eleven.

The First Fifty Suttas are complete.
154:
Eleventh Sutta.
The fifth, Cūḷa Vagga, is finished.
The first fifty suttas are finished.

## (6) Brāhmaṇa Vagga
## 1. Paṭhama Dvebrāhmaṇa Sutta

52. Then two brahmins, aged, elderly, advanced in years, having reached the final stage of life, one hundred and twenty years of age, went to the Blessed One and exchanged greetings with him. When they had concluded their greetings and cordial talk, they sat down to one side and said to the Blessed One: "Master Gotama, we are brahmins, aged, elderly, advanced in years, having reached the final stage of life, one hundred and twenty years of age. Yet, we have not performed any deeds that are beautiful, any deeds that are wholesome, any deeds that provide protection against the fear of a miserable destination. Let Master Gotama exhort us, let Master Gotama instruct us in what may be for our welfare and happiness for a long time."

"Indeed, brahmins, you are aged, elderly, advanced in years, having reached the final stage of life, one hundred and twenty years of age. And you have not performed any deeds that are beautiful, any deeds that are wholesome, any deeds that provide protection against the fear of a miserable destination. Brahmins, this world is being led on by old age, sickness, and death. While the world is thus being led on by old age, sickness, and death, whatever restraint of body, restraint of speech, and restraint of mind one has here in this present life, that is the shelter, the cave, the island, the refuge, and the resort for one who has passed away."

"Life is led on, its span is short,
There are no shelters for one led on by old age.
Beholding this danger in death,
One should perform merits that bring happiness.

Whatever restraint of body, speech, and mind one has here,
And whatever merit one performs while living,
That leads to happiness for the one who has passed away."
155:
First Sutta.

## 2. Second Dvebrāhmaṇa Sutta

53. Then two brahmins, who were aged, elderly, advanced in years, having reached the final stage of life, and being one hundred and twenty years old from birth, approached the Blessed One. Having approached, they exchanged greetings with the Blessed One. After concluding the pleasant and memorable conversation, they sat at one side. Sitting at one side, those brahmins said to the Blessed One: "Master Gotama, we are aged, elderly, advanced in years, having reached the final stage of life, and are one hundred and twenty years old from birth. Yet, we have not performed any meritorious deeds that serve as a protection against the danger of an unhappy destination. May Master Gotama instruct us; may Master Gotama exhort us in a way that will lead to our welfare and happiness for a long time."

"Indeed, brahmins, you are aged, elderly, advanced in years, having reached the final stage of life, and are one hundred and twenty years old from birth. And indeed, you have not performed any meritorious deeds that serve as a protection against the danger of an unhappy destination. Brahmins, this world is ablaze with aging, sickness, and death. Brahmins, when the world is thus ablaze with aging, sickness, and death, whatever restraint of body, restraint of speech, and restraint of mind one practices here, that serves as a protection, a shelter, an island, a refuge, and a resort for one who has passed away."

"When a house is ablaze, the vessel that is taken out is the one that becomes useful, not the one that is burnt therein.

In the same way, the world is ablaze with aging and death; one should take out [one's wealth] by giving. What is given is well taken out.

Whatever restraint of body, speech, or mind one practices here, and whatever merit one performs while alive, that leads to the happiness of the one who has passed away."

Second Sutta.

## 3. Aññatara Brāhmaṇa Sutta

54. Then a certain brahmin approached the Blessed One. Having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Blessed One... (Pe) ... Sitting at one side, he...
156:
Sitting to one side, he said to the Blessed One: "Venerable Gotama, it is said, 'The Dhamma is visible here and now, the Dhamma is visible here and now.' In what way, Venerable Gotama, is the Dhamma visible here and now, immediate, inviting one to come and see, worthy of application, and to be personally realized by the wise?"

"Brahmin, a person who is lustful, overcome by lust, with a mind obsessed by it, intends for his own affliction, intends for the affliction of others, and intends for the affliction of both. He experiences mental suffering and grief. When lust is abandoned, he does not intend for his own affliction, nor for the affliction of others, nor for the affliction of both. He does not experience mental suffering and grief. (Brahmin, a person who is lustful... [Pe]... commits misconduct by body, speech, and mind. When lust is abandoned, he does not commit misconduct by body, speech, or mind. Brahmin, a person who is lustful... [Pe]... does not understand as it really is his own good, the good of others, or the good of both. When lust is abandoned, he understands as it really is his own good, the good of others, and the good of both.) Brahmin, in this way the Dhamma is visible here and now... [Pe]... (The passages within these parentheses are not found in the Sinhalese, Siamese, Cambodian, or PTS editions.)"

"Brahmin, a person who is corrupted by hatred, overcome by hatred, with a mind obsessed by it, intends for his own affliction, for the affliction of others, and for the affliction of both. He experiences mental suffering and grief. When hatred is abandoned, he does not intend for his own affliction, nor for the affliction of others, nor for the affliction of both. He does not experience mental suffering and grief. Brahmin, in this way the Dhamma is visible here and now... [Pe]..."

"Brahmin, a person who is deluded by ignorance, overcome by ignorance, with a mind obsessed by it, intends for his own affliction, for the affliction of others, and for the affliction of both. He experiences mental suffering and grief. When ignorance is abandoned, he does not intend for his own affliction, nor for the affliction of others, nor for the affliction of both. He does not experience mental suffering and grief. Brahmin, in this way the Dhamma is visible here and now, immediate, inviting one to come and see, worthy of application,"
157:
"...and to be personally realized by the wise."

"Excellent, Venerable Gotama! Excellent, Venerable Gotama! Just as one might set upright what had been overturned, or reveal what was hidden, or show the way to one who is lost, or hold up a lamp in the darkness so that those with eyes might see forms, even so has the Dhamma been made clear in many ways by the Venerable Gotama. I go to the Venerable Gotama for refuge, to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha of monks. May the Venerable Gotama accept me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge from this day forward for as long as life lasts."

The Third Sutta.

## 4. Paribbājaka Sutta

55. Then a certain Brahmin wanderer approached the Blessed One. [Pe]... Sitting to one side, that Brahmin wanderer said to the Blessed One: "Venerable Gotama, it is said, 'The Dhamma is visible here and now, the Dhamma is visible here and now.' In what way, Venerable Gotama, is the Dhamma visible here and now, immediate, inviting one to come and see, worthy of application, and to be personally realized by the wise?"

"Brahmin, a person who is lustful, overcome by lust, with a mind obsessed by it, intends for his own affliction, for the affliction of others, and for the affliction of both. He experiences mental suffering and grief. When lust is abandoned, he does not intend for his own affliction, nor for the affliction of others, nor for the affliction of both. He does not experience mental suffering and grief. Brahmin, a person who is lustful... [Pe]... commits misconduct by body, speech, and mind. When lust is abandoned, he does not commit misconduct by body, speech, or mind. Brahmin, a person who is lustful... [Pe]... does not understand as it really is his own good, the good of others, or the good of both. When lust is abandoned, he understands as it really is his own good, the good of others, and the good of both."
158:
Brahmin, in this way the Dhamma is visible here and now... [pe]...

Brahmin, one who is corrupted by hatred... [pe]... Brahmin, one who is deluded by delusion, overcome and with mind obsessed by delusion, intends for his own affliction, intends for the affliction of others, intends for the affliction of both, and experiences mental suffering and grief. When delusion is abandoned, he does not intend for his own affliction, nor for the affliction of others, nor for the affliction of both, and he does not experience mental suffering and grief.

Brahmin, one who is deluded by delusion, overcome and with mind obsessed by delusion, engages in misconduct by body, engages in misconduct by speech, and engages in misconduct by mind. When delusion is abandoned, he does not engage in misconduct by body, nor by speech, nor by mind.

Brahmin, one who is deluded by delusion, overcome and with mind obsessed by delusion, does not understand his own welfare as it really is, does not understand the welfare of others as it really is, and does not understand the welfare of both as it really is. When delusion is abandoned, he understands his own welfare as it really is, he understands the welfare of others as it really is, and he understands the welfare of both as it really is. Brahmin, in this way the Dhamma is visible here and now, timeless, inviting one to come and see, worthy of being applied, to be personally realized by the wise.

'Excellent, Master Gotama! ... [pe] ... May Master Gotama accept me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge from this day forward for as long as life lasts.'

The Fourth Sutta.

## 5. Nibbuta Sutta

56. Then the Brahmin Jāṇussoṇi approached the Blessed One. Having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Blessed One and sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, the Brahmin Jāṇussoṇi said to the Blessed One: 'Master Gotama, it is said "Nirvana is visible here and now, Nirvana is visible here and now." In what way, Master Gotama, is Nirvana visible here and now, timeless, inviting one to come and see, worthy of being applied, to be personally realized by the wise?'
159:
Brahmin, one who is lustful with lust, overcome and with mind obsessed by lust, intends for his own affliction, intends for the affliction of others, intends for the affliction of both, and experiences mental suffering and grief. When lust is abandoned, he does not intend for his own affliction, nor for the affliction of others, nor for the affliction of both, and he does not experience mental suffering and grief. Brahmin, in this way Nirvana is visible here and now.

Brahmin, one who is corrupted by hatred... [pe]... Brahmin, one who is deluded by delusion, overcome and with mind obsessed by delusion, intends for his own affliction, intends for the affliction of others, intends for the affliction of both, and experiences mental suffering and grief. When delusion is abandoned, he does not intend for his own affliction, nor for the affliction of others, nor for the affliction of both, and he does not experience mental suffering and grief. Brahmin, in this way too Nirvana is visible here and now. Brahmin, when one experiences the destruction of lust without remainder, the destruction of hatred without remainder, and the destruction of delusion without remainder; in this way, Brahmin, Nirvana is visible here and now, timeless, inviting one to come and see, worthy of being applied, to be personally realized by the wise.

'Excellent, Master Gotama! ... [pe] ... May Master Gotama accept me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge from this day forward for as long as life lasts.'

The Fifth Sutta.

## 6. Paloka Sutta

57. Then a certain wealthy Brahmin approached the Blessed One... [pe]... Sitting to one side, that wealthy Brahmin said to the Blessed One: 'Master Gotama, I have heard this from the ancient Brahmins, the aged and elderly, the teachers and teachers of teachers: "In the past, this world was as if crowded with people like the Avīci hell, and villages, market towns, and royal capitals were as close as a cock's flight." Why is it, Master Gotama, what is the cause, what is the reason, that now humans are being depleted, their numbers are thinning, villages are no longer villages, market towns are no longer market towns, cities are no longer cities, and districts are no longer districts?'
160:
“Brahmin, at present, people are infatuated with unrighteous passion (adhamma-rāga), overcome by excessive greed (visama-lobha), and obsessed with wrong Dhamma (micchā-dhamma). Being infatuated with unrighteous passion, overcome by excessive greed, and obsessed with wrong Dhamma, they take up sharp weapons and take each other's lives. Because of that, many people die. This, Brahmin, is a cause, this is a reason why at present there is a depletion of humans, their scarcity is apparent, and villages are no longer villages, market towns are no longer market towns, cities are no longer cities, and districts are no longer districts.

“Furthermore, Brahmin, at present, people are infatuated with unrighteous passion, overcome by excessive greed, and obsessed with wrong Dhamma. For those people who are infatuated with unrighteous passion, overcome by excessive greed, and obsessed with wrong Dhamma, the sky does not rain properly. Because of that, there is famine, poor crops, blight, and only stalks remain. Because of that, many people die. This, Brahmin, is a cause, this is a reason why at present there is a depletion of humans, their scarcity is apparent, and villages are no longer villages, market towns are no longer market towns, cities are no longer cities, and districts are no longer districts.

“Furthermore, Brahmin, at present, people are infatuated with unrighteous passion, overcome by excessive greed, and obsessed with wrong Dhamma. For those people who are infatuated with unrighteous passion, overcome by excessive greed, and obsessed with wrong Dhamma, the chief yakkhas unleash fierce non-human beings. Because of that, many people die. This, Brahmin, is a cause, this is a reason why at present there is a depletion of humans, their scarcity is apparent, and villages are no longer villages, market towns are no longer market towns, cities are no longer cities, and districts are no longer districts.”

“Excellent, Master Gotama! ... May Master Gotama accept me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge from this day forward for as long as life lasts.” Sixth Sutta.
161:
Sixth Sutta.
## 7. Vacchagotta Sutta
58. Then the wanderer Vacchagotta approached the Blessed One and exchanged greetings with him. After exchanging pleasant and memorable words, he sat down to one side. Sitting there, the wanderer Vacchagotta said to the Blessed One: “Master Gotama, I have heard it said: ‘The ascetic Gotama says: "Gifts should be given only to me, not to others. Gifts should be given only to my disciples, not to the disciples of others. Only a gift given to me is of great fruit, not a gift given to others. Only a gift given to my disciples is of great fruit, not a gift given to the disciples of others."' Now, Master Gotama, do those who say this speak what has been said by Master Gotama, and not misrepresent Master Gotama with what is false? Do they explain in accordance with the Dhamma, so that no legitimate ground for censure arises? For we do not wish to misrepresent Master Gotama.”

“Vaccha, those who say: ‘The ascetic Gotama says: "Gifts should be given only to me... [as above] ... not to the disciples of others"’ do not speak what I have said. They misrepresent me with what is untrue and false. Vaccha, whoever prevents another from giving a gift creates an obstacle for three people, a danger for three people. Which three? He creates an obstacle to the merit of the donor; he creates an obstacle to the gain of the recipients; and he has already uprooted and harmed himself. Vaccha, whoever prevents another from giving a gift creates an obstacle for these three, a danger for these three.

“Vaccha, I say this: even if one throws away the rinsings of a pot or a bowl into a cesspool or a drain where there are living beings, saying, ‘May the living beings here be sustained by this’—Vaccha, I say that even that is a source of merit,”
162:
What need is there to speak of giving to a human being? Indeed, I say that giving to one who is virtuous is of great fruit, but I do not say so of giving to one who is immoral. And that virtuous person must be one who has abandoned five factors and is possessed of five factors.

Which five factors must be abandoned? He must be one who has abandoned sensual desire (kāmacchanda), abandoned ill will (byāpāda), abandoned sloth and torpor (thina-middha), abandoned restlessness and remorse (uddhacca-kukkucca), and abandoned doubt (vicikiccā). These five factors must be abandoned.

With which five factors must he be possessed? He must be one who is possessed of the aggregate of virtue of one beyond training (asekha-sīlakkhandha), possessed of the aggregate of concentration of one beyond training (asekha-samādhikkhandha), possessed of the aggregate of wisdom of one beyond training (asekha-paññākkhandha), possessed of the aggregate of liberation of one beyond training (asekha-vimuttikkhandha), and possessed of the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation of one beyond training (asekha-vimuttiñāṇadassanakkhandha). He must be possessed of these five factors. I say that a gift given to such a person who has abandoned these five factors and is possessed of these five factors is of great fruit.

Among cows—whether black, white, red, tawny, spotted, or pigeon-colored—whichever bull is born among them that is tamed, a burden-bearer, possessed of strength, and moves with a good and swift pace; they yoke that very bull to the load, and they do not examine its color.

Even so, among humans, in whatever birth one is born—whether among the khattiyas, brahmins, vessas, suddas, caṇḍālas, or pukkusas—whichever person among them is tamed, of good conduct, established in Dhamma, possessed of virtue, a speaker of truth, and conscientious; who has abandoned birth and death, has fulfilled the holy life in its entirety, has laid down the burden, is detached, has done what was to be done, is taintless (anāsava), has reached the far shore of all dhammas, and is extinguished (nibbuta) without clinging to any object (through craving or views); the gift given to that Arahant, who is like a stainless and fertile field, is of great fruit.
163:
Fools, who are ignorant, unwise, and lacking in learning, give gifts outside [the dispensation]; they do not attend upon the peaceful ones. But those who attend upon the peaceful ones, the wise who are esteemed as sages, their faith in the Sugata is rooted and established. Those wise ones go to the heavenly world or are born here in a noble family; and gradually, they reach Nibbāna.

Seventh Sutta.

## 8. Tikaṇṇa Sutta

59. Then the brahmin Tikaṇṇa approached the Blessed One. Having approached, he [exchanged greetings] with the Blessed One... and while sitting to one side, the brahmin Tikaṇṇa spoke in praise of the 'tevijja' (three-knowledge) brahmins in the presence of the Blessed One: "In this way, the tevijja brahmins are [wise]; for this reason, the tevijja brahmins are [wise]."

"But brahmin, how do the brahmins describe a brahmin as one who possesses the three knowledges (tevijja)?"

"Master Gotama, here a brahmin is well-born on both the mother's and the father's side, of pure descent as far back as the seventh paternal generation, unrejected and unreproached in terms of birth; he is a reciter and a master of the mantras, a master of the three Vedas with their glossaries (nighaṇḍu), rituals (keṭubha), phonology (akkharappabheda), and history (itihāsa) as the fifth; he is an expert in word-analysis (padaka) and grammar (veyyākaraṇa), and is fully proficient in the Lokāyata and the marks of a Great Man. It is in this way, Master Gotama, that the brahmins describe a brahmin as one who possesses the three knowledges."

"Brahmin, the way the brahmins describe a brahmin as one who possesses the three knowledges is one thing, but the one who possesses the three knowledges in the Noble One's Discipline is quite another."

"But Master Gotama, how is one a possessor of the three knowledges in the Noble One's Discipline? It would be good if Master Gotama would teach me the Dhamma in such a way that one becomes a possessor of the three knowledges in the Noble One's Discipline."

"Then listen, brahmin, and pay close attention; I will speak."

"Yes, sir," the brahmin Tikaṇṇa replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this:

"Here, brahmin, a bhikkhu, secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by thought (vitakka) and examination (vicāra), with rapture (pīti) and happiness (sukha) born of seclusion. With the stilling of thought and examination, he enters and dwells in the second jhāna, which has internal confidence and unification of mind, is without thought and examination, and has rapture and happiness born of concentration. Because of the fading away of rapture, he dwells equanimous, mindful and clearly comprehending..."
164:
He experiences happiness with the body. Because of that (third jhāna), the Noble Ones declare: ‘He is equanimous, mindful, and dwells in happiness.’ He enters and dwells in the third jhāna. With the abandoning of pleasure and pain, and with the previous disappearance of joy and grief, he enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna, which has neither-pain-nor-pleasure and has purity of mindfulness due to equanimity.

When the mind is thus concentrated, purified, bright, unblemished, rid of defilements, pliant, malleable, steady, and attained to imperturbability, he directs his mind to the knowledge of recollecting past lives (pubbenivāsanussatiñāṇa). He recollects his manifold past lives, that is, one birth, two births, three births, four births, five births, ten births, twenty births, thirty births, forty births, fifty births, a hundred births, a thousand births, a hundred thousand births, many aeons of world-contraction, many aeons of world-expansion, many aeons of world-contraction and expansion, thus: ‘In such a place I had such a name, such a clan, such an appearance, such food, such experience of pleasure and pain, and such a lifespan. Passing away from there, I reappeared in such a place. There too I had such a name, such a clan, such an appearance, such food, such experience of pleasure and pain, and such a lifespan. Passing away from there, I reappeared here.’ Thus he recollects his manifold past lives with their aspects and particulars. This is the first true knowledge (vijjā) attained by him. Ignorance is dispelled, true knowledge has arisen; darkness is dispelled, light has arisen, as happens in one who dwells heedful, ardent, and resolute.

When the mind is thus concentrated, purified, bright, unblemished, rid of defilements, pliant, malleable, steady, and attained to imperturbability, he directs his mind to the knowledge of the passing away and reappearance of beings (cutūpapātañāṇa). With the divine eye (dibbacakkhu), purified and surpassing the human, he sees beings passing away and reappearing—inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate. He understands how beings fare according to their kamma: ‘These worthy beings, indeed, were possessed of misconduct by body, misconduct by speech, and misconduct by mind; they were revilers of the Noble Ones, held wrong views, and undertook actions based on wrong views. With the breakup of the body, after death, they have reappeared in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a state of ruin, even in hell. But these worthy beings were possessed of good conduct by body, good conduct by speech, and good conduct by mind; they were not revilers of the Noble Ones...
165:
...they held right views and undertook actions based on right views. With the breakup of the body, after death, they have reappeared in a good destination, in a heavenly world.’ Thus, with the divine eye, purified and surpassing the human, he sees beings passing away and reappearing—inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate. He understands how beings fare according to their kamma. This is the second true knowledge attained by him. Ignorance is dispelled, true knowledge has arisen; darkness is dispelled, light has arisen, as happens in one who dwells heedful, ardent, and resolute.

When the mind is thus concentrated, purified, bright, unblemished, rid of defilements, pliant, malleable, steady, and attained to imperturbability, he directs his mind to the knowledge of the destruction of the taints (āsavakkhayañāṇa).
