He understands as it really is: ‘This is suffering’; he understands as it really is: ‘This is the origin of suffering’; he understands as it really is: ‘This is the cessation of suffering’; he understands as it really is: ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering.’ He understands as it really is: ‘These are the taints’; he understands as it really is: ‘This is the origin of the taints’; he understands as it really is: ‘This is the cessation of the taints’; he understands as it really is: ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of the taints.’ When he knows and sees thus, his mind is liberated from the taint of sensual desire, from the taint of being, and from the taint of ignorance. When it is liberated, the knowledge arises: ‘It is liberated.’ He understands: ‘Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more for this state of being.’ This is the third true knowledge attained by him. Ignorance is dispelled, true knowledge has arisen; darkness is dispelled, light has arisen, as happens in one who dwells heedful, ardent, and resolute.

For one whose virtue is consistent, who is prudent and a meditator, whose mind is mastered, one-pointed, and well-concentrated.

They call him a sage, a dispeller of darkness, one with the threefold knowledge, who has abandoned death, who is beneficial to gods and humans, who has abandoned everything.

They pay homage to that Gotama, the Buddha, who is possessed of the threefold knowledge, who dwells undeluded, who bears his final body. He who knows his past lives, and sees heaven and the states of deprivation...
166:
“Furthermore, he reaches the end of birth (the fruit of Arahantship); having known through higher knowledge, he reaches the end; he is a sage possessed of the practice of a silent one (moneyya). By these three knowledges, he is a Brahmin of the threefold knowledge. I call only him one who is accomplished in the threefold knowledge, not another who merely repeats what others say.”

“Brahmin, thus is one accomplished in the threefold knowledge in the discipline of the Noble One.”

“Master Gotama, the threefold knowledge of the Brahmins is one thing, and the threefold knowledge in the discipline of the Noble One is quite another. Master Gotama, the threefold knowledge of the Brahmins is not worth even a sixteenth part of this threefold knowledge in the discipline of the Noble One. Excellent, Master Gotama! [...] May Master Gotama accept me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge from this day forward for as long as life lasts.”

The Eighth Sutta.

1. Ancient historical epics and legends such as the Mahabharata.
2. Texts that extract and analyze the roots of Vedic words.
3. Texts that show the formation of words through roots, suffixes, and inflections.
4. Materialist philosophy that shows only the visible world, such as the materialism of the Carvaka teachers.

## 9. Jāṇussoṇi Sutta

60. Then Jāṇussoṇi the Brahmin approached the Blessed One. Having approached, he [exchanged greetings] with the Blessed One... and while sitting at one side, Jāṇussoṇi the Brahmin said to the Blessed One: “Master Gotama, if a person has a sacrifice to offer, or a meal for the dead (saddha), or a dish of milk-rice (thālipāka), or a gift to give, he should give that gift to Brahmins who possess the threefold knowledge.”

“But Brahmin, how do the Brahmins describe a Brahmin who possesses the threefold knowledge?”

“Master Gotama, here a Brahmin is well-born on both sides, of pure descent from both the mother’s and the father’s side, purified as far back as the seventh paternal generation, unassailable and irreproachable in terms of birth; he is a repeater and master of the hymns, a master of the three Vedas with their vocabularies (Nighaṇḍu), rituals (Keṭubha), phonology (Akkhara-pabbheda), and the epics as the fifth (Itihāsa); he is a philologist and a grammarian, and is fully proficient in cosmology (Lokāyata) and the marks of a Great Man (Mahāpurisa-lakkhaṇa). Master Gotama, it is in this way that the Brahmins describe a Brahmin who possesses the threefold knowledge.”

“Brahmin, the way the Brahmins describe a Brahmin with the threefold knowledge is one thing, but the threefold knowledge in the discipline of the Noble One is quite another.”

“How then, Master Gotama, is there threefold knowledge in the discipline of the Noble One? Please, Master Gotama, teach me the Dhamma in such a way that there is threefold knowledge in the discipline of the Noble One.”

“In that case, Brahmin, listen and pay close attention; I will speak.” “Yes, sir,” Jāṇussoṇi the Brahmin replied to the Blessed One.
167:
The Blessed One said this: “Brahmin, here in this teaching, a bhikkhu, secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states... enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna. With a mind thus concentrated, purified, bright, unblemished, rid of defilements, malleable, wieldy, steady, and attained to imperturbability, he directs his mind to the knowledge of recollecting past lives (pubbenivāsānussati-ñāṇa). He recollects his manifold past lives, that is, one birth, two births... thus he recollects his manifold past lives with their aspects and details. This is the first knowledge he attains. Ignorance is dispelled, knowledge has arisen; darkness is dispelled, light has arisen, as happens in one who dwells diligent, ardent, and resolute.

With a mind thus concentrated, purified, bright, unblemished, rid of defilements, malleable, wieldy, steady, and attained to imperturbability, he directs his mind to the knowledge of the passing away and rebirth of beings (cutūpapāta-ñāṇa). With the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans... he understands how beings fare according to their karma. This is the second knowledge he attains. Ignorance is dispelled, knowledge has arisen; darkness is dispelled, light has arisen, as happens in one who dwells diligent, ardent, and resolute.

With a mind thus concentrated, purified, bright, unblemished, rid of defilements, malleable, wieldy, steady, and attained to imperturbability, he directs his mind to the knowledge of the destruction of the taints (āsavakkhaya-ñāṇa). He understands as it really is: ‘This is suffering’... ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering’; he understands as it really is: ‘These are the taints’... ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of the taints.’ When he knows and sees thus, his mind is liberated from the taint of sensual desire, from the taint of existence, and from the taint of ignorance. When it is liberated, there comes the knowledge: ‘It is liberated.’ He understands: ‘Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more for this state of being.’ This is the third knowledge he attains. Ignorance is dispelled, knowledge has arisen; darkness is dispelled, light has arisen, as happens in one who dwells diligent, ardent, and resolute.”
168:
[Ignorance] darkness vanished and [knowledge] light arose, [he said].

He who is perfect in virtue and conduct, with a mind directed [towards Nibbāna] and concentrated, whose mind is mastered, one-pointed, and well-composed. He who knows his former lives, sees heaven and the states of woe, and has reached the destruction of birth (the fruit of Arahantship), a sage who has reached the end through higher knowledge. By these three knowledges, he is a 'Threefold-Knowledge' Brahmin; him alone I call a 'Threefold-Knowledge' one, not another who merely repeats what others say.

Brahmin, thus is one a 'Threefold-Knowledge' one in the Noble One's Discipline. [The Brahmin replied:] "Master Gotama, the 'Threefold-Knowledge' of the Brahmins is one thing, and the 'Threefold-Knowledge' in the Noble One's Discipline is another. Master Gotama, the 'Threefold-Knowledge' of the Brahmins does not even equal a sixteenth part of this 'Threefold-Knowledge' in the Noble One's Discipline. Excellent, Master Gotama! ... May Master Gotama accept me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge from this day forth as long as life lasts."

Ninth Sutta.

1. Kubbhī rice refers to rice offered for the deceased.
2. Thālipāka is described in Sanskrit dictionaries as a special rice cooked with milk.

## 10. Saṅgārava Sutta

61. Then the Brahmin Saṅgārava approached the Blessed One and exchanged greetings with him. Having concluded the friendly and memorable conversation, he sat to one side. Sitting there, the Brahmin Saṅgārava said to the Blessed One: "Master Gotama, we are Brahmins. We perform sacrifices and make others perform them. Master Gotama, in that sacrifice, both the one who performs it and the one who makes others perform it are practicing a path of merit for many people, because of that sacrifice. But Master Gotama, whoever has gone forth from home to homelessness from this or that family, tames himself alone, calms himself alone, and extinguishes [the fires of defilements] in himself alone; thus, this person is practicing a path of merit for only one person, because of that going forth."

Brahmin, in that case, I will question you in return. Answer as you see fit. What do you think, Brahmin? Here, a Tathāgata...
169:
...arises in the world, an Arahant, a Perfectly Enlightened One, perfect in knowledge and conduct, well-gone, knower of the worlds, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One. He says: 'Come, this is the path, this is the way. Having personally realized through higher knowledge the unsurpassed holy life, I make it known. Come, you too practice in such a way that you too will personally realize through higher knowledge the unsurpassed holy life and dwell having attained it.' Thus the Teacher himself teaches the Dhamma, and others practice for that goal; and those who practice are many hundreds, many thousands, many hundreds of thousands.

Brahmin, what do you think of what I have just said? This being so, is this practice of going forth a practice for one or a practice for many? Master Gotama, this being so, this practice of going forth is a practice for many.

When this was said, the Venerable Ānanda said to the Brahmin Saṅgārava: "Brahmin, of these two practices, which do you prefer? Which involves less work, less effort, but has greater fruit and greater benefit?" When this was said, the Brahmin Saṅgārava said to the Venerable Ānanda: "Master Gotama and Master Ānanda are those I worship and praise."

For a second time, the Venerable Ānanda said to the Brahmin Saṅgārava: "Brahmin, I am not asking you who you worship or who you praise. I am asking you this: Brahmin, of these two practices, which do you prefer? Which involves less work, less effort, but has greater fruit and greater benefit?" For a second time, the Brahmin Saṅgārava said to the Venerable Ānanda: "Master Gotama and Master Ānanda are those I worship and praise."

For a third time, the Venerable Ānanda said to the Brahmin Saṅgārava: "Brahmin, I am not asking you who you worship...
170:
“Brahmin, I did not ask you, ‘Whom do you praise?’ I only asked you, ‘Brahmin, of these two practices, which do you prefer? Which has fewer duties? Which involves less effort? Which has greater fruit? Which has greater benefit?’” Even for the third time, Saṅgārava the Brahmin said to the Venerable Ānanda, “I revere and praise persons like the Venerable Gotama and the Venerable Ānanda.”

Then the Blessed One thought: “Even for the third time, Saṅgārava the Brahmin, though asked a righteous question by Ānanda, evades it and does not answer. Let me release them both from this difficulty.” Then the Blessed One said to Saṅgārava the Brahmin: “Brahmin, what was the topic of conversation that arose today among the royal officers assembled and gathered in the palace?”

“Venerable Gotama, today this conversation arose among the royal officers assembled and gathered in the palace: ‘In the past, there were fewer monks, yet more of them displayed miracles of psychic power surpassing human states. Now, there are more monks, yet fewer of them display miracles of psychic power surpassing human states.’ This was the conversation, Venerable Gotama, that arose today among the royal officers assembled and gathered in the palace.”

“Brahmin, there are these three kinds of miracles. What three? The miracle of psychic power (iddhipāṭihāriya), the miracle of telepathy (ādesanāpāṭihāriya), and the miracle of instruction (anusāsanīpāṭihāriya).

“And what, Brahmin, is the miracle of psychic power? Here, Brahmin, someone experiences various kinds of psychic power: having been one, he becomes many; having been many, he becomes one; he appears and disappears; he goes unhindered through a wall, through an enclosure, through a mountain as if through space; he dives in and out of the earth as if in water; he walks on water without sinking as if on earth; he travels through the sky cross-legged like a winged bird; he touches and strokes with his hand these sun and moon, so mighty and powerful; he exercises mastery with his body even as far as the Brahma world. This, Brahmin, is called the miracle of psychic power.

“And what, Brahmin, is the miracle of telepathy? Here, Brahmin, someone predicts by means of a sign: ‘Such is your mind, such is your thought, such is your state of mind.’ Even if he predicts much, it is exactly so and not otherwise.”
171:
“Even if he predicts much, it is exactly so and not otherwise. Furthermore, Brahmin, here someone does not predict by means of a sign, but by hearing the sounds of humans, non-humans, or deities, he predicts: ‘Such is your mind, such is your thought, such is your state of mind.’ Even if he predicts much, it is exactly so and not otherwise.

“Furthermore, Brahmin, here someone does not predict by means of a sign, nor by hearing the sounds of humans, non-humans, or deities, but by hearing the sound of the vibration of thought and reflection of one who is thinking and reflecting, he predicts: ‘Such is your mind, such is your thought, such is your state of mind.’ Even if he predicts much, it is exactly so and not otherwise.

“Furthermore, Brahmin, here someone does not predict by means of a sign, nor by hearing the sounds of humans, non-humans, or deities, nor by hearing the sound of the vibration of thought and reflection, but by encompassing with his own mind the mind of one who has attained a concentration without thought and reflection, he understands: ‘According to the way the mental formations of this worthy one are directed, immediately following this mind, he will think such and such a thought.’ Even if he predicts much, it is exactly so and not otherwise. This, Brahmin, is called the miracle of telepathy.

“And what, Brahmin, is the miracle of instruction? Here, Brahmin, someone instructs thus: ‘Think thus, do not think thus; attend thus, do not attend thus; abandon this, attain and dwell in that.’ This, Brahmin, is called the miracle of instruction. These, Brahmin, are the three kinds of miracles. Of these three miracles, Brahmin, which miracle do you prefer as being more excellent and more sublime?”

“Venerable Gotama, regarding the miracle where someone experiences various kinds of psychic power... and exercises mastery with his body even as far as the Brahma world—this miracle, Venerable Gotama, is experienced only by the one who performs it; it belongs only to the one who performs it. This miracle, Venerable Gotama, appears to me to be like a magic trick.

“Venerable Gotama, regarding the miracle where someone predicts by means of a sign: ‘Such is your mind, such is your state of mind...’"
172:
‘Your mind is such, your thought is such, your mind is thus’—he declares exactly. Even if he declares much, it is just so and not otherwise. Master Gotama, here some person does not declare by a sign, but rather, having heard the sound of humans, non-humans, or deities, he declares... [Pe] ...he does not declare by hearing the sound of humans, non-humans, or deities, but rather, having heard the sound of the vibration of thought of one who is thinking and pondering, he declares... [Pe] ...he does not declare by hearing the sound of the vibration of thought of one who is thinking and pondering, but rather, he discerns with his own mind the mind of one who has attained a concentration without thought and pondering, and understands: ‘According to the way the mental formations of this venerable one are directed, immediately after this mind, he will think such and such a thought.’ Even if he declares much, it is just so and not otherwise. Master Gotama, this too is a miracle. Only the one who performs it experiences it; it belongs only to the one who performs it. Master Gotama, this miracle also appears to me like something of the nature of magic.

Master Gotama, here some person instructs thus: ‘Think thus, do not think thus; attend thus, do not attend thus; abandon this, enter and dwell in that.’ Master Gotama, of these three miracles, I find this miracle of instruction to be the most excellent and sublime.

Wonderful, Master Gotama! Marvelous, Master Gotama! How well-spoken this is by Master Gotama. We regard Master Gotama as one endowed with these three miracles. For Master Gotama experiences various modes of psychic power... [Pe] ...even as far as the Brahma world, he exercises mastery with his body. For Master Gotama discerns with his own mind the mind of one who has attained a concentration without thought and pondering, and understands: ‘According to the way the mental formations of this venerable one are well-directed, immediately after this mind, he will think such and such a thought.’ For Master Gotama instructs thus: ‘Think thus, do not think thus; attend thus, do not attend thus; abandon this, enter and dwell in that.’
173:
“Certainly, Brahmin, you have spoken these words in a confrontational and offensive manner; nevertheless, I will answer you. For I, Brahmin, experience various modes of psychic power... [Pe] ...even as far as the Brahma world, I exercise mastery with my body. For I, Brahmin, discern with my own mind the mind of one who has attained a concentration without thought and pondering, and understand: ‘According to the way the mental formations of this venerable one are directed, immediately after this mind, he will think such and such a thought.’ For I, Brahmin, instruct thus: ‘Think thus, do not think thus; attend thus, do not attend thus; abandon this, enter and dwell in that.’”

“But Master Gotama, is there even one other monk, besides Master Gotama, who is endowed with these three miracles?” “Brahmin, it is not just one hundred, nor two hundred, nor three hundred, nor four hundred, nor five hundred, but rather there are many more monks who are endowed with these three miracles.” “But where, Master Gotama, do those monks now dwell?” “Brahmin, they dwell in this very Sangha of monks.”

“Excellent, Master Gotama! Excellent, Master Gotama! Just as, Master Gotama, one might set upright what had been overturned, or reveal what was hidden, or show the way to one who was lost, or hold up a lamp in the darkness so that those with eyes might see forms, in the same way, the Dhamma has been made clear in many ways by Master Gotama. I go to Master Gotama for refuge, and to the Dhamma, and to the Sangha of monks. May Master Gotama accept me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge from this day forward for as long as life lasts.”

The Tenth [Sutta].
The First Chapter on Brahmins.
Its summary:
Two Brahmins and another, the Wanderer, and Nibbuta,
Palokavaccha, Tikanna, Soni, and with Sangarava.
174:
The tenth discourse.
The first section, the Brāhmaṇa Vagga, is finished.

## (7) 2. Mahāvagga

## 1. Titthāyatana Sutta

62. Monks, there are these three sectarian views which, when questioned, examined, and scrutinized by the wise, end in a doctrine of inaction (akiriya), even when followed to their conclusion. What are the three?

Monks, there are some ascetics and brahmins who speak thus and hold this view: 'Whatever this person experiences—whether pleasure, pain, or neither-pleasure-nor-pain—all that is caused by what was done in the past (pubbekata-hetu).'

Monks, there are some ascetics and brahmins who speak thus and hold this view: 'Whatever this person experiences—whether pleasure, pain, or neither-pleasure-nor-pain—all that is caused by the creation of a Supreme Lord (issara-nimmāna-hetu).'

Monks, there are some ascetics and brahmins who speak thus and hold this view: 'Whatever this person experiences—whether pleasure, pain, or neither-pleasure-nor-pain—all that is without cause or condition (ahetu-appaccayā).'

Monks, among those three, I approach those ascetics and brahmins who speak thus and hold this view: 'Whatever this person experiences—whether pleasure, pain, or neither-pleasure-nor-pain—all that is caused by what was done in the past,' and I ask them: 'Is it true, venerable sirs, that you speak thus and hold this view: "Whatever this person experiences—whether pleasure, pain, or neither-pleasure-nor-pain—all that is caused by what was done in the past"?' When I ask them this, they acknowledge it, saying, 'Yes.' Then I say to them: 'In that case, venerable sirs, people will be killers of living beings because of what was done in the past; they will be takers of what is not given because of what was done in the past; they will be unchaste because of what was done in the past; they will be liars because of what was done in the past; they will be slanderers because of what was done in the past; they will be harsh speakers because of what was done in the past; they will be idle chatterers because of what was done in the past; they will be covetous because of what was done in the past; they will be ill-willed because of what was done in the past; they will be holders of wrong view because of what was done in the past.'

Monks, for those who fall back on what was done in the past as the essential truth, there is no desire (chanda) or effort (vāyāma) regarding 'this should be done' or 'this should not be done'...
175:
...there is no desire (chanda) or effort (viriya). When what should be done and what should not be done are not truly and firmly established, for those who live unmindful and unguarded, a legitimate ascetic doctrine (samaṇavāda) cannot exist for themselves. This, monks, is my first legitimate refutation (sahadhammika niggaha) of those ascetics and brahmins who hold such a view. (1)

Monks, among those three, I approach those ascetics and brahmins who speak thus and hold this view: 'Whatever this person experiences—whether pleasure, pain, or neither-pleasure-nor-pain—all that is caused by the creation of a Supreme Lord,' and I ask them: 'Is it true, venerable sirs, that you speak thus and hold this view: "Whatever this person experiences—whether pleasure, pain, or neither-pleasure-nor-pain—all that is caused by the creation of a Supreme Lord"?' When I ask them this, they acknowledge it, saying, 'Yes.' Then I say to them: 'In that case, venerable sirs, people will be killers of living beings because of the creation of a Supreme Lord; they will be takers of what is not given because of the creation of a Supreme Lord; they will be unchaste because of the creation of a Supreme Lord; they will be liars because of the creation of a Supreme Lord; they will be slanderers because of the creation of a Supreme Lord; they will be harsh speakers because of the creation of a Supreme Lord; they will be idle chatterers because of the creation of a Supreme Lord; they will be covetous because of the creation of a Supreme Lord; they will be ill-willed because of the creation of a Supreme Lord; they will be holders of wrong view because of the creation of a Supreme Lord.'

Monks, for those who fall back on the creation of a Supreme Lord as the essential truth, there is no desire (chanda) or effort (viriya) regarding 'this should be done' or 'this should not be done.' When what should be done and what should not be done are not truly and firmly established, for those who live unmindful and unguarded, a legitimate ascetic doctrine cannot exist for themselves. This, monks, is my second legitimate refutation of those ascetics and brahmins who hold such a view. (2)

Monks, among those three, I approach those ascetics and brahmins who speak thus and hold this view: 'Whatever this person experiences—whether pleasure, pain, or neither-pleasure-nor-pain—all that is without cause or condition...'
176: "All these feelings are without cause or condition." I approached those ascetics and brahmins who speak and hold such views and asked: "Is it true, venerable sirs, that you speak and hold the view that whatever a being experiences—whether pleasure (sukha), pain (dukkha), or neither-pleasure-nor-pain (upekkhā)—all that is without cause or condition?" When I asked this, they acknowledged it, saying, "It is true." Then I said to them: "In that case, venerable sirs, those who kill living beings would do so without cause or condition... [etc.] ... those who hold wrong views would do so without cause or condition."## Monks, for those who fall back on non-causality as the essential truth, there is no desire (chanda) or effort (vīriya) [to think], "This should be done" or "This should not be done." Thus, when what should and should not be done is not truly and firmly established, for those who live unmindful and unguarded, there can be no legitimate ascetic discourse (samaṇavāda) with its specific causes. Monks, this is my third legitimate refutation of those ascetics and brahmins who speak and hold such views. (3)## Monks, these are the three sectarian tenets which, when questioned, examined, and scrutinized by the wise, even if they go further, end up in a doctrine of non-action (akiriya).## Monks, this Dhamma taught by me is unrefuted, untarnished, irreproachable, and uncensored by wise ascetics and brahmins. And what, monks, is this Dhamma taught by me that is unrefuted, untarnished, irreproachable, and uncensored by wise ascetics and brahmins? "Monks, these are the six elements (dhātu)"—this is the Dhamma taught by me... "Monks, these are the six bases of contact (phassāyatana)"—this is the Dhamma taught by me... "Monks, these are the eighteen mental explorations (manopavicāra)"—this is the Dhamma taught by me... "Monks, these are the four Noble Truths (ariyasacca)"—this is the Dhamma taught by me...## "Monks, these are the six elements"—this was said. In reference to what was this said? Monks, there are these six elements: the earth element (pathavīdhātu), the water element (āpodhātu), the fire element (tejodhātu), the air element (vāyodhātu), the space element (ākāsadhātu), and the consciousness element (viññāṇadhātu). "Monks, these are the six elements"—this was said in reference to this.## "Monks, these are the six bases of contact"—this was said. In reference to what was this said?
177: Monks, these are the six bases of contact: the eye base of contact, the ear base of contact, the nose base of contact, the tongue base of contact, the body base of contact, and the mind base of contact. "Monks, these are the six bases of contact"—this was said in reference to this.## "Monks, these are the eighteen mental explorations"—this was said. In reference to what was this said? Having seen a form with the eye, one explores a form that is a basis for joy (somanassa), one explores a form that is a basis for grief (domanassa), one explores a form that is a basis for equanimity (upekkhā). Having heard a sound with the ear... Having smelled an odor with the nose... Having tasted a flavor with the tongue... Having felt a tactile object with the body... Having cognized a mental phenomenon with the mind, one explores a mental phenomenon that is a basis for joy, one explores a mental phenomenon that is a basis for grief, one explores a mental phenomenon that is a basis for equanimity. "Monks, these are the eighteen mental explorations"—this was said in reference to this.## "Monks, these are the four Noble Truths"—this was said. In reference to what was this said? Monks, depending on the six elements, there is the descent of the embryo (gabbhassāvakkanti). When there is descent, there is name-and-form (nāmarūpa). With name-and-form as condition, the six sense bases (saḷāyatana). With the six sense bases as condition, contact (phassa). With contact as condition, feeling (vedanā). Monks, for one who feels, I declare: "This is suffering (dukkha)"; I declare: "This is the origin of suffering (dukkhasamudaya)"; I declare: "This is the cessation of suffering (dukkhanirodha)"; I declare: "This is the path leading to the cessation of suffering (dukkhanirodhagāminī paṭipadā)."## And what, monks, is the Noble Truth of Suffering? Birth is suffering, aging is suffering, sickness is suffering, death is suffering; sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair are suffering; not getting what one wants is suffering; in short, the five aggregates of clinging (upādānakkhandhā) are suffering. Monks, this is called the Noble Truth of Suffering.
178:
Monks, what is the Noble Truth of the Origin of Suffering? With ignorance (avijjā) as condition, volitional formations (saṅkhāra) come to be; with volitional formations as condition, consciousness (viññāṇa) comes to be; with consciousness as condition, name-and-form (nāmarūpa) comes to be; with name-and-form as condition, the six sense bases (saḷāyatana) come to be; with the six sense bases as condition, contact (phassa) comes to be; with contact as condition, feeling (vedanā) comes to be; with feeling as condition, craving (taṇhā) comes to be; with craving as condition, clinging (upādāna) comes to be; with clinging as condition, becoming (bhava) comes to be; with becoming as condition, birth (jāti) comes to be; with birth as condition, aging and death (jarāmaraṇa), sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair come to be. Thus is the origin of this whole mass of suffering. Monks, this is called the Noble Truth of the Origin of Suffering.

Monks, what is the Noble Truth of the Cessation of Suffering? With the remainderless fading away and cessation of that same ignorance (avijjā), volitional formations (saṅkhāra) cease; with the cessation of volitional formations, consciousness (viññāṇa) ceases; with the cessation of consciousness, name-and-form (nāmarūpa) ceases; with the cessation of name-and-form, the six sense bases (saḷāyatana) cease; with the cessation of the six sense bases, contact (phassa) ceases; with the cessation of contact, feeling (vedanā) ceases; with the cessation of feeling, craving (taṇhā) ceases; with the cessation of craving, clinging (upādāna) ceases; with the cessation of clinging, becoming (bhava) ceases; with the cessation of becoming, birth (jāti) ceases; with the cessation of birth, aging and death (jarāmaraṇa), sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair cease. Thus is the cessation of this whole mass of suffering. Monks, this is called the Noble Truth of the Cessation of Suffering.

Monks, what is the Noble Truth of the Way Leading to the Cessation of Suffering? It is this Noble Eightfold Path, namely: Right View (sammā-diṭṭhi), Right Intention (sammā-saṅkappa), Right Speech (sammā-vācā), Right Action (sammā-kammanta), Right Livelihood (sammā-ājīva), Right Effort (sammā-vāyāma), Right Mindfulness (sammā-sati), and Right Concentration (sammā-samādhi). Monks, this is called the Noble Truth of the Way Leading to the Cessation of Suffering. Monks, when I said, 'These are the Four Noble Truths,' this Dhamma taught by me is unrefuted, untarnished, irreproachable, and uncensored by wise recluses and brahmins; it was said in reference to this.

First Sutta.

## 2. Bhaya Sutta

63. Monks, the uninstructed worldling speaks of these three as fears where mother and son cannot protect each other (amātāputtika bhaya). What three?
179:
What three? Monks, there is a time when a great fire breaks out. When a great fire breaks out, it burns villages, market towns, and cities. While villages, market towns, and cities are burning, there a mother does not find her son to protect him, and a son does not find his mother to protect her. Monks, the uninstructed worldling speaks of this as the first fear where mother and son cannot protect each other (amātāputtika bhaya).

Again, monks, there is a time when a great rain falls. When a great rain falls, a great flood of water arises. When a great flood of water arises, it carries away villages, market towns, and cities. While villages, market towns, and cities are being carried away, there a mother does not find her son to protect him, and a son does not find his mother to protect her. Monks, the uninstructed worldling speaks of this as the second fear where mother and son cannot protect each other (amātāputtika bhaya).

Again, monks, there is a time when there is the danger of a forest uprising, and the people of the countryside, mounting their vehicles, flee in all directions. When there is the danger of a forest uprising and the people of the countryside, mounting their vehicles, are fleeing in all directions, there a mother does not find her son to protect him, and a son does not find his mother to protect her. Monks, the uninstructed worldling speaks of this as the third fear where mother and son cannot protect each other (amātāputtika bhaya). Monks, the uninstructed worldling speaks of these three as fears where mother and son cannot protect each other.

But monks, these three are actually fears where mother and son can protect each other (samātāputtika bhaya), yet the uninstructed worldling speaks of them as fears where mother and son cannot protect each other. What three? Monks, there is a time when a great fire breaks out. When a great fire breaks out, it burns villages, market towns, and cities. While villages, market towns, and cities are burning, there comes a time, occasionally and at some point, when a mother finds her son to protect him, and a son finds his mother to protect her. Monks, the uninstructed worldling speaks of this first fear, which is actually one where mother and son can protect each other, as a fear where mother and son cannot protect each other.
180:
Bhikkhus, there is another occasion when a great rainstorm pours down. When a great rainstorm pours down, a great flood of water arises. When a great flood of water arises, it sweeps away villages, market towns, and cities. While villages, market towns, and cities are being swept away, there is an occasion when, at some time or other, a mother might find her son [to protect him], and a son might find his mother [to protect her]. Bhikkhus, an uninstructed worldling speaks of this second danger, which is actually one where mother and son can protect each other, as 'a danger where mother and son cannot protect each other.'

Bhikkhus, there is another occasion when there is the danger of a forest uprising, and the country folk, mounting their vehicles [with their belongings], flee in all directions. Bhikkhus, when there is the danger of a forest uprising and the country folk are fleeing in all directions on their vehicles, there is an occasion when, at some time or other, a mother might find her son [to protect him], and a son might find his mother [to protect her]. Bhikkhus, an uninstructed worldling speaks of this third danger, which is actually one where mother and son can protect each other, as 'a danger where mother and son cannot protect each other.' Bhikkhus, these are the three dangers where mother and son can protect each other that an uninstructed worldling speaks of as 'dangers where mother and son cannot protect each other.'

Bhikkhus, these three are the dangers where mother and son truly cannot protect each other. What three? The danger of aging, the danger of sickness, and the danger of death. Bhikkhus, a mother cannot obtain [her wish] for her aging son by saying, 'Let me age, but let my son not age.' Nor can a son obtain [his wish] for his aging mother by saying, 'Let me age, but let my mother not age.'

Bhikkhus, a mother cannot obtain [her wish] for her sick son by saying, 'Let me be sick, but let my son not be sick.' Nor can a son obtain [his wish] for his sick mother by saying, 'Let me be sick, but let my mother not be sick.'

Bhikkhus, a mother cannot obtain [her wish] for her dying son by saying, 'Let me die, but let my son not die.' Nor can a son obtain [his wish] for his dying mother by saying, 'Let me die, but let my mother not die.' Bhikkhus, these are the three dangers where mother and son cannot protect each other.

Bhikkhus, there is a path, there is a practice that leads to the abandoning and overcoming of these three dangers where mother and son can protect each other and these three dangers where mother and son cannot protect each other. Bhikkhus, what is that path, what is that practice that leads to the abandoning and overcoming of these three dangers where mother and son can protect each other and these three dangers where mother and son cannot protect each other?
181:
It is this Noble Eightfold Path. What is this path? It is Right View (Sammādiṭṭhi), Right Intention (Sammāsaṅkappa), Right Speech (Sammāvāစာ), Right Action (Sammākammanta), Right Livelihood (Sammā-ājīva), Right Effort (Sammāvāyāma), Right Mindfulness (Sammāsati), and Right Concentration (Sammāsamādhi). Bhikkhus, this is the path, this is the practice that leads to the abandoning and overcoming of these three dangers where mother and son can protect each other and these three dangers where mother and son cannot protect each other.

Second Sutta.

## 3. Venāgapura Sutta

64. On one occasion, the Blessed One was wandering on tour among the Kosalans with a large Saṅgha of monks and arrived at a Kosalan Brahmin village named Venāgapura. The Brahmin householders of Venāgapura heard: "It is said that the ascetic Gotama, the son of the Sakyans who went forth from the Sakyan clan, has arrived at Venāgapura. A good report of that Master Gotama has spread thus: 'That Blessed One is an Arahant, perfectly self-enlightened, endowed with knowledge and conduct, well-gone, knower of the worlds, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One.' Having realized it for himself with direct knowledge, he makes known this world with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās, this generation with its ascetics and Brahmins, its devas and humans. He teaches the Dhamma that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with the right meaning and phrasing; he reveals a holy life that is utterly complete and pure. It is good to see such Arahants."

Then the Brahmin householders of Venāgapura approached the Blessed One. Having approached, some paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side; some exchanged friendly greetings with the Blessed One and, after the exchange of pleasant and memorable words, sat down to one side; some extended their hands in reverential salutation toward the Blessed One and sat down to one side; some announced their name and clan and sat down to one side; and some sat down to one side in silence. When he was seated to one side, the Brahmin Vacchagotta of Venāgapura said this to the Blessed One:
182:
Some announced their name and clan and sat down; some sat down in silence.

Sitting to one side, the Brahmin of Venāgapura, of the Vacchagotta lineage, said to the Blessed One: "It is wonderful, Master Gotama! It is marvelous, Master Gotama! How exceptionally clear are Master Gotama’s faculties! How pure and radiant is the complexion of his skin! Just as a ripe jujube fruit in the autumn month of Kattika is pure and radiant, so too are Master Gotama’s faculties clear and his complexion pure and radiant. Just as a ripe palm fruit just fallen from its stalk is pure and radiant, so too are Master Gotama’s faculties clear and his complexion pure and radiant.

Master Gotama, just as a single nikkha of Jambonada gold, well-wrought by a skilled goldsmith, deftly purified in the mouth of the furnace, and placed on a red blanket, shines, blazes, and radiates, so too are Master Gotama’s faculties clear and his complexion pure and radiant. Master Gotama, there are these high and luxurious beds and seats. What are they? Namely: a high couch, a throne, a long-fleeced coverlet, a variegated woolen coverlet, a white woolen coverlet, a wool-flower coverlet, a cotton-stuffed quilt, a woolen coverlet embroidered with animal figures, a double-fringed woolen coverlet, a single-fringed woolen coverlet, a silk-thread coverlet, a silk coverlet, a large woolen carpet, an elephant rug, a horse rug, a chariot rug, an antelope-skin rug, a rug of choice kadali-deer hide, with a red canopy above and red pillows at both ends. Does Master Gotama not obtain such high and luxurious beds and seats at will, without trouble or difficulty?"

"Brahmin, there are indeed those high and luxurious beds and seats. What are they? Namely: a high couch, a throne, a long-fleeced coverlet, a variegated woolen coverlet, a white woolen coverlet, a wool-flower coverlet, a cotton-stuffed quilt, a woolen coverlet embroidered with animal figures, a double-fringed woolen coverlet, a single-fringed woolen coverlet, a silk-thread coverlet, a silk coverlet, a large woolen carpet, an elephant rug, a horse rug, a chariot rug, an antelope-skin rug, a rug of choice kadali-deer hide, with a red canopy above and red pillows at both ends. Those high and luxurious beds and seats are difficult for recluses to obtain, and even if obtained, they are not allowable.

Brahmin, there are these three high and luxurious beds and seats that I now obtain at will, without trouble or difficulty. Which three? The divine high and luxurious bed and seat, the brahma high and luxurious bed and seat, and the noble high and luxurious bed and seat. Brahmin, these are the three high and luxurious beds and seats that I now obtain at will, without trouble or difficulty."

"Master Gotama, what is that divine high and luxurious bed and seat that Master Gotama now obtains at will, without trouble or difficulty?"

"Brahmin, here, in whatever village or town I live in dependence upon,
183:
in the morning, having dressed and taking my bowl and robe, I enter that village or town for alms. After the meal, returning from the alms round, I enter the forest. There, I gather grass or leaves into one place and sit down, having folded my legs cross-legged, set my body erect, and established mindfulness before me. Secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, I enter and dwell in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by thought and examination, with rapture and happiness born of seclusion. With the subsiding of thought and examination, I enter and dwell in the second jhāna, which has internal confidence and unification of mind, is without thought and examination, and has rapture and happiness born of concentration. With the fading away as well of rapture, I dwell equanimous, mindful, and clearly comprehending, and I experience happiness with the body; I enter and dwell in the third jhāna of which the noble ones declare: 'He is equanimous, mindful, and dwells happily.'

I enter and dwell in that third jhāna. With the abandoning of pleasure and pain, and with the previous disappearance of joy and grief, I enter and dwell in the fourth jhāna, which has neither-pain-nor-pleasure and has purity of mindfulness due to equanimity. Brahmin, when I am in such a state, if I walk, my walking at that time is a divine walking. Brahmin, when I am in such a state, if I stand, my standing at that time is a divine standing. Brahmin, when I am in such a state, if I sit, my sitting at that time is a divine sitting. Brahmin, when I am in such a state, if I lie down, my lying down at that time is a divine high and luxurious bed and seat. Brahmin, this is that divine high and luxurious bed and seat that I now obtain at will, without trouble or difficulty."

"It is wonderful, Master Gotama! It is marvelous, Master Gotama! Who else but Master Gotama could obtain such a divine high and luxurious bed and seat at will, without trouble or difficulty?

But Master Gotama, what is that brahma high and luxurious bed and seat that Master Gotama now obtains at will, without trouble or difficulty?"

"Brahmin, here, in whatever village or town I live in dependence upon, in the morning, having dressed and taking my bowl and robe, I enter that village or town for alms. After the meal, returning from the alms round, I enter the forest.
184:
In that forest, I gather grass and leaves together, sit down cross-legged, set my body erect, and establish mindfulness in front of me. I dwell pervading one direction with a mind imbued with loving-kindness, likewise the second, likewise the third, likewise the fourth. Thus, above, below, and across, everywhere and in every way, identifying myself with all, I dwell pervading the entire world with a mind imbued with loving-kindness—abundant, exalted, immeasurable, without hostility, and without ill will.

With a mind imbued with compassion... [p]... With a mind imbued with appreciative joy... [p]... I dwell pervading one direction with a mind imbued with equanimity, likewise the second, likewise the third, likewise the fourth. Thus, above, below, and across, everywhere and in every way, identifying myself with all, I dwell pervading the entire world with a mind imbued with equanimity—abundant, exalted, immeasurable, without hostility, and without ill will.

Brahmin, when I am in such a state, if I walk, at that time my walking is divine. Brahmin, when I am in such a state, if I stand... [p]... sit... [p]... or lie down, at that time this is my divine high and luxurious couch. This, Brahmin, is the divine high and luxurious couch which I now obtain at will, without difficulty or trouble."

"It is wonderful, Master Gotama! It is marvelous, Master Gotama! Who else besides Master Gotama could obtain such a divine high and luxurious couch at will, without difficulty or trouble? But what, Master Gotama, is that noble high and luxurious couch which Master Gotama now obtains at will, without difficulty or trouble?"

"Brahmin, here, I live depending on a certain village or market town. In the morning, I dress, take my bowl and outer robe, and enter that village or market town for alms. After the meal, when I have returned from the alms round, I enter the forest. In that forest, I gather grass and leaves together, sit down cross-legged, set my body erect, and establish mindfulness in front of me. Then I know: 'Lust has been abandoned by me, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, obliterated, so that it is no longer subject to future arising. Hatred has been abandoned by me, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, obliterated, so that it is no longer subject to future arising.'
185:
Delusion has been abandoned by me, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, obliterated, so that it is no longer subject to future arising.' Brahmin, when I am in such a state, if I walk, at that time my walking is noble. Brahmin, when I am in such a state, if I stand... [p]... sit... [p]... or lie down, at that time this is my noble high and luxurious couch. This, Brahmin, is the noble high and luxurious couch which I now obtain at will, without difficulty or trouble."

"It is wonderful, Master Gotama! It is marvelous, Master Gotama! Who else besides Master Gotama could obtain such a noble high and luxurious couch at will, without difficulty or trouble? Excellent, Master Gotama! Excellent, Master Gotama! Just as, Master Gotama, one might set upright what had been overturned, or reveal what was hidden, or show the way to one who was lost, or hold up a lamp in the dark so that those with eyes might see forms, in the same way, the Dhamma has been made clear in many ways by Master Gotama. I go to Master Gotama for refuge, to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha of monks. May Master Gotama accept me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge from this day forward for as long as life lasts."

The Third Sutta.

## 4. Sarabha Sutta

65. Thus have I heard: At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha on Gijjhakūṭa Hill. Now at that time, a wanderer named Sarabha had recently left this Dhamma-Vinaya. In the midst of the assembly in Rājagaha, he was making this statement: "I have understood the Dhamma of the Sakyan ascetics. It is because I have understood the Dhamma of the Sakyan ascetics that I have left that Dhamma-Vinaya." Then a number of monks dressed in the morning, took their bowls and outer robes, and entered Rājagaha for alms.
186:
Those monks heard the wanderer Sarabha speaking in the midst of an assembly in the city of Rājagaha: "I have understood the Dhamma of the Sakyaputtiya ascetics. It is because I have understood the Dhamma of the Sakyaputtiya ascetics that I have departed from that Dhamma-Vinaya."

Then those monks, having wandered for alms in Rājagaha and returned from their alms round after the meal, approached the Blessed One. Having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, they sat down to one side. Sitting there, those monks said to the Blessed One: "Venerable Sir, a wanderer named Sarabha has recently departed from this Dhamma-Vinaya. In the midst of an assembly in Rājagaha, he speaks thus: 'I have understood the Dhamma of the Sakyaputtiya ascetics. It is because I have understood the Dhamma of the Sakyaputtiya ascetics that I have departed from that Dhamma-Vinaya.' We pray, Venerable Sir, may the Blessed One approach the wanderers' park on the bank of the Sappinī River, where the wanderer Sarabha is, out of compassion."

The Blessed One consented by remaining silent.

Then, in the evening, the Blessed One emerged from his seclusion and approached the wanderers' park on the bank of the Sappinī River where the wanderer Sarabha was. Having approached, he sat down on the prepared seat. Having sat down, the Blessed One said to the wanderer Sarabha: "Is it true, Sarabha, as it is said, that you speak thus: 'I have understood the Dhamma of the Sakyaputtiya ascetics. It is because I have understood the Dhamma of the Sakyaputtiya ascetics that I have departed from that Dhamma-Vinaya'?"

When this was said, the wanderer Sarabha remained silent.

A second time, the Blessed One said to the wanderer Sarabha: "Speak, Sarabha! In what way have you understood the Dhamma of the Sakyaputtiya ascetics? If your understanding is incomplete, I will complete it for you. But if it is complete, I will rejoice in it."

A second time, the wanderer Sarabha remained silent.

A third time, the Blessed One said to the wanderer Sarabha: "Speak, Sarabha! In what way have you understood the Dhamma of the Sakyaputtiya ascetics? If your understanding is incomplete, I will complete it for you."
187:
"But if it is complete, I will rejoice in it." Even for the third time, the wanderer Sarabha remained silent.

Then those wanderers said to the wanderer Sarabha: "Friend Sarabha, whatever you might ask of the ascetic Gotama, he is offering you that very opportunity. Speak, friend Sarabha! In what way have you understood the Dhamma of the Sakyaputtiya ascetics? If your understanding is incomplete, the ascetic Gotama will complete it for you. But if it is complete, the ascetic Gotama will rejoice in it."

When this was said, the wanderer Sarabha sat silent, crestfallen, with drooping shoulders and downcast face, brooding and speechless.

Then the Blessed One, knowing that the wanderer Sarabha was silent, crestfallen, with drooping shoulders and downcast face, brooding and speechless, addressed those wanderers:

"Wanderers, if anyone were to say to me: 'While you claim to be a Fully Enlightened One, these things are not fully understood by you,' I would cross-examine him, press him, and question him closely on that matter. Being thus cross-examined, pressed, and questioned by me, it is impossible, there is no chance, that he would not fall into one of these three situations: he would either prevaricate, leading the talk aside, or show anger, aversion, and discontent, or he would sit silent, crestfallen, with drooping shoulders and downcast face, brooding and speechless, just like the wanderer Sarabha.

"Wanderers, if anyone were to say to me: 'While you claim to be one whose taints are destroyed, these taints are not destroyed in you,' I would cross-examine him, press him, and question him closely on that matter. Being thus cross-examined, pressed, and questioned by me, it is impossible, there is no chance, that he would not fall into one of these three situations: he would either prevaricate, leading the talk aside, or..."
188:
He will manifest anger, ill-will, and displeasure. There is no possibility or chance that he would not fall into one of these three states; or he would sit silent, confused, with shoulders slumped and head down, brooding and speechless, just like the wanderer Sarabha.

“Wanderers, if anyone were to say to me: ‘The Dhamma taught by you for the purpose of ending suffering does not lead one who practices it to the complete destruction of suffering,’ I would question him closely, examine him, and cross-examine him. If he were thus questioned, examined, and cross-examined by me, there is no possibility or chance that he would not fall into one of these three states: he would either prevaricate, or lead the talk aside, or manifest anger, ill-will, and displeasure; or he would sit silent, confused, with shoulders slumped and head down, brooding and speechless, just like the wanderer Sarabha.” Thus the Blessed One spoke. Then the Blessed One, having roared his lion’s roar three times in the wanderers’ park on the banks of the Sippinikā River, departed through the air.

Then, not long after the Blessed One had departed, those wanderers surrounded the wanderer Sarabha and poked him with the goad of their tongues: “Friend Sarabha, just as an old jackal in the great forest thinks ‘I will roar a lion’s roar,’ but only lets out a jackal’s howl, a yelp; so too, you, friend Sarabha, away from the presence of the recluse Gotama, think ‘I will roar a lion’s roar,’ but only let out a jackal’s howl, a yelp. Friend Sarabha, just as a young hen thinks ‘I will crow like a rooster,’ but only lets out a hen’s cackle; so too, you, friend Sarabha, away from the presence of the recluse Gotama, think ‘I will crow like a rooster,’ but only let out a hen’s cackle. Friend Sarabha, just as a bull in an empty cow-pen thinks he can bellow a deep roar; so too, you, friend Sarabha, away from the presence of the recluse Gotama, think you can bellow a deep roar.”
189:
In this way, those wanderers surrounded the wanderer Sarabha and poked him with the goad of their tongues.

The Fourth Sutta.

## 5 - Kesamutti Sutta

66. Thus have I heard: At one time the Blessed One was wandering in the Kosala country with a large community of monks and arrived at a market town of the Kālāmas named Kesamutta. The Kālāmas of Kesamutta heard: “The recluse Gotama, a son of the Sakyans who went forth from the Sakyan clan, has arrived at Kesamutta. A good report concerning that Master Gotama has spread: ‘That Blessed One is an Arahant... [etc]... It is good to see such Arahants.’”

Then the Kālāmas of Kesamutta approached the Blessed One. Having approached, some paid homage to the Blessed One and sat to one side. Some exchanged friendly greetings with the Blessed One and, after finishing the cordial and memorable conversation, sat to one side. Some extended their joined palms toward the Blessed One and sat to one side. Some announced their name and clan and sat to one side. Some sat to one side in silence. Sitting to one side, those Kālāmas of Kesamutta said to the Blessed One:

“Venerable sir, there are some recluses and brahmins who come to Kesamutta. They explain and illuminate only their own doctrines, but they attack, despise, disparage, and debunk the doctrines of others. Then, venerable sir, other recluses and brahmins come to Kesamutta. They too explain and illuminate only their own doctrines, but they attack, despise, disparage, and debunk the doctrines of others. Venerable sir, we have doubt and uncertainty: ‘Which of these reverend recluses and brahmins spoke the truth, and which spoke falsehood?’”

“It is fitting for you to doubt, Kālāmas, it is fitting for you to be uncertain. Uncertainty has arisen in you about a matter that is doubtful.

Come, Kālāmas,
do not go by oral tradition,
do not go by lineage,
do not go by hearsay,
do not go by the authority of scriptures,
do not go by logical reasoning,
do not go by inferential reasoning,
do not go by reasoned reflection,
do not go by acceptance of a view after pondering it,”
190:
Do not go by the appearance of probability, nor by the thought, 'The ascetic is our guru.' Kālāmas, when you yourselves know: 'These things are unwholesome; these things are blameworthy; these things are censured by the wise; these things, when accepted and undertaken, lead to harm and suffering,' then you should abandon them.

"What do you think, Kālāmas? When greed (lobha) arises within a person internally (ajjhatta), does it arise for their welfare or for their harm?"
"For their harm, Bhante."
"Kālāmas, a person who is greedy, overcome by greed, with mind obsessed, kills living beings, takes what is not given, commits adultery, speaks falsehood, and encourages others to do the same. Does this lead to their harm and suffering for a long time?"
"Yes, Bhante."

"What do you think, Kālāmas? When hatred (dosa) arises within a person internally (ajjhatta), does it arise for their welfare or for their harm?"
"For their harm, Bhante."
"Kālāmas, a person who is hateful, overcome by hatred, with mind obsessed, kills living beings, takes what is not given, commits adultery, speaks falsehood, and encourages others to do the same. Does this lead to their harm and suffering for a long time?"
"Yes, Bhante."

"What do you think, Kālāmas? When delusion (moha) arises within a person internally (ajjhatta), does it arise for their welfare or for their harm? ... (etc.) ... Does it lead to suffering?"
"Yes, Bhante."

"What do you think, Kālāmas? Are these things wholesome or unwholesome?"
"Unwholesome, Bhante."
"Are they blameworthy or blameless?"
"Blameworthy, Bhante."
"Are they censured by the wise or praised by the wise?"
"Censured by the wise, Bhante."
"When accepted and undertaken, do they lead to harm and suffering, or not? How does it seem to you here?"
"Bhante, when accepted and well-undertaken, they lead to harm and suffering. This is how it seems to us here."

"Kālāmas, do not go by oral tradition,
191:
nor by lineage of teaching, nor by hearsay, nor by accordance with scriptures, nor by logical reasoning, nor by inferential reasoning, nor by reflection on reasons, nor by agreement with a pondered view, nor by the appearance of probability, nor by the thought, 'The ascetic is our guru.' Kālāmas, when you yourselves know: 'These things are unwholesome; these things are blameworthy; these things are censured by the wise; these things, when accepted and undertaken, lead to harm and suffering,' then you should abandon them. This is what I meant when I said that.

Kālāmas, do not go by oral tradition, nor by lineage of teaching, nor by hearsay, nor by accordance with scriptures, nor by logical reasoning, nor by inferential reasoning, nor by reflection on reasons, nor by agreement with a pondered view, nor by the appearance of probability, nor by the thought, 'The ascetic is our guru.' Kālāmas, when you yourselves know: 'These things are wholesome; these things are blameless; these things are praised by the wise; these things, when accepted and undertaken, lead to welfare and happiness,' then you should live having undertaken them.

"What do you think, Kālāmas? When non-greed (alobha) arises within a person internally (ajjhatta), does it arise for their welfare or for their harm?"
"For their welfare, Bhante."
"Kālāmas, a person who is not greedy, not overcome by greed, with mind not obsessed, does not kill living beings, does not take what is not given, does not commit adultery, does not speak falsehood, and does not encourage others to do the same. Does this lead to their welfare and happiness for a long time?"
"Yes, Bhante."

"What do you think, Kālāmas? When non-hatred (adosa) arises within a person internally (ajjhatta) ... (etc.) ... When non-delusion (amoha) arises within a person internally (ajjhatta) ... (etc.) ... Does it lead to welfare and happiness?"
"Yes, Bhante."

"What do you think, Kālāmas? Are these things wholesome or unwholesome?"
"Wholesome, Bhante."
192:
"Are they blameworthy or blameless?" (the Buddha asked). "They are blameless, Bhante." "Are they censured by the wise or praised by the wise?" "They are praised by the wise, Bhante." "When these things are fulfilled and undertaken, do they lead to welfare and happiness, or not? What is your thought on this?" "Bhante, when these things are fulfilled and undertaken, they lead to welfare and happiness. This is our thought on this."

"Kālāmas, do not go by oral tradition, nor by lineage, nor by hearsay, nor by the authority of scriptures, nor by logical reasoning, nor by inferential reasoning, nor by reflection on appearances, nor by acceptance of a view after pondering it, nor by the appearance of competence, nor by the thought: 'The ascetic is our teacher.' Kālāmas, when you know for yourselves: 'These things are wholesome; these things are blameless; these things are praised by the wise; these things, when fulfilled and undertaken, lead to welfare and happiness,' then, Kālāmas, you should fulfill them and dwell in them. What I have said was said for this reason."

Kālāmas, that noble disciple, thus free from longing (abhijjhā), free from ill will (byāpāda), unconfused, clearly comprehending, and mindful, dwells pervading one direction with a mind imbued with loving-kindness (mettā); likewise the second, likewise the third, likewise the fourth. Thus above, below, across, everywhere, and to all as to himself, he dwells pervading the entire world with a mind imbued with loving-kindness—abundant, exalted, immeasurable, without hostility, and without ill will. With a mind imbued with compassion (karuṇā)... [pe]... With a mind imbued with altruistic joy (muditā)... [pe]... With a mind imbued with equanimity (upekkhā), he dwells pervading one direction; likewise the second, likewise the third, likewise the fourth. Thus above, below, across, everywhere, and to all as to himself, he dwells pervading the entire world with a mind imbued with equanimity—abundant, exalted, immeasurable, without hostility, and without ill will.

Kālāmas, for that noble disciple whose mind is thus without hostility, without ill will, undefiled, and pure, four assurances are attained in this very life.
193:
"'If there is a world beyond, and if there is the fruit and result of deeds well done and ill done, then after the breaking up of the body, after death, I will be reborn in a good destination, in a heavenly world.' This is the first assurance attained by that noble disciple.

'If there is no world beyond, and if there is no fruit and result of deeds well done and ill done, then in this very life I maintain myself free from hostility, free from ill will, free from suffering, and happy.' This is the second assurance attained by that noble disciple.

'If evil comes to one who does evil, but I do not intend evil toward anyone, then how can suffering touch me who does no evil deed?' This is the third assurance attained by that noble disciple.

'If evil does not come to one who does evil, then I see myself pure in both ways.' This is the fourth assurance attained by that noble disciple. Kālāmas, for that noble disciple whose mind is thus without hostility, without ill will, undefiled, and pure, these four assurances are attained in this very life." (the Buddha said).

"It is so, Blessed One! It is so, Fortunate One! Bhante, for that noble disciple whose mind is thus without hostility, without ill will, undefiled, and pure, four assurances are attained in this very life. 'If there is a world beyond, and if there is the fruit and result of deeds well done and ill done, then after the breaking up of the body, after death, I will be reborn in a good destination, in a heavenly world.' This is the first assurance attained by that noble disciple.

'If there is no world beyond, and if there is no fruit and result of deeds well done and ill done, then in this very life I maintain myself free from hostility, free from ill will, free from suffering, and happy.' This is the second assurance attained by that noble disciple.

'If evil comes to one who does evil, but I do not intend evil toward anyone, then how can suffering touch me who does no evil deed?' This is the third assurance he attains."
194:
This is the third assurance attained by that noble disciple.

If, while doing [evil], no evil is done, then I see myself purified in both ways (by not doing evil and by no evil being done). This is the fourth assurance attained by that noble disciple. Venerable sir, for that noble disciple whose mind is thus free from enmity, free from ill-will, undefiled, and purified, these four assurances are attained in this very life.

Excellent, venerable sir! [Excellent, venerable sir!] ... We go to the Blessed One for refuge, to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha. May the Blessed One accept us as lay followers who have gone for refuge from this day forward for as long as life lasts.

Fifth Sutta.

## 6. Sāḷha Sutta

67. Thus have I heard—At one time the venerable Nandaka was staying at Sāvatthī in the Eastern Monastery, the palace of Migāra's mother. Then Sāḷha, the grandson of Migāra, and Sāṇa, the grandson of Sekhuniya, approached the venerable Nandaka. Having approached and paid homage to the venerable Nandaka, they sat down to one side. As Sāḷha, the grandson of Migāra, was sitting there, the venerable Nandaka said this to him:

"Come, Sāḷha,
do not go by oral tradition,
do not go by lineage of teaching,
do not go by hearsay,
do not go by a collection of scriptures,
do not go by logical reasoning,
do not go by inferential reasoning,
do not go by reasoned reflection,
do not go by acceptance of a view after pondering it,
do not go by the appearance of competence,
do not go by the thought, 'The ascetic is our teacher.'

Sāḷha, when you know for yourselves: 'These things are unwholesome; these things are blameworthy; these things are censured by the wise; these things, when accepted and undertaken, lead to harm and suffering,' then, Sāḷha, you should abandon them.

What do you think, Sāḷha? Is there greed?"
"There is, venerable sir."
"Sāḷha, I call this 'covetousness' (abhijjhā). Sāḷha, a greedy person, overcome by covetousness, kills living beings, takes what is not given, commits adultery, speaks falsehood, and encourages others to do the same. Does this lead to his harm and suffering for a long time?"
"Yes, venerable sir."
195:
"It can, venerable sir."

What do you think, Sāḷha? Is there hatred (dosa)?" "There is, venerable sir." "Sāḷha, I call this 'ill-will' (byāpāda). Sāḷha, a hateful person, with a mind of ill-will, kills living beings, takes what is not given, commits adultery, speaks falsehood, and encourages others to do the same. Does this lead to his harm and suffering for a long time?" "It can, venerable sir."

What do you think, Sāḷha? Is there delusion (moha)?" "There is, venerable sir." "Sāḷha, I call this 'ignorance' (avijjā). Sāḷha, a deluded person, possessed of ignorance, kills living beings, takes what is not given, commits adultery, speaks falsehood, and encourages others to do the same. Does this lead to his harm and suffering for a long time?" "It can, venerable sir."

What do you think, Sāḷha? Are these things wholesome or unwholesome?" "Unwholesome, venerable sir." "Are they blameworthy or blameless?" "Blameworthy, venerable sir." "Are they censured by the wise or praised by the wise?"
"Censured by the wise, venerable sir."

"When accepted and undertaken, do they lead to harm and suffering, or not? Or how is it in this case?" "When accepted and undertaken, they lead to harm and suffering, venerable sir. That is how it appears to us in this case."

"So, Sāḷha, when it was said: 'Come, Sāḷha, do not go by oral tradition, do not go by lineage of teaching, do not go by hearsay, do not go by a collection of scriptures, do not go by logical reasoning, do not go by inferential reasoning, do not go by reasoned reflection, do not go by acceptance of a view after pondering it, do not go by the appearance of competence, do not go by the thought, "The ascetic is our teacher." When you know for yourselves: "These things are unwholesome; these things are blameworthy; these things are censured by the wise; these things, when accepted and undertaken, lead to harm and suffering," then, Sāḷha, you should abandon them,' it was for this reason that it was said.

Come, Sāḷha, do not go by oral tradition, do not go by lineage of teaching, do not go by hearsay, do not go by a collection of scriptures, do not go by logical reasoning, do not go by inferential reasoning, do not go by reasoned reflection, do not go by acceptance of a view after pondering it, do not go by the appearance of competence, do not go by the thought, 'The ascetic is our teacher.' When you know for yourselves: 'These things are wholesome, these things are blameless, these things are praised by the wise, these things...'
196:
Do not go by the thought, 'The ascetic is our respected teacher.' But, Sāḷhas, when you know for yourselves: 'These things are wholesome; these things are blameless; these things are praised by the wise; these things, when accepted and undertaken, lead to welfare and to happiness,' then you should live having attained them.

What do you think, Sāḷhas? Is there such a thing as non-greed (alobha)?" "There is, venerable sir." "Sāḷhas, I call this 'non-covetousness' (anabhijjhā). A man who is not greedy, being free from covetousness, does not kill living beings, does not take what is not given, does not go to another's wife, does not speak falsehood, and does not incite others to do likewise. Can this (abstaining from killing, etc.) lead to welfare and happiness for a long time?" "It can, venerable sir."

What do you think, Sāḷhas? Is there such a thing as non-hatred (adosa)?" "There is, venerable sir." "Sāḷhas, I call this 'non-ill will' (avyāpāda). A man who is not hateful, having a mind free from ill will, does not kill living beings, does not take what is not given, does not go to another's wife, does not speak falsehood, and does not incite others to do likewise. Can this lead to welfare and happiness for a long time?" "It can, venerable sir."

What do you think, Sāḷhas? Is there such a thing as non-delusion (amoha)?" "There is, venerable sir." "Sāḷhas, I call this 'knowledge' (vijjā). A man who is not deluded, having attained knowledge, does not kill living beings, does not take what is not given, does not go to another's wife, does not speak falsehood, and does not incite others to do likewise. Can this lead to welfare and happiness for a long time?" "It can, venerable sir."

What do you think, Sāḷhas? Are these things wholesome or unwholesome?" "Wholesome, venerable sir." "Are they blameworthy or blameless?" "Blameless, venerable sir." "Are they censured or praised by the wise?" "Praised by the wise, venerable sir." "When accepted and undertaken, do they lead to welfare and happiness, or not? How does it appear to you in this matter?"

"When accepted and undertaken, they lead to welfare and happiness, venerable sir; thus it appears to us in this matter, venerable sir."

"So, Sāḷhas, as to what I said: 'Come, Sāḷhas, do not go by oral tradition, by lineage of teaching, by hearsay, by a collection of scriptures, by logical reasoning, by inferential reasoning, by reflection on appearances, by acceptance of a view after pondering it, by the seeming competence of a speaker, or by the thought: "The ascetic is our respected teacher." But, Sāḷhas, when you know for yourselves: "These things are wholesome; these things are blameless; these things are praised by the wise; these things..."
197:
"...when accepted and undertaken, lead to welfare and to happiness," then you should live having attained them.' It was for this reason that this was said.

Sāḷhas, that noble disciple, thus free from covetousness, free from ill will, undeluded, clearly comprehending, and mindful, dwells pervading one quarter with a mind imbued with loving-kindness (mettā)... with compassion (karuṇā)... with appreciative joy (muditā)... with equanimity (upekkhā). Likewise the second, likewise the third, likewise the fourth. Thus above, below, across, everywhere, and to all as to himself, he dwells pervading the entire world with a mind imbued with equanimity—abundant, exalted, measureless, without hostility, and without ill will. That noble disciple understands thus: 'There is this (suffering); there is the low; there is the sublime; there is an escape beyond this perception.' When he knows and sees thus, his mind is liberated from the taint of sensual desire (kāmāsava), from the taint of existence (bhavāsava), and from the taint of ignorance (avijjāsava). When it is liberated, there comes the knowledge: 'It is liberated.' He understands: 'Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more for this state of being.'

He understands thus: 'Formerly there was greed, and that was unwholesome; now it is not there, and that is wholesome. Formerly there was hatred... Formerly there was delusion, and that was unwholesome; now it is not there, and that is wholesome.' Thus, in this very life, being without the hunger (of craving), extinguished, cooled, experiencing happiness, he dwells with a self that has become sublime.

The Sixth Sutta.

## 7. Kathāvatthu Sutta

68. "Bhikkhus, there are these three topics of conversation. Which three? One might speak a discourse concerning the past, saying: 'Thus it was in the past.' Or one might speak a discourse concerning the future, saying: 'Thus it will be in the future.' Or one might speak a discourse concerning the present, saying: 'Thus it is now in the present.'

Bhikkhus, by his engagement in conversation, a person is to be known as one fit to talk with or one unfit to talk with. Bhikkhus, if a person, when asked a question, does not give a direct answer to a question that should be answered directly; does not give an analytical answer to a question that should be answered analytically; does not give a counter-question to a question that should be answered with a counter-question; and does not set aside a question that should be set aside..."
198:
Monks, in such a case, this person is one unfit to talk with. Monks, if this person, when asked a question, does not answer a question that should be answered categorically with a categorical answer; does not answer a question that should be answered analytically with an analytical answer; does not answer a question that should be answered with a counter-question with a counter-question; and does not set aside a question that should be set aside; then, monks, such a person is unfit to talk with. But if, monks, this person, when asked a question, answers a categorical question categorically, an analytical question analytically, a counter-question with a counter-question, and sets aside a question that should be set aside; then, monks, such a person is fit to talk with.

Monks, a person should be known through the engagement in talk as to whether they are fit or unfit to talk with. Monks, if this person, when asked a question, does not stand by what is possible and impossible, does not stand by assumptions, does not stand by acknowledged positions, and does not stand by the course of practice; then, monks, such a person is unfit to talk with. But if, monks, this person, when asked a question, stands by what is possible and impossible, stands by assumptions, stands by acknowledged positions, and stands by the course of practice; then, monks, such a person is fit to talk with.

Monks, a person should be known through the engagement in talk as to whether they are fit or unfit to talk with. Monks, if this person, when asked a question, evades one thing with another, leads the talk aside, and manifests anger, malice, and resentment; then, monks, such a person is unfit to talk with. But if, monks, this person, when asked a question, does not evade one thing with another, does not lead the talk aside, and does not manifest anger, malice, and resentment; then, monks, such a person is fit to talk with.

Monks, a person should be known through the engagement in talk as to whether they are fit or unfit to talk with. Monks, if this person, when asked a question, overwhelms, crushes, laughs at (to cause doubt in the questioner), and seizes upon minor mistakes; then, monks, such a person is unfit to talk with. But if, monks, this person, when asked a question, does not overwhelm, does not crush, does not laugh at, and does not seize upon minor mistakes; then, monks, such a person is fit to talk with.

Monks, a person should be known through the engagement in talk as to whether they have the supporting condition (saupaniso) or lack the supporting condition (anupaniso). Monks, one who does not lend an ear lacks the supporting condition; one who lends an ear has the supporting condition. If that person has the supporting condition, they know one thing with higher knowledge (the Noble Path), they fully understand one thing (the truth of suffering),
199:
they abandon one thing (unwholesome states), and they realize one thing (Nibbāna). That person, having known one thing with higher knowledge (the Noble Path), fully understanding one thing (the truth of suffering), abandoning one thing (unwholesome states), and realizing one thing (Nibbāna), touches the fruit of Arahantship, which is right liberation. Monks, there is the fruit of Arahantship, the liberation of the mind through non-clinging; talk has this as its purpose, consultation has this as its purpose, the supporting condition has this as its purpose, and lending an ear has this as its purpose.

Those who converse with hostility, being biased and arrogant, attacking the virtues of the Noble Ones, seeking each other's faults—they rejoice in each other's poorly spoken words, minor slips, confusion, and defeat. A Noble One does not engage in such talk. If a wise person wishes to speak, knowing the right time, they should speak words connected with the Dhamma and its meaning, the kind of talk practiced by the Noble Ones. A wise person should speak that talk without hostility or arrogance, with an unruffled mind, without rivalry or violence. Without envy, they speak with right knowledge; they should rejoice in what is well-spoken and not rebuke what is poorly spoken. They should not practice picking holes or seize upon slips; they should not overwhelm or crush, nor speak words that are deceptive. The consultation of the virtuous is indeed for the sake of knowledge and confidence; thus the Noble Ones consult. This is the consultation of the Noble Ones. Knowing this, a wise person should consult without arrogance.

The Seventh Sutta.

## 8. Aññatitthiya Sutta
69. Monks, if wanderers of other sects should ask: 'Friends, there are these three things. Which three? Lust (rāga), hatred (dosa),'
200:
...hatred (dosa) and delusion (moha). Friends, these are the three things. Friends, what is the distinction, what is the disparity, what is the difference between these three things? If asked thus, bhikkhus, how would you answer those wanderers of other sects?"
