"Venerable Sir, our teachings are rooted in the Blessed One, guided by the Blessed One, and have the Blessed One as their refuge. It would be good, Venerable Sir, if the Blessed One himself would explain the meaning of this statement. Having heard it from the Blessed One, the bhikkhus will remember it."

"In that case, bhikkhus, listen and pay close attention; I will speak." "Yes, Venerable Sir," the bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this:

"Bhikkhus, if wanderers of other sects should ask: 'Friends, there are these three things. Which three? Lust (rāga), hatred (dosa), and delusion (moha). Friends, these are the three things. Friends, what is the distinction, what is the disparity, what is the difference between these three things?' If asked thus, bhikkhus, you should answer those wanderers of other sects in this way: 'Friends, lust is less blameworthy and slow to fade. Hatred is very blameworthy and quick to fade. Delusion is very blameworthy and slow to fade.'

'But friends, what is the cause, what is the reason, why unarisen lust arises, or why arisen lust increases and expands?' It should be said: 'The sign of the beautiful (subhanimitta).' For one who attends unwisely to the sign of the beautiful, unarisen lust arises, and arisen lust increases and expands. Friends, this is the cause, this is the reason, why unarisen lust arises, or why arisen lust increases and expands.

'But friends, what is the cause, what is the reason, why unarisen hatred arises, or why arisen hatred increases and expands?' It should be said: 'The sign of irritation (paṭighanimitta).' For one who attends unwisely to the sign of irritation, unarisen hatred arises, and arisen hatred increases and expands. Friends, this is the cause, this is the reason, why unarisen hatred arises, or why arisen hatred increases and expands.

'But friends, what is the cause, what is the reason, why unarisen delusion arises, or why arisen delusion increases and expands?' It should be said: 'Unwise attention (ayoniso manasikāra).' For one who attends unwisely, unarisen delusion arises, and arisen delusion...
201:
...increases and expands. Friends, this is the cause, this is the reason, why unarisen delusion arises, or why arisen delusion increases and expands.'

'But friends, what is the cause, what is the reason, why unarisen lust does not arise, and arisen lust is abandoned?' It should be said: 'The sign of the unattractive (asubhanimitta).' For one who attends wisely to the sign of the unattractive, unarisen lust does not arise, and arisen lust is abandoned. Friends, this is the cause, this is the reason, why unarisen lust does not arise, and arisen lust is abandoned.

'But friends, what is the cause, what is the reason, why unarisen hatred does not arise, and arisen hatred is abandoned?' It should be said: 'The deliverance of mind through loving-kindness (mettā cetovimutti).' For one who attends wisely to the deliverance of mind through loving-kindness, unarisen hatred does not arise, and arisen hatred is abandoned. Friends, this is the cause, this is the reason, why unarisen hatred does not arise, and arisen hatred is abandoned.

'But friends, what is the cause, what is the reason, why unarisen delusion does not arise, and arisen delusion is abandoned?' It should be said: 'Wise attention (yoniso manasikāra).' For one who attends wisely, unarisen delusion does not arise, and arisen delusion is abandoned. Friends, this is the cause, this is the reason, why unarisen delusion does not arise, and arisen delusion is abandoned."

(Eighth Sutta)
202:
The Eighth Sutta.

## 9. Akusalamūla Sutta

70. "Monks, there are these three roots of the unwholesome. Which three? Greed as a root of the unwholesome, hatred as a root of the unwholesome, and delusion as a root of the unwholesome.

Monks, there is greed; that greed is a root of the unwholesome. A greedy person makes an effort through body, speech, and mind; that effort is unwholesome. A greedy person, overcome by greed, with a mind obsessed, causes suffering to another through a manifest matter—by killing, or by binding, or by loss, or by reproach, or by banishment—thinking 'I have power, I am capable.' That too is unwholesome. Thus, many evil unwholesome states, born of greed, caused by greed, originating from greed, and conditioned by greed, arise in that person.

Monks, there is hatred; that hatred is a root of the unwholesome. A hateful person makes an effort through body, speech, and mind; that effort is also unwholesome. A hateful person, overcome by hatred, with a mind obsessed, causes suffering to another through a non-manifest matter—by killing, or by binding, or by loss, or by reproach, or by banishment—thinking 'I have power, I am capable.' That too is unwholesome. Thus, many evil unwholesome states, born of hatred, caused by hatred, originating from hatred, and conditioned by hatred, arise in that person.

Monks, there is delusion; that delusion is a root of the unwholesome. A deluded person makes an effort through body, speech, and mind; that effort is indeed unwholesome. A deluded person, overcome by delusion, with a mind obsessed, causes suffering to another through a non-manifest matter—by killing, or by binding, or by loss, or by reproach, or by banishment—thinking 'I have power, I am capable.' That too is unwholesome. Thus, many evil unwholesome states, born of delusion, caused by delusion, originating from delusion, and conditioned by delusion, arise in that person."
203:
"Monks, such a person is called 'one who speaks at the wrong time,' 'one who speaks what is not true,' 'one who speaks what is useless,' 'one who speaks what is not Dhamma,' and 'one who speaks what is not Vinaya.'

Monks, why is such a person called 'one who speaks at the wrong time,' 'one who speaks what is not true,' 'one who speaks what is useless,' 'one who speaks what is not Dhamma,' and 'one who speaks what is not Vinaya'? Monks, this person causes suffering to another through a non-manifest matter—by killing, or by binding, or by loss, or by reproach, or by banishment—thinking 'I have power, I am capable.' When spoken to with the truth, he denies it and does not acknowledge it. When spoken to with what is not true, he makes no effort to untangle it, saying 'This is not true for this reason, this is not so for this reason.' Therefore, such a person is called 'one who speaks at the wrong time,' 'one who speaks what is not true,' 'one who speaks what is useless,' 'one who speaks what is not Dhamma,' and 'one who speaks what is not Vinaya.'

Monks, such a person, with a mind overcome and obsessed by evil unwholesome states born of greed, dwells in suffering in this very life, with distress, with great anguish, and with fever. After the breakup of the body, after death, a bad destination is to be expected.

With a mind overcome and obsessed by evil unwholesome states born of hatred... (Pe)... born of delusion, dwells in suffering in this very life, with distress, with great anguish, and with fever. After the breakup of the body, after death, a bad destination is to be expected.

Monks, just as a Sāla tree, a Dhava tree, or a Phandana tree, when destroyed, enveloped, and smothered by three Māluva creepers, comes to ruin, comes to destruction, comes to ruin and destruction; even so, monks, such a person, with a mind overcome and obsessed by evil unwholesome states born of greed, dwells in suffering in this very life, with distress, with great anguish, and with fever. After the breakup of the body, after death, a bad destination is to be expected.

With a mind overcome and obsessed by evil unwholesome states born of hatred... (Pe)... born of delusion, dwells in suffering in this very life, with distress, with great anguish, and with fever. After the breakup of the body, after death, a bad destination is to be expected.

These, monks, are the three roots of the unwholesome.

Monks, there are these three roots of the wholesome. Which three? Non-greed as a root of the wholesome, non-hatred as a root of the wholesome, and non-delusion as a root of the wholesome."
204:
“Monks, these are the three roots of the unwholesome,” (He said).

Monks, there are these three roots of the wholesome. Which three? Non-greed as a root of the wholesome, non-hatred as a root of the wholesome, and non-delusion as a root of the wholesome.

Monks, there is non-greed (alobha); that non-greed is a root of the wholesome. When a person who is not greedy makes an effort by way of body, speech, or mind, that effort is wholesome. When a person who is not greedy—being neither overcome nor possessed by greed—does not cause suffering to another through false accusation, by killing, binding, confiscating, censuring, or banishing, thinking ‘I have power, I am capable,’ that too is wholesome. Thus, many wholesome states arise in him, born of non-greed, caused by non-greed, originating from non-greed, and conditioned by non-greed.

Monks, there is non-hatred (adosa); that non-hatred is a root of the wholesome. When a person who is without hatred makes an effort by way of body, speech, or mind, that effort is wholesome. When a person who is without hatred—being neither overcome nor possessed by hatred—does not cause suffering to another through false accusation, by killing, binding, confiscating, censuring, or banishing, thinking ‘I have power, I am capable,’ that too is wholesome. Thus, many wholesome states arise in him, born of non-hatred, caused by non-hatred, originating from non-hatred, and conditioned by non-hatred.

Monks, there is non-delusion (amoha); that non-delusion is a root of the wholesome. When a person who is not deluded makes an effort by way of body, speech, or mind, that effort is wholesome. When a person who is not deluded—being neither overcome nor possessed by delusion—does not cause suffering to another through false accusation, by killing, binding, confiscating, censuring, or banishing, thinking ‘I have power, I am capable,’ that too is wholesome. Thus, many wholesome states arise in him, born of non-delusion, caused by non-delusion, originating from non-delusion, and conditioned by non-delusion. Monks, such a person is called one who speaks at the right time, one who speaks the truth, one who speaks what is beneficial, one who speaks the Dhamma, and one who speaks the Vinaya.
205:
“Monks, why is such a person called one who speaks at the right time, one who speaks the truth, one who speaks what is beneficial, one who speaks the Dhamma, and one who speaks the Vinaya? Monks, this person does not cause suffering to another through false accusation, by killing, binding, confiscating, censuring, or banishing, thinking ‘I have power, I am capable.’ When spoken to with what is true, he admits it and does not deny it. When spoken to with what is untrue, he makes an effort to clarify it, saying: ‘For this reason, this is not true; for this reason, this is not so.’ Therefore, such a person is called one who speaks at the right time, one who speaks the truth, one who speaks what is beneficial, one who speaks the Dhamma, and one who speaks the Vinaya.

Monks, for such a person, the evil, unwholesome states born of greed have been abandoned, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, obliterated, so that they are no longer subject to future arising. He dwells happily in this very life, without distress, without despair, without fever. In this very life, he attains Nibbāna.

Those born of hatred... (as above) ...he attains Nibbāna. Those born of delusion... (as above) ...he attains Nibbāna. Monks, suppose three Māluva creepers were to overspread, entwine, and envelop a Sāla tree, a Dhava tree, or a Phandana tree. Then a man would come along with a hoe and a basket. He would cut the Māluva creeper at the root. Having cut it at the root, he would dig it up. Having dug it up, he would pull out the roots, even the fine rootlets the size of usīra-grass. He would cut the Māluva creeper into pieces. Having cut it into pieces, he would split them. Having split them, he would make them into splinters. Having made them into splinters, he would dry them in the wind and sun. Having dried them in the wind and sun, he would burn them with fire. Having burned them with fire, he would make them into ashes. Having made them into ashes, he would winnow them in a strong wind or let them be carried away by a swift-flowing river. Monks, in this way, those Māluva creepers would be cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, obliterated, so that they are no longer subject to future arising.

In the same way, monks, for such a person, the evil, unwholesome states born of greed have been abandoned, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, obliterated, so that they are no longer subject to future arising. He dwells happily in this very life, without distress, without despair, without fever. In this very life, he attains Nibbāna.

Those born of hatred... (as above) ...The evil, unwholesome states born of delusion have been abandoned, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, obliterated, so that they are no longer subject to future arising. He dwells happily in this very life, without distress, without despair, without fever. In this very life, he attains Nibbāna. Monks, these are the three roots of the wholesome.” (He said).
206:
Ninth Sutta.

## 10. Uposatha Sutta

71. Thus have I heard— At one time the Blessed One was staying in Sāvatthī at the Eastern Monastery, the palace of Visākhā, Migāra’s mother. Then, on that Uposatha day, Visākhā, Migāra’s mother, approached the Blessed One. Having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, she sat down at one side. As she was sitting there, the Blessed One said to Visākhā, Migāra’s mother: “Now then, Visākhā, from where do you come in the middle of the day?”

“Venerable Sir, today is the Uposatha day; I am observing the Uposatha.”

“Visākhā, there are these three kinds of Uposatha. What three? The Herdsman’s Uposatha (Gopālaka Uposatha), the Nigaṇṭha’s Uposatha, and the Noble Uposatha (Ariya Uposatha).

And how, Visākhā, is the Herdsman’s Uposatha? Just as, Visākhā, a herdsman, having returned the cattle to their owners in the evening, reflects: ‘Today the cattle grazed in such and such a place and drank water in such and such a place; tomorrow the cattle will graze in such and such a place and drink water in such and such a place.’ In the same way, Visākhā, some person here observing the Uposatha reflects: ‘Today I ate such and such hard food and such and such soft food; tomorrow I will eat such and such hard food and such and such soft food.’ He spends the day with a mind accompanied by that covetousness (abhijjhā). Such, Visākhā, is the Herdsman’s Uposatha. Visākhā, the Herdsman’s Uposatha observed in this way is not of great fruit, not of great benefit, not of great brilliance, and not of great radiance. (1)

And how, Visākhā, is the Nigaṇṭha’s Uposatha? Visākhā, there are ascetics called Nigaṇṭhas. They encourage their disciples thus: ‘Come, good man, lay down the weapon regarding all beings beyond a hundred yojanas to the east; lay down the weapon regarding all beings beyond a hundred yojanas to the west; lay down the weapon regarding all beings beyond a hundred yojanas to the north; lay down the weapon regarding all beings beyond a hundred yojanas to the south.’ Thus, they encourage compassion and protection for some beings, but they do not encourage compassion and protection for other beings. On the Uposatha day, they encourage their disciples thus: ‘Come, good man, take off all your clothes and say this: “I have no concern for anyone or anything in any place, and there is no concern for me by anyone or anything in any place.”’ Even though they encourage them in this way, his parents still know, ‘This is our son,’ and he also knows, ‘These are my parents.’ His wife and children also know, ‘This is our provider and husband,’ and he also knows, ‘These are my wife and children.’
207:
His slaves, workers, and men also know, ‘This is our master,’ and he also knows, ‘These are my slaves, workers, and men.’ Thus, at the very time when they should be encouraged in truth, they are encouraged in falsehood. I call this his ‘false speech.’ After that night has passed, he enjoys possessions that were not given to him. I call this his ‘taking what is not given.’ Such, Visākhā, is the Nigaṇṭha’s Uposatha. Visākhā, the Nigaṇṭha’s Uposatha observed in this way is not of great fruit, not of great benefit, not of great brilliance, and not of great radiance. (2)

And how, Visākhā, is the Noble Uposatha (Ariya Uposatha)? Visākhā, it is the cleansing of a defiled mind through effort. And how, Visākhā, is a defiled mind cleansed through effort? Here, Visākhā, a noble disciple recollects the qualities of the Tathāgata: ‘That Blessed One is an Arahat, perfectly enlightened, accomplished in true knowledge and conduct, fortunate, knower of the world, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of devas and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One.’ As he recollects the qualities of the Tathāgata, his mind becomes clear, joy arises, and the defilements of the mind are abandoned. Visākhā, it is just like the cleansing of a dirty head through effort.

And how, Visākhā, is a dirty head cleansed through effort? It is cleansed by means of cleansing paste, clay, water, and the appropriate effort of a person. Such, Visākhā, is the cleansing of a dirty head through effort. In the same way, Visākhā, a defiled mind is cleansed through effort.

And how, Visākhā, is a defiled mind cleansed through effort? Here, Visākhā, a noble disciple recollects the qualities of the Tathāgata: ‘That Blessed One is an Arahat, perfectly enlightened,
208:
"He is called 'Vijjācaraṇasampanno' because he is accomplished in knowledge and conduct; he is called 'Sugato' because he has gone well; he is called 'Lokavidū' because he is the knower of the worlds; he is called 'Anuttaro purisadammasārathi' because he is the incomparable leader of persons to be tamed; he is called 'Satthā devamanussānaṃ' because he is the teacher of gods and humans; he is called 'Buddho' because he is the Awakened One (who knows the Four Noble Truths); he is called 'Bhagavā' because he is the Blessed One." (Thus he repeatedly recollects the qualities of the Buddha). As he repeatedly recollects the qualities of the Buddha, his mind becomes clear, joy arises, and the defilements that corrupt the mind are abandoned. Visākhā, this noble disciple is said to be observing the Brahma-Uposatha, dwelling with the Buddha; by taking the Buddha as the object, his mind becomes clear, joy arises, and the defilements that corrupt the mind are abandoned. In this way, Visākhā, a corrupted mind is purified through effort. (3-a)

Visākhā, a corrupted mind is purified through effort. And how, Visākhā, is a corrupted mind purified through effort? Here, Visākhā, a noble disciple repeatedly recollects the qualities of the Dhamma: "The Dhamma is well-expounded by the Blessed One, visible here and now, timeless, inviting one to come and see, leading onward, to be personally realized by the wise." He repeatedly recollects the qualities of the Dhamma. As he repeatedly recollects the qualities of the Dhamma, his mind becomes clear, joy arises, and the defilements that corrupt the mind are abandoned. Just as, Visākhā, a soiled body is purified through effort.

And how, Visākhā, is a soiled body purified through effort? It is purified by means of a scouring stone, powder, water, and the appropriate effort of a person. In this way, Visākhā, a soiled body is purified through effort. Even so, Visākhā, how is a corrupted mind purified through effort? Here, Visākhā, a noble disciple repeatedly recollects the qualities of the Dhamma: "The Dhamma is well-expounded by the Blessed One, visible here and now, timeless, inviting one to come and see, leading onward, to be personally realized by the wise." He repeatedly recollects the qualities of the Dhamma.
209:
As he repeatedly recollects the qualities of the Dhamma, his mind becomes clear, joy arises, and the defilements that corrupt the mind are abandoned. Visākhā, this noble disciple is said to be observing the Dhamma-Uposatha, dwelling with the Dhamma; by taking the Dhamma as the object, his mind becomes clear, joy arises, and the defilements that corrupt the mind are abandoned. In this way, Visākhā, a corrupted mind is purified through effort. (3-b)

Visākhā, a corrupted mind is purified through effort. And how, Visākhā, is a corrupted mind purified through effort? Here, Visākhā, a noble disciple repeatedly recollects the qualities of the Saṅgha: "The Saṅgha of the Blessed One's disciples is practicing well; the Saṅgha of the Blessed One's disciples is practicing uprightly; the Saṅgha of the Blessed One's disciples is practicing correctly; the Saṅgha of the Blessed One's disciples is practicing properly. This Saṅgha of the Blessed One's disciples—consisting of the four pairs of persons, the eight individual persons—is worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, the unsurpassed field of merit for the world." Thus he repeatedly recollects the qualities of the Saṅgha. As he repeatedly recollects the qualities of the Saṅgha, his mind becomes clear, joy arises, and the defilements that corrupt the mind are abandoned. Just as, Visākhā, a soiled garment is purified through effort.

And how, Visākhā, is a soiled garment purified through effort? It is purified by means of heat, alkali, cow dung, water, and the appropriate effort of a person. In this way, Visākhā, a soiled garment is purified through effort. Even so, Visākhā, a corrupted mind is purified through effort. And how, Visākhā, is a corrupted mind purified through effort? Here, Visākhā, a noble disciple repeatedly recollects the qualities of the Saṅgha: "The Saṅgha of the Blessed One's disciples is practicing well; the Saṅgha of the Blessed One's disciples is practicing uprightly; the Saṅgha of the Blessed One's disciples is practicing correctly; the Saṅgha of the Blessed One's disciples is practicing properly. This Saṅgha of the Blessed One's disciples—consisting of the four pairs of persons, the eight individual persons—is worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation..."
210:
“The Saṅgha is the incomparable field of merit for the world”—thus he repeatedly recollects the qualities of the Saṅgha. As he repeatedly recollects the qualities of the Saṅgha, his mind becomes clear, joy arises, and the defilements of the mind are abandoned. Visākhā, this noble disciple is called one who observes the Saṅgha-uposatha, who dwells with the Saṅgha, and whose mind is cleared, joy arises, and defilements are abandoned by focusing on the Saṅgha. Visākhā, in this way, a soiled mind is cleansed by effort. (3-c)

Visākhā, a soiled mind is cleansed by effort. And how, Visākhā, is a soiled mind cleansed by effort? Here, Visākhā, a noble disciple repeatedly recollects his own virtues—virtues that are unbroken, untorn, unblemished, unmottled, freeing (from the slavery of craving), praised by the wise, ungrasped, and leading to concentration. As he repeatedly recollects them, his mind becomes clear, joy arises, and the defilements of the mind are abandoned. Just as, Visākhā, a soiled mirror is cleansed by effort.

And how, Visākhā, is a soiled mirror cleansed by effort? It is cleansed by means of oil, ash, a brush, and the appropriate effort of a person. In this way, Visākhā, a soiled mirror is cleansed by effort. Even so, Visākhā, a soiled mind is cleansed by effort. And how, Visākhā, is a soiled mind cleansed by effort? Here, Visākhā, a noble disciple repeatedly recollects his own virtues—virtues that are unbroken, untorn, unblemished, unmottled, freeing, praised by the wise, ungrasped, and leading to concentration. As he repeatedly recollects his virtues, his mind becomes clear, joy arises, and the defilements of the mind are abandoned. Visākhā, this noble disciple is called one who observes the Sīla-uposatha, who dwells with virtue, and whose mind is cleared, joy arises, and defilements are abandoned by focusing on virtue. Visākhā, in this way, a soiled mind is cleansed by effort. (3-d)

Visākhā, a soiled mind is cleansed by effort. And how, Visākhā, is a soiled mind cleansed by effort? Here, Visākhā, a noble disciple repeatedly recollects the deities (taking them as witnesses to his own qualities such as faith): “There are the Devas of the Four Great Kings, the Devas of the Thirty-three, the Yāma Devas, the Tusita Devas, the Devas who Delight in Creation, the Devas who Wield Power over Others' Creations, the Devas of the Brahma-group, and Devas beyond these. Such faith as those deities possessed, because of which they passed away from here and were reborn there, such faith is also found in me. Such virtue as those deities possessed, because of which they passed away from here and were reborn there, such virtue is also found in me. Such learning as those deities possessed, because of which they passed away from here and were reborn there, such learning is also found in me. Such generosity as those deities possessed, because of which they passed away from here and were reborn there, such generosity is also found in me.”
211:
“Such generosity is also found in me. Such wisdom as those deities possessed, because of which they passed away from here and were reborn there, such wisdom is also found in me.” As he repeatedly recollects the faith, virtue, learning, generosity, and wisdom of both himself and those deities, his mind becomes clear, joy arises, and the defilements of the mind are abandoned. Just as, Visākhā, soiled gold or silver is cleansed by effort.

And how, Visākhā, is soiled gold or silver cleansed by effort? It is cleansed by means of a crucible, salt, red chalk, a blowpipe and tongs, and the appropriate effort of a person. In this way, Visākhā, soiled gold or silver is cleansed by effort. Even so, Visākhā, a soiled mind is cleansed by effort. And how, Visākhā, is a soiled mind cleansed by effort? Here, Visākhā, a noble disciple repeatedly recollects the deities (taking them as witnesses): “There are the Devas of the Four Great Kings, the Devas of the Thirty-three, the Yāma Devas, the Tusita Devas, the Devas who Delight in Creation, the Devas who Wield Power over Others' Creations, the Devas of the Brahma-group, and Devas beyond these. Such faith as those deities possessed, because of which they passed away from here and were reborn there, such faith is also found in me. Such virtue... such learning... such generosity... such wisdom as those deities possessed, because of which they passed away from here and were reborn there, such wisdom is also found in me.” As he repeatedly recollects the faith, virtue (sīla), learning (suta), generosity (cāga), and wisdom (paññā) of both himself and those deities, his mind becomes clear, joy arises, and the defilements of the mind are abandoned. Visākhā, this noble disciple is called one who observes the Devatā-uposatha, who dwells with the deities, and whose mind is cleared, joy arises, and defilements are abandoned by focusing on the deities (taking them as witnesses to his own qualities such as faith). Visākhā, in this way, a soiled mind is cleansed by effort. (3-e)

Visākhā, that noble disciple reflects thus: “For as long as they live, the Arahants, having abandoned the destruction of life, abstain from the destruction of life. They have laid aside the rod and the sword. They are conscientious, merciful, and dwell compassionate for the welfare of all living beings.”
212:
Today, I too, for this night and this day, having abandoned the destruction of life, dwell refraining from the destruction of life, with stick laid down, with weapon laid down, conscientious, compassionate, and desiring the welfare of all living beings. By this factor, I imitate the Arahants, and the Uposatha will be observed by me.

For as long as they live, the Arahants, having abandoned the taking of what is not given, refrain from taking what is not given; they take only what is given, expect only what is given, and dwell with a self that is pure and not thieving. Today, I too, for this night and this day, having abandoned the taking of what is not given, refrain from taking what is not given; being one who takes only what is given, expecting only what is given, I shall dwell with a self that is pure and not thieving. By this factor, I imitate the Arahants, and the Uposatha will be observed by me.

For as long as they live, the Arahants, having abandoned unchaste conduct, lead a chaste life, living apart, refraining from the sexual act which is the practice of villagers. Today, I too, for this night and this day, having abandoned unchaste conduct, shall lead a chaste life, living far apart from unchaste conduct, and refrain from the sexual act which is the practice of villagers. By this factor, I imitate the Arahants, and the Uposatha will be observed by me.

For as long as they live, the Arahants, having abandoned false speech, refrain from false speech; they speak the truth, are bound to the truth, are firm in speech, are trustworthy, and are not deceivers of the world. Today, I too, for this night and this day, having abandoned false speech, refrain from false speech; speaking only the truth, being bound to the truth, being firm in speech, being trustworthy, I shall dwell without deceiving the world. By this factor, I imitate the Arahants, and the Uposatha will be observed by me.

For as long as they live, the Arahants, having abandoned the use of wine, liquor, and intoxicants which cause heedlessness, refrain from the use of wine, liquor, and intoxicants which cause heedlessness. Today, I too, for this night and this day, having abandoned the use of wine, liquor, and intoxicants which cause heedlessness, shall refrain from the use of wine, liquor, and intoxicants which cause heedlessness. By this factor, I imitate the Arahants, and the Uposatha will be observed by me.

For as long as they live, the Arahants eat only one meal a day, refraining from eating at night, refraining from eating at the wrong time.
213:
refraining from eating at the wrong time. Today, I too, for this night and this day, shall eat only one meal, refraining from eating at night, and refraining from eating at the wrong time. By this factor, I imitate the Arahants, and the Uposatha will be observed by me.

For as long as they live, the Arahants refrain from dancing, singing, music, and witnessing unseemly shows which are thorns (to the Dhamma), and from wearing garlands, using perfumes, and beautifying themselves with ointments. Today, I too, for this night and this day, shall refrain from dancing, singing, music, and witnessing unseemly shows which are thorns (to the Dhamma), and from wearing garlands, using perfumes, and beautifying myself with ointments. By this factor, I imitate the Arahants, and the Uposatha will be observed by me.

For as long as they live, the Arahants, having abandoned high and large beds, refrain from high and large beds; they sleep on low beds, either on a small couch or a straw mat. Today, I too, for this night and this day, having abandoned high and large beds, shall refrain from high and large beds, and sleep on a low bed, either on a small couch or a straw mat. By this factor, I imitate the Arahants, and the Uposatha will be observed by me (thus one reflects).

Visākhā, such is the Noble Uposatha. The Noble Uposatha observed in this way, Visākhā, is of great fruit, great benefit, great splendor, and great pervasiveness. How great is the fruit, how great the benefit, how great the splendor, and how great the pervasiveness? Visākhā, suppose someone were to exercise sovereign power and kingship over these sixteen great nations abounding in many desirable treasures—namely, Aṅga, Magadha, Kāsī, Kosala, Vajjī, Mallā, Cetiya, Vaṅga, Kuru, Pañcāla, Maccha, Sūrasena, Assaka, Avanti, Gandhāra, and Kamboja—this is not worth even a sixteenth part of the Uposatha endowed with eight factors. For what reason? Visākhā, human kingship is insignificant compared to celestial happiness.

Visākhā, fifty human years are but a single night and day for the Cātumahārājikā devas. Thirty such nights make a month. Twelve such months make a year.
214:
By that year, five hundred celestial years is the lifespan of the devas of the Realm of the Four Great Kings. Visākhā, it is possible that some woman or man, having observed the Uposatha endowed with eight factors, after the breaking up of the body, after death, may be reborn in the company of the devas of the Realm of the Four Great Kings. Visākhā, it was with reference to this that it was said: 'Miserable is human kingship compared to celestial happiness.'

Visākhā, one hundred human years are but a single day and night for the Tāvatiṃsa devas; thirty such nights make a month; twelve such months make a year; by that year, one thousand celestial years is the lifespan of the Tāvatiṃsa devas. Visākhā, it is possible that some woman or man, having observed the Uposatha endowed with eight factors, after the breaking up of the body, after death, may be reborn in the company of the Tāvatiṃsa devas. Visākhā, it was with reference to this that it was said: 'Miserable is human kingship compared to celestial happiness.'

Visākhā, two hundred human years are but a single day and night for the Yāma devas; thirty such nights make a month; twelve such months make a year; by that year, two thousand celestial years is the lifespan of the Yāma devas. Visākhā, it is possible that some woman or man, having observed the Uposatha endowed with eight factors, after the breaking up of the body, after death, may be reborn in the company of the Yāma devas. Visākhā, it was with reference to this that it was said: 'Miserable is human kingship compared to celestial happiness.'

Visākhā, four hundred human years are but a single day and night for the Tusita devas; thirty such nights make a month; twelve such months make a year; by that year, four thousand celestial years is the lifespan of the Tusita devas. Visākhā, it is possible that some woman or man, having observed the Uposatha endowed with eight factors, after the breaking up of the body, after death, may be reborn in the company of the Tusita devas. Visākhā, it was with reference to this that it was said: 'Miserable is human kingship compared to celestial happiness.'

Visākhā, eight hundred human years are but a single day and night for the Nimmānarati devas; thirty such nights make a month; twelve such months make a year; by that year, eight thousand celestial years is the lifespan of the Nimmānarati devas. Visākhā, it is possible that some woman or man, having observed the Uposatha endowed with eight factors, after the breaking up of the body, after death, may be reborn in the company of the Nimmānarati devas.
215:
Visākhā, it was with reference to this that it was said: 'Miserable is human kingship compared to celestial happiness.'

Visākhā, sixteen hundred human years are but a single day and night for the Paranimmita-vasavatti devas; thirty such nights make a month; twelve such months make a year; by that year, sixteen thousand celestial years is the lifespan of the Paranimmita-vasavatti devas. Visākhā, it is possible that some woman or man, having observed the Uposatha endowed with eight factors, after the breaking up of the body, after death, may be reborn in the company of the Paranimmita-vasavatti devas. Visākhā, it was with reference to this that it was said: 'Miserable is human kingship compared to celestial happiness.'

(The Uposatha observer) should not kill living beings, nor take what is not given, nor speak falsely, nor be a drinker of intoxicants. One should abstain from unchaste conduct, from sexual intercourse. One should not eat at night, at the wrong time. One should not wear garlands or use perfumes. One should sleep on a couch, or on the ground, or on a grass mat. This is called the eight-factored Uposatha, proclaimed by the Buddha who has reached the end of suffering. The sun and moon, both beautiful to see, wandering as far as they illuminate, those dispellers of darkness, moving through the sky, shine in the heavens, brightening the quarters.
216:
Whatever wealth exists within the reach of the sun and moon—pearls, gems, beryl, auspicious stones, singī gold, kañcana gold, or the gold found in its natural state called haṭaka gold—all these are not worth a sixteenth part of the Uposatha endowed with eight factors, just as the light of all the stars is not worth a sixteenth part of the moonlight. Therefore, a virtuous woman or man should observe the Uposatha endowed with eight factors. Having performed meritorious deeds that result in happiness, they go to the heavenly realm, free from blame.

The Tenth Sutta.
The Second Great Chapter (Mahāvagga) is finished.
1. Meaning: Do not oppress or kill living beings.

## (8) 3-Ānanda-vagga
## 1-Channa Sutta

72. At one time the Blessed One was staying at Sāvatthī in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's monastery. Then Channa the Wanderer approached the Venerable Ānanda and exchanged greetings with him. When they had concluded their greetings and cordial talk, he sat down to one side. Sitting there, Channa the Wanderer said to the Venerable Ānanda: "Friend Ānanda, do you also prescribe the abandonment of lust, the abandonment of hatred, and the abandonment of delusion?" "Friend Channa, we do prescribe the abandonment of lust, the abandonment of hatred, and the abandonment of delusion."

"Friend Ānanda, seeing what danger in lust do you prescribe its abandonment? Seeing what danger in hatred do you prescribe its abandonment? Seeing what danger in delusion do you prescribe its abandonment?"

"Friend Channa, a person who is lustful, being overcome and obsessed by lust, intends for his own affliction, intends for the affliction of others, and intends for the affliction of both..."
217:
One also experiences mental suffering and grief born of the mind. When lust is abandoned, one does not intend for one's own harm, nor for the harm of others, nor for the harm of both; one does not experience mental suffering and grief born of the mind. Friend Channa, a person who is lustful, being overcome and his mind obsessed by lust, commits misconduct by body, commits misconduct by speech, and commits misconduct by mind. When lust is abandoned, he does not commit misconduct by body, speech, or mind. Friend Channa, a person who is lustful, being overcome and his mind obsessed by lust, does not understand his own welfare as it really is, does not understand the welfare of others as it really is, and does not understand the welfare of both as it really is. When lust is abandoned, he understands his own welfare as it really is, understands the welfare of others as it really is, and understands the welfare of both as it really is. Friend Channa, lust causes blindness, causes lack of vision, causes lack of knowledge, destroys wisdom, is on the side of distress, and does not lead to Nibbāna.

Friend Channa, a person who is hateful, being overcome by hatred... [Pe]... Friend Channa, a person who is deluded, being overcome and his mind obsessed by delusion, intends for his own harm, intends for the harm of others, and intends for the harm of both; he also experiences mental suffering and grief born of the mind. When delusion is abandoned, he does not intend for his own harm, nor for the harm of others, nor for the harm of both; he does not experience mental suffering and grief born of the mind. Friend Channa, a person who is deluded, being overcome and his mind obsessed by delusion, commits misconduct by body, commits misconduct by speech, and commits misconduct by mind. When delusion is abandoned, he does not commit misconduct by body, speech, or mind. Friend Channa, a person who is deluded, being overcome and his mind obsessed by delusion, does not understand his own welfare as it really is, does not understand the welfare of others as it really is, and does not understand the welfare of both as it really is. When delusion is abandoned, he understands his own welfare as it really is, understands the welfare of others as it really is, and understands the welfare of both as it really is. Friend Channa, delusion causes blindness, causes lack of vision, causes lack of knowledge, destroys wisdom, is on the side of distress, and does not lead to Nibbāna. Friend Channa, seeing this danger in lust, we prescribe the abandoning of lust,
218:
Seeing this danger in hatred, we prescribe the abandoning of hatred. Seeing this danger in delusion, we prescribe the abandoning of delusion.

'But friend (Ānanda), is there a path, is there a way for the abandoning of this lust, hatred, and delusion?'

'There is, friend Channa, a path, there is a way for the abandoning of this lust, hatred, and delusion.' 'And what, friend Ānanda, is that path, what is that way for the abandoning of this lust, hatred, and delusion?' 'It is this Noble Eightfold Path itself, namely: Right View (Sammā-diṭṭhi), Right Thought (Sammā-saṅkappa), Right Speech (Sammā-vācā), Right Action (Sammā-kammanta), Right Livelihood (Sammā-ājīva), Right Effort (Sammā-vāyāma), Right Mindfulness (Sammā-sati), and Right Concentration (Sammā-samādhi). This, friend (Channa), is the path, this is the way for the abandoning of this lust, hatred, and delusion.' 'Friend Ānanda, the path is excellent, the way is excellent for the abandoning of this lust, hatred, and delusion. And friend Ānanda, it is fitting to be diligent.'

The First Sutta.

## 2. Ājīvaka Sutta

73. At one time, the Venerable Ānanda was staying at Kosambī in Ghosita’s Monastery. Then a certain householder, a disciple of the Ājīvakas, approached the Venerable Ānanda, paid homage to him, and sat down to one side. Sitting there, that householder, the disciple of the Ājīvakas, said to the Venerable Ānanda: "Venerable Ānanda, whose Dhamma is well-expounded? Who in the world are practicing well? Who in the world have fared well?"

"In that case, householder, I will question you in return on this matter. Answer as you see fit. What do you think, householder? Those who teach the Dhamma for the abandoning of lust, for the abandoning of hatred, and for the abandoning of delusion—is their Dhamma well-expounded or not? Or how does it appear to you in this matter?" "Venerable sir, those who teach the Dhamma for the abandoning of lust, for the abandoning of hatred, and for the abandoning of delusion—their Dhamma is well-expounded. This is how it appears to me in this matter."

"What do you think, householder? Those who are practicing for the abandoning of lust, for the abandoning of hatred, and for the abandoning of delusion—are they practicing well in the world or not? Or how does it appear to you in this matter?" "Venerable sir, those who are practicing for the abandoning of lust, for the abandoning of hatred, and for the abandoning of delusion—they are practicing well in the world. This is how it appears to me in this matter."
219:
"Householder, what do you think? Those who have abandoned lust, cut it off at the root, made it like a palm stump, done away with it so that it is no longer subject to future arising; those who have abandoned hatred, cut it off at the root, made it like a palm stump, done away with it so that it is no longer subject to future arising; those who have abandoned delusion, cut it off at the root, made it like a palm stump, done away with it so that it is no longer subject to future arising—are they those who have done well in the world, or not? What is your view on this?"

"Venerable sir, those who have abandoned lust, cut it off at the root, made it like a palm stump, done away with it so that it is no longer subject to future arising; those who have abandoned hatred... (as above)... those who have abandoned delusion, cut it off at the root, made it like a palm stump, done away with it so that it is no longer subject to future arising—they are those who have done well in the world. This is my view on this."

"Householder, thus you have answered: 'Venerable sir, those who teach the Dhamma for the abandoning of lust, for the abandoning of hatred, for the abandoning of delusion—their Dhamma is well-expounded.' You have answered: 'Venerable sir, those who practice for the abandoning of lust, for the abandoning of hatred, for the abandoning of delusion—they are well-practiced in the world.' You have answered: 'Venerable sir, those for whom lust is abandoned, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, done away with, no longer subject to future arising; those for whom hatred... (as above)... those for whom delusion is abandoned, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, done away with, no longer subject to future arising—they are those who have done well in the world.'"

"It is wonderful, venerable sir! It is marvelous, venerable sir! There is no extolling of one's own doctrine, nor disparaging of another's doctrine. The Dhamma is taught only in its proper scope; the meaning is stated, and the self is not uplifted. Venerable Ānanda, you teach the Dhamma for the abandoning of lust, for the abandoning of hatred, for the abandoning of delusion. Venerable Ānanda, your Dhamma is well-expounded. Venerable Ānanda, you practice for the abandoning of lust, for the abandoning of hatred, for the abandoning of delusion. Venerable Ānanda, you are well-practiced in the world. Venerable Ānanda, you have abandoned lust in the world..."
220:
"...cut it off at the root, made it like a palm stump, done away with it so that it is no longer subject to future arising. Venerable sir, you have abandoned hatred... (as above)... you have abandoned delusion, cut it off at the root, made it like a palm stump, done away with it so that it is no longer subject to future arising. You are those who have done well in the world."

"Excellent, venerable sir! Excellent, venerable sir! Just as if, venerable sir, one were to set upright what had been overturned, or to reveal what had been hidden, or to show the way to one who was lost, or to hold up a lamp in the dark so that those with eyes could see forms—even so has the Dhamma been clarified in many ways by the venerable Ānanda. Venerable Ānanda, I go to the Blessed One for refuge, to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha of monks. May the venerable Ānanda accept me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge from this day forward for as long as life lasts."

The Second Sutta.

## 3. Mahānāmasakka Sutta

74. Thus have I heard: At one time the Blessed One was staying among the Sakyans at Kapilavatthu in Nigrodha’s Park. At that time the Blessed One had recently recovered from an illness. Then Mahānāma the Sakyan approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, and sat down to one side. Sitting there, Mahānāma the Sakyan said to the Blessed One: "Venerable sir, for a long time I have understood the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One thus: 'Knowledge is for one who is concentrated, not for one who is unconcentrated.' Venerable sir, does concentration come first and knowledge afterwards, or does knowledge come first and concentration afterwards?"

Then the venerable Ānanda thought: "The Blessed One has recently recovered from an illness. This Mahānāma the Sakyan is asking the Blessed One a very deep question. What if I were to take Mahānāma the Sakyan aside and teach him the Dhamma?"

Then the venerable Ānanda took Mahānāma the Sakyan by the arm, led him aside, and said to him: "Mahānāma, the Blessed One has spoken of the virtue of a trainee (sekha) and the virtue of one beyond training (asekha). The Blessed One has spoken of the concentration of a trainee and the concentration of one beyond training. The Blessed One has spoken of the wisdom of a trainee and the wisdom of one beyond training."
221:
“Mahānāma, what is the virtue of a trainee (sekha)? Here, Mahānāma, a monk is virtuous; he dwells restrained by the restraint of the Pātimokkha... [etc.] ...he trains in the training rules he has undertaken. This, Mahānāma, is called the virtue of a trainee.

“And what, Mahānāma, is the concentration of a trainee? Here, Mahānāma, a monk, secluded from sensual pleasures... [etc.] ...enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna. This, Mahānāma, is called the concentration of a trainee.

“And what, Mahānāma, is the wisdom of a trainee? Here, Mahānāma, a monk understands as it really is: ‘This is suffering’... [etc.] ...he understands as it really is: ‘This is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering.’ This, Mahānāma, is called the wisdom of a trainee.

“Mahānāma, that noble disciple, being thus possessed of virtue, thus possessed of concentration, and thus possessed of wisdom, through the destruction of the taints, enters and dwells in the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, having realized it for himself by direct knowledge in this very life. Thus, Mahānāma, the virtue of a trainee has been spoken of by the Blessed One, and the virtue of one beyond training (asekha) has also been spoken of by the Blessed One; the concentration of a trainee has been spoken of by the Blessed One, and the concentration of one beyond training has also been spoken of by the Blessed One; the wisdom of a trainee has been spoken of by the Blessed One, and the wisdom of one beyond training has also been spoken of by the Blessed One.”

The Third Sutta.

## 4. Nigaṇṭha Sutta

75. On one occasion the Venerable Ānanda was dwelling at Vesālī in the Great Wood in the Hall with the Peaked Roof. Then Abhaya the Licchavi and Paṇḍitakumāraka the Licchavi approached the Venerable Ānanda, paid homage to him, and sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, Abhaya the Licchavi said to the Venerable Ānanda:

“Venerable sir, the Nigaṇṭha Nāṭaputta claims to be all-knowing and all-seeing, professing to have complete knowledge and vision, saying: ‘Whether I am walking, standing, sleeping, or awake, knowledge and vision are constantly and continuously present to me.’ He prescribes the wearing away of old kammas through asceticism and the non-doing of new kammas as a bridge-destruction. Thus, with the exhaustion of kamma, there is the exhaustion of suffering; with the exhaustion of suffering, there is the exhaustion of feeling; and with the exhaustion of feeling, all suffering will be worn away. He teaches that by this purification through wearing away (nijjara), which is visible here and now, one transcends [the round of suffering].”
222:
“Venerable sir, what does the Blessed One say regarding this?”

“Abhaya, these three purifications through wearing away have been well-proclaimed by that Blessed One who knows and sees, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One, for the purification of beings, for the overcoming of sorrow and lamentation, for the disappearance of pain and grief, for the attainment of the true way, and for the realization of Nibbāna. What are the three?

“Here, Abhaya, a monk is virtuous... [etc.] ...he trains in the training rules he has undertaken. He does not perform new kamma, and he wears away old kamma by experiencing it again and again. This purification through wearing away is visible here and now, timeless, inviting one to come and see, onward-leading, to be experienced by the wise for themselves.

“Abhaya, that monk, being thus possessed of virtue, secluded from sensual pleasures... [etc.] ...enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna. He does not perform new kamma, and he wears away old kamma by experiencing it again and again. This purification through wearing away is visible here and now, timeless, inviting one to come and see, onward-leading, to be experienced by the wise for themselves.

“Abhaya, that monk, being thus possessed of concentration, through the destruction of the taints, enters and dwells in the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, having realized it for himself by direct knowledge in this very life. He does not perform new kamma, and he wears away old kamma by experiencing it again and again. This purification through wearing away is visible here and now, timeless, inviting one to come and see, onward-leading, to be experienced by the wise for themselves. These, Abhaya, are the three purifications through wearing away well-proclaimed by that Blessed One who knows and sees, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One, for the purification of beings, for the overcoming of sorrow and lamentation, for the disappearance of pain and grief, for the attainment of the true way, and for the realization of Nibbāna.”

When this was said, Paṇḍitakumāraka the Licchavi said to Abhaya the Licchavi: “Friend Abhaya, why do you not applaud the well-spoken words of the Venerable Ānanda as well-spoken?”

“Friend Paṇḍitakumāraka, how could I not applaud the well-spoken words of the Venerable Ānanda as well-spoken? The head of anyone who would not applaud the well-spoken words of the Venerable Ānanda as well-spoken would surely fall off.”

The Fourth Sutta.
223:
Fourth Sutta.

## 5. Nivesaka Sutta

76. Then, the Venerable Ānanda approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, and sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, the Blessed One said to him:

“Ānanda, those whom you have compassion for, and those who think they should listen—whether friends, colleagues, relatives, or kinsmen—should be exhorted, settled, and established in three things. In which three?

They should be exhorted, settled, and established in unwavering faith in the Buddha: ‘The Blessed One is an Arahant, a Perfectly Enlightened One, accomplished in true knowledge and conduct, fortunate, knower of the world, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of devas and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One.’

They should be exhorted, settled, and established in unwavering faith in the Dhamma: ‘The Dhamma is well-expounded by the Blessed One, directly visible, immediate, inviting one to come and see, applicable, to be personally experienced by the wise.’

They should be exhorted, settled, and established in unwavering faith in the Saṅgha: ‘The Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is practicing well, the Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is practicing uprightly, the Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is practicing methodically, the Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is practicing properly. This Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples—consisting of the four pairs of persons, the eight individuals—is worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, the unsurpassed field of merit for the world.’

“Ānanda, there might be change in the four great elements—the earth element, the water element, the fire element, or the air element—but there could never be change in a noble disciple endowed with unwavering faith in the Buddha. Herein, this is the meaning of ‘change’: Ānanda, it is impossible that a noble disciple endowed with unwavering faith in the Buddha would be reborn in hell, the animal realm, or the realm of hungry ghosts.

“Ānanda, there might be change in the four great elements—the earth element, the water element, the fire element, or the air element—but there could never be change in a noble disciple endowed with unwavering faith in the Dhamma... (as above) ...but there could never be change in a noble disciple endowed with unwavering faith in the Saṅgha. Herein, this is the meaning of ‘change’: Ānanda, a noble disciple endowed with unwavering faith in the Saṅgha..."
224:
Herein, this is the meaning of ‘change’: Ānanda, it is impossible that a noble disciple endowed with unwavering faith in the Saṅgha would be reborn in hell, the animal realm, or the realm of hungry ghosts.

“Ānanda, those whom you have compassion for, and those who think they should listen—whether friends, colleagues, relatives, or kinsmen—should be exhorted, settled, and established in these three things.”

Fifth Sutta.

## 6. Paṭhama Bhava Sutta

77. Then, the Venerable Ānanda approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, sat down to one side, and said to the Blessed One: “Venerable Sir, it is said, ‘existence, existence’ (bhava). To what extent, Venerable Sir, is there existence?”

“Ānanda, if there were no kamma ripening in the sensual realm (kāmadhātu), would sensual existence (kāmabhava) be manifested?” “No, Venerable Sir.” “Thus, Ānanda, kamma is the field, consciousness is the seed, and craving is the moisture. For beings hindered by ignorance and fettered by craving, consciousness is established in the lower realm. Thus, there is the production of renewed existence in the future.

“Ānanda, if there were no kamma ripening in the fine-material realm (rūpadhātu), would fine-material existence (rūpabhava) be manifested?” “No, Venerable Sir.” “Thus, Ānanda, kamma is the field, consciousness is the seed, and craving is the moisture. For beings hindered by ignorance and fettered by craving, consciousness is established in the middle realm. Thus, there is the production of renewed existence in the future.

“Ānanda, if there were no kamma ripening in the immaterial realm (arūpadhātu), would immaterial existence (arūpabhava) be manifested?” “No, Venerable Sir.” “Thus, Ānanda, kamma is the field, consciousness is the seed, and craving is the moisture. For beings hindered by ignorance and fettered by craving, consciousness is established in the superior realm. Thus, there is the production of renewed existence in the future. In this way, Ānanda, there is existence.”

Sixth Sutta.
225:
Sixth Sutta.
## 7. Dutiya Bhava Sutta
78. Then the Venerable Ānanda approached the Blessed One... [and] said to the Blessed One: "Venerable Sir, it is said, 'existence, existence' (bhava). To what extent, Venerable Sir, is there existence?"

"Ānanda, if there were no kamma ripening in the sense-sphere (kāmadhātu), would sense-sphere existence (kāmabhava) be manifested?" "No, Venerable Sir." "Thus, Ānanda, kamma is the field, consciousness (viññāṇa) is the seed, and craving (taṇhā) is the moisture. For beings hindered by ignorance (avijjā) and fettered by craving, intention (cetanā) is established and aspiration (patthanā) is established in the lower element, the sense-sphere (kāmadhātu). Thus, there is the production of renewed existence in the future."

"Ānanda, if there were no kamma ripening in the fine-material sphere (rūpadhātu), would fine-material existence (rūpabhava) be manifested?" "No, Venerable Sir." "Thus, Ānanda, kamma is the field, consciousness is the seed, and craving is the moisture. For beings hindered by ignorance and fettered by craving, intention is established and aspiration is established in the middle element, the fine-material sphere (rūpadhātu). Thus, there is the production of renewed existence in the future."

"Ānanda, if there were no kamma ripening in the immaterial sphere (arūpadhātu), would immaterial existence (arūpabhava) be manifested?" "No, Venerable Sir." "Thus, Ānanda, kamma is the field, consciousness is the seed, and craving is the moisture. For beings hindered by ignorance and fettered by craving, intention is established and aspiration is established in the superior element, the immaterial sphere (arūpadhātu). Thus, there is the production of renewed existence in the future. In this way, Ānanda, there is existence."

Seventh Sutta.
## 8. Sīlabbata Sutta
79. Then the Venerable Ānanda approached the Blessed One, paid homage, and sat to one side. As he was sitting there, the Blessed One said to him: "Ānanda, are all ardent religious observances and vows, the practice of the holy life, and service regarded as the essence—is all that fruitful?" "Venerable Sir, this cannot be answered categorically (ekāṃsena)." "Then, Ānanda, analyze it."

"Venerable Sir, when one follows such ardent religious observances and vows, the practice of the holy life, and service regarded as the essence, and unwholesome states increase while wholesome states decline, such ardent religious observances and vows, the practice of the holy life, and service regarded as the essence are not fruitful."
226:
"Venerable Sir, when one follows such ardent religious observances and vows, the practice of the holy life, and service regarded as the essence, and unwholesome states decline while wholesome states increase, such ardent religious observances and vows, the practice of the holy life, and service regarded as the essence are fruitful." Venerable Ānanda said this, and the Teacher approved.

Then the Venerable Ānanda, [thinking] "The Teacher has approved of my words," rose from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, and keeping him on his right, departed. Soon after Venerable Ānanda had left, the Blessed One addressed the monks: "Monks, Ānanda is a trainee (sekha). However, even though he is a trainee, it is not easy to find one who is his equal in wisdom."

Eighth Sutta.
## 9. Gandhajāta Sutta
80. Then the Venerable Ānanda approached the Blessed One, paid homage, and sat to one side. Sitting there, Venerable Ānanda said to the Blessed One: "Venerable Sir, there are these three kinds of scents whose fragrance goes only with the wind, but not against the wind. What three? The scent of roots, the scent of heartwood, and the scent of flowers. These, Venerable Sir, are the three kinds of scents whose fragrance goes with the wind, but not against the wind. Is there, Venerable Sir, any kind of scent whose fragrance goes with the wind, goes against the wind, and goes both with and against the wind?"

"There is, Ānanda, a kind of scent whose fragrance goes with the wind, goes against the wind, and goes both with and against the wind." "And what, Venerable Sir, is that kind of scent...?"

"Ānanda, here in this world, in whatever village or town, a man or a woman has gone for refuge to the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha; abstains from taking life, from taking what is not given, from sexual misconduct, from false speech, and from the use of intoxicants; is virtuous and of good character; dwells at home with a heart free from the stain of stinginess, is open-handed, with hands washed (ready to give), delighting in giving,"
227:
...is accessible to those who ask, and delights in giving and sharing.

Recluses and brahmins speak of his praise in the four directions: 'In such a village or town, such a man or woman has gone for refuge to the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha. He or she abstains from taking life, from taking what is not given, from sexual misconduct, from false speech, and from the use of intoxicants which cause heedlessness. He or she is virtuous, of good character, and dwells at home with a mind free from the stain of stinginess, being open-handed, delighting in relinquishment, accessible to those who ask, and delighting in giving and sharing.'

Deities also speak of his praise: 'In such a village or town, such a man or woman has gone for refuge to the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha. He or she abstains from taking life... (Pe) ...from the use of intoxicants which cause heedlessness. He or she is virtuous, of good character, and dwells at home with a mind free from the stain of stinginess, being open-handed, delighting in relinquishment, accessible to those who ask, and delighting in giving and sharing.' Ānanda, the kind of fragrance that can go with the wind, against the wind, and in both directions is this very reputation (of being endowed with the refuges, virtue, etc.).

The fragrance of flowers does not go against the wind, nor does the scent of sandalwood, tagara, or jasmine. But the fragrance of the virtuous goes against the wind; the virtuous person pervades all directions with the fragrance of his reputation.

Ninth Sutta.

## 10. Cūḷanikā Sutta

81. Then the Venerable Ānanda approached the Blessed One, paid homage, and sat at one side. Sitting at one side, the Venerable Ānanda said to the Blessed One: "Venerable Sir, I have heard and learned this from the presence of the Blessed One: 'Ānanda, the disciple named Abhibhū of the Blessed One Sikhī, while staying in the Brahma realm, could make his voice heard throughout a thousandfold world system.'"
228: 'Venerable Sir, how far can the Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, make his voice heard?' 'He was a disciple, Ānanda; the Tathāgatas are immeasurable.' For a second time, the Venerable Ānanda said to the Blessed One: 'Venerable Sir, I have heard and learned this in the presence of the Blessed One: "Ānanda, the disciple of the Blessed One Sikhī, named Abhibhū, while standing in the Brahma world, could make his voice heard throughout a thousandfold world system." Venerable Sir, how far can the Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, make his voice heard?' 'He was a disciple, Ānanda; the Tathāgatas are immeasurable.' For a third time, the Venerable Ānanda said to the Blessed One: 'Venerable Sir, I have heard and learned this in the presence of the Blessed One: "Ānanda, the disciple of the Blessed One Sikhī, named Abhibhū, while standing in the Brahma world, could make his voice heard throughout a thousandfold world system." Venerable Sir, how far can the Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, make his voice heard?' 'Ānanda, have you heard of the thousandfold minor world system?' 'It is the time, Blessed One; it is the time, Sugata, for the Blessed One to speak. Having heard it from the Blessed One, the monks will remember it.' 'Then listen, Ānanda, and pay close attention; I will speak.' 'Yes, Venerable Sir,' the Venerable Ānanda replied. The Blessed One said: 'Ānanda, as far as the sun and moon revolve and illuminate the quarters with their light, that is a thousandfold world. In that thousandfold world, there are a thousand moons, a thousand suns, a thousand Sinerus, kings of mountains, a thousand Jambudīpas, a thousand Aparagoyānas, a thousand Uttarakurus, a thousand Pubbavidehas, four thousand great oceans, four thousand Great Kings, a thousand Cātumahārājika heavens, a thousand Tāvatiṃsa, a thousand Yāma, a thousand Tusita, a thousand Nimmānarati, a thousand Paranimmitavasavatti, and a thousand Brahma worlds. This, Ānanda, is called a thousandfold minor world system.'
229:
“Ānanda, a world system that is a thousandfold is called a small world system (Cūḷanikā loka-dhātu). Ānanda, a world that encompasses a thousand small world systems is called a twice-thousandfold middle world system (Majjhimikā loka-dhātu).

Ānanda, a world that encompasses a thousand twice-thousandfold middle world systems is called a thrice-thousandfold great world system (Mahāsahassī loka-dhātu). Ānanda, if the Tathāgata so desires, he can make his voice heard throughout the thrice-thousandfold great world system (comprising a hundred billion universes), or even as far as he wishes.”

“But how, Bhante, can the Blessed One make his voice heard throughout the thrice-thousandfold great world system, or even as far as he wishes?” “Here, Ānanda, the Tathāgata would pervade the thrice-thousandfold great world system with radiance. When those beings perceive that light, the Tathāgata would then make a sound and cause his voice to be heard. In this way, Ānanda, the Tathāgata can make his voice heard throughout the thrice-thousandfold great world system, or even as far as he wishes.”

When this was said, the Venerable Ānanda said to the Venerable Udāyī (Lāḷudāyī): “It is a gain for me, it is a great blessing for me, that my teacher, the Blessed One, is so powerful and so majestic!” When this was said, Udāyī said to the Venerable Ānanda: “Friend Ānanda, what benefit is it to you that your teacher is so powerful and so majestic?” When this was said, the Blessed One said to the Venerable Udāyī: “Do not say so, Udāyī! Do not say so, Udāyī! Udāyī, if Ānanda were to pass away without being free from lust (rāga), he would, by virtue of that settled faith (in the Buddha), rule as a king of devas in the celestial realms seven times, and rule as a great wheel-turning monarch (Cakkavatti) right here in this Jambudīpa seven times. However, Udāyī, Ānanda will surely attain Parinibbāna in this very life.”
230:
The Tenth Discourse.
The third chapter, the Ānanda Vagga, is finished.

1. One universe exists; multiplied by a thousand, it becomes one small world system (Cūḷanikā loka-dhātu). One small world system (a thousand universes) exists; multiplied by a thousand, it becomes one middle world system (Majjhimikā loka-dhātu, a million universes). One middle world system (a million universes) exists; multiplied by a thousand small world systems (a thousand), it becomes one great world system (Mahā loka-dhātu, a hundred billion universes).

## (9) 4. Samaṇa Vagga

## 1. Samaṇa Sutta

82. Monks, there are these three duties of an ascetic that are the property of an ascetic and must be performed by an ascetic. What three? The undertaking of the training in higher virtue (adhisīla-sikkhā), the undertaking of the training in higher mind (adhicitta-sikkhā), and the undertaking of the training in higher wisdom (adhipaññā-sikkhā). Monks, these are the three duties of an ascetic that are the property of an ascetic and must be performed by an ascetic.

Monks, therefore, in this Dispensation, you should train yourselves thus: 'Our desire shall be intense for the undertaking of the training in higher virtue; our desire shall be intense for the undertaking of the training in higher mind; our desire shall be intense for the undertaking of the training in higher wisdom.' Monks, thus should you train yourselves.

The First Discourse.

## 2. Gadrabha Sutta

83. Monks, suppose a donkey follows behind a herd of cattle, thinking, 'I too am a cow, I too am a cow.' Yet its color is not like that of cattle, its voice is not like that of cattle, and its hoof is not like that of cattle. That donkey just follows behind the herd of cattle, thinking, 'I too am a cow, I too am a cow.'

In the same way, monks, here a certain monk follows behind the Saṅgha of monks, thinking, 'I too am a monk, I too am a monk.' Yet he does not have the same kind of desire for the undertaking of the training in higher virtue as other monks do; he does not have the same kind of desire for the undertaking of the training in higher mind as other monks do; and he does not have the same kind of desire for the undertaking of the training in higher wisdom as other monks do. That monk just follows behind the Saṅgha of monks, thinking, 'I too am a monk, I too am a monk.'

Monks, therefore, in this Dispensation, you should train yourselves thus: 'Our desire shall be intense for the undertaking of the training in higher virtue...'
231:
"'We will have a strong desire for the undertaking of the training in higher mind; we will have a strong desire for the undertaking of the training in higher wisdom.' This is how you should train. Monks, this is how you must train."
Second Sutta.

## 3. Khetta Sutta
84. "Monks, there are these three things to be done beforehand by a householder farmer. What three? Here, monks, a householder farmer first plows and levels the field well. Having first plowed and leveled the field well, he sows the seeds at the proper time. Having sown the seeds at the proper time, he lets water in and out at the appropriate time. Monks, these are the three things to be done beforehand by a householder farmer.

"In the same way, monks, there are these three things to be done beforehand by a monk. What three? The undertaking of the training in higher virtue, the undertaking of the training in higher mind, and the undertaking of the training in higher wisdom. Monks, these are the three things to be done beforehand by a monk.

"Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus: 'We will have a strong desire for the undertaking of the training in higher virtue; we will have a strong desire for the undertaking of the training in higher mind; we will have a strong desire for the undertaking of the training in higher wisdom.' This is how you should train. Monks, this is how you must train."
Third Sutta.

## 4. Vajjiputta Sutta
85. On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Vesālī in the Gabled Hall in the Great Wood. Then a certain Vajjiputta monk approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, and sat down to one side. Sitting there, that Vajjiputta monk said to the Blessed One: "Venerable sir, more than a hundred and fifty training rules¹ come for recitation every fortnight.
232:
"Venerable sir, I am not able to train in these training rules."

"But are you able, monk, to train in the three trainings: the training in higher virtue, the training in higher mind, and the training in higher wisdom?"

"Venerable sir, I am able to train in these three trainings: the training in higher virtue, the training in higher mind, and the training in higher wisdom."

"Therefore, monk, you should train in these three trainings: the training in higher virtue, the training in higher mind, and the training in higher wisdom. Monk, as you train in higher virtue, higher mind, and higher wisdom, lust, hatred, and delusion will be abandoned. With the abandoning of lust, hatred, and delusion, you will not perform what is unwholesome, nor will you indulge in evil."

Then, at a later time, that monk trained in higher virtue, higher mind, and higher wisdom. As he trained in these three, lust was abandoned, hatred was abandoned, and delusion was abandoned. With the abandoning of lust, hatred, and delusion, he did not perform what is unwholesome, nor did he indulge in evil.
Fourth Sutta.

1. At the time this discourse was taught, only over 150 Pātimokkha training rules had been laid down. Therefore, instead of saying 227 training rules as they appear in the Pātimokkha, it was said "more than a hundred and fifty training rules" (sādhikaṃ idaṃ bhante diyaḍḍhasikkhāpadasataṃ) referring to those already laid down.

## 5. Sekkha Sutta
86. Then a certain monk approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, and sat down to one side. Sitting there, that monk said to the Blessed One: "Venerable sir, it is said, 'a trainee, a trainee' (sekkha). In what way, venerable sir, is one a trainee?"

"Monk, one is called a trainee because one trains (sikkhati). In what does one train? One trains in higher virtue, one trains in higher mind, and one trains in higher wisdom. One is called a trainee, monk, because one trains."

"For the trainee who is training,
Following the straight path,
First, knowledge of destruction arises,
And immediately after, final knowledge.

"Then, for the one liberated by final knowledge,
The knowledge of such a stable one arises:
'My liberation is unshakable,'
With the destruction of the fetters of existence."
Fifth Sutta.
233:
The Fifth Sutta.

## 6. Paṭhama Sikkhā Sutta

87. "Monks, these more than a hundred and fifty training rules come for recitation every fortnight, in which sons of good family who are desirous of their own welfare train themselves. Monks, there are these three trainings in which all these training rules are encompassed. What are the three? The training in higher virtue, the training in higher mind, and the training in higher wisdom. These, monks, are the three trainings in which all these training rules are encompassed.

"Here, monks, a bhikkhu is one who fulfills virtue, but practices only to a limited extent in concentration and only to a limited extent in wisdom. Regarding those minor and lesser training rules, he both commits offenses and rehabilitates himself from them. Why is that? Because, monks, I have not declared any incapability [for a Noble One] in this matter of committing and rehabilitating from such offenses. However, regarding those training rules that are fundamental to the holy life and suitable for the holy life, he is of firm virtue and steady virtue; he trains himself by undertaking the training rules. With the total destruction of the three fetters, he becomes a Stream-enterer (Sotāpanna), no longer subject to rebirth in the lower worlds, fixed in destiny, and bound for enlightenment.

"Furthermore, monks, here a bhikkhu is one who fulfills virtue, but practices only to a limited extent in concentration and only to a limited extent in wisdom. Regarding those minor and lesser training rules, he both commits offenses and rehabilitates himself from them. Why is that? Because, monks, I have not declared any incapability in this matter of committing and rehabilitating from such offenses. However, regarding those training rules that are fundamental to the holy life and suitable for the holy life, he is of firm virtue and steady virtue; he trains himself by undertaking the training rules. With the total destruction of the three fetters and the weakening of lust, hatred, and delusion, he becomes a Once-returner (Sakadāgāmī), who returns to this world only once more to make an end of suffering.

"Furthermore, monks, here a bhikkhu is one who fulfills virtue and fulfills concentration, but practices only to a limited extent in wisdom. Regarding those minor and lesser training rules, he both commits offenses and rehabilitates himself from them. Why is that? Because, monks, I have not declared any incapability in this matter of committing and rehabilitating from such offenses. However, regarding those training rules that are fundamental to the holy life and suitable for the holy life, he is of firm virtue and steady virtue; he trains himself by undertaking the training rules. With the total destruction of the five lower fetters [that bind one to the sensual realm], he becomes a Non-returner (Anāgāmī),
234:
who is reborn spontaneously [in the Brahma realm] and attains final Nibbāna there, not being subject to return from that world.

"Furthermore, monks, here a bhikkhu is one who fulfills virtue, fulfills concentration, and fulfills wisdom. Regarding those minor and lesser training rules, he both commits offenses and rehabilitates himself from them. Why is that? Because, monks, I have not declared any incapability in this matter of committing and rehabilitating from such offenses. However, regarding those training rules that are fundamental to the holy life and suitable for the holy life, he is of firm virtue and steady virtue; he trains himself by undertaking the training rules. Through the destruction of the taints, he enters and dwells in the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, having realized them for himself in this very life through direct knowledge; he is an Arahant.

"Thus, monks, one who practices partially achieves partially; one who practices fully achieves fully. Monks, I declare that these training rules are not in vain."

The Sixth Sutta.

1. By saying that he has not declared it impossible to commit offenses, it implies that offenses can be committed. Therefore, various commentaries explain that Arahants do not commit worldly faults (loka-vajja), but they may still commit minor or major disciplinary faults (dhamma-vajja/paṇṇatti-vajja). This is more clearly and fully explained in the Vinaya.

## 7. Dutiya Sikkhā Sutta

88. "Monks, these more than a hundred and fifty training rules come for recitation every fortnight, in which sons of good family who are desirous of their own welfare train themselves. Monks, there are these three trainings in which all these training rules are encompassed. What are the three? The training in higher virtue, the training in higher mind, and the training in higher wisdom. These, monks, are the three trainings in which all these training rules are encompassed.

"Here, monks, a bhikkhu is one who fulfills virtue, but practices only to a limited extent in concentration and only to a limited extent in wisdom. Regarding those minor and lesser training rules, he both commits offenses and rehabilitates himself from them. Why is that?
