Because, monks, I have not declared any incapability in this matter of committing and rehabilitating from such offenses. However, regarding those training rules that are fundamental to the holy life and suitable for the holy life, he is of firm virtue and steady virtue; he trains himself by undertaking the training rules. With the total destruction of the three fetters, he becomes a 'seven-times-at-most' (Sattakkhattuparama) Stream-enterer, who, after wandering and circling through the worlds of devas and humans for seven times at most, makes an end of suffering. With the total destruction of the three fetters, he becomes a 'family-to-family' (Kolaṃkola) Stream-enterer, who, after wandering and circling through two or three [noble] families, makes an end of suffering. With the total destruction of the three fetters, he becomes a 'one-seed' (Ekabījī) Stream-enterer, who, after being reborn only once more in the human world, makes an end of suffering. Also, with the total destruction of the three fetters and the weakening of lust, hatred,
235:
...and through the attenuation of greed, hatred, and delusion, he becomes a Once-returner (Sakadāgāmī), returning to this world only once to make an end of suffering.

"Furthermore, monks, here a monk is one who fulfills virtue, fulfills concentration, and practices wisdom to a limited extent. He commits some minor and lesser offenses and amends them. Why is that? Because, monks, I have not declared it impossible for him to do so. But as for those training rules that are fundamental to the holy life and suitable for the holy life, he is of firm virtue and steadfast virtue; he trains in them, having undertaken the training rules. With the total destruction of the five lower fetters, he is one who goes upstream to the Akaniṭṭha realm (Uddhaṃsoto Akaniṭṭhagāmī). With the total destruction of the five lower fetters, he is one who attains Nibbāna with exertion (Sasaṅkhāra-parinibbāyī). With the total destruction of the five lower fetters, he is one who attains Nibbāna without exertion (Asaṅkhāra-parinibbāyī). With the total destruction of the five lower fetters, he is one who attains Nibbāna after passing the middle of the lifespan (Upahacca-parinibbāyī). With the total destruction of the five lower fetters, he is one who attains Nibbāna in the interval (Antarā-parinibbāyī).

"Furthermore, monks, here a monk is one who fulfills virtue, fulfills concentration, and fulfills wisdom. He commits some minor and lesser offenses and amends them. Why is that? Because, monks, I have not declared it impossible for him to do so. But as for those training rules that are fundamental to the holy life and suitable for the holy life, he is of firm virtue and steadfast virtue; he trains in them, having undertaken the training rules. With the destruction of the taints (āsavas), he realizes for himself with direct knowledge, in this very life, the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, and having entered upon them, he dwells in them. Thus, monks, one who practices partially achieves partially; one who practices fully achieves fully. Monks, I say that the training rules are not barren."

The Seventh Sutta.

## 8. Tatiya Sikkha Sutta
89. "Monks, these more than one hundred and fifty training rules come up for recitation every fortnight, in which clansmen desiring their own welfare train. Monks, there are these three trainings, in which all those training rules are included."
236:
What are the three? They are the training in higher virtue (adhisīla-sikkhā), the training in higher mind (adhicitta-sikkhā), and the training in higher wisdom (adhipaññā-sikkhā). Bhikkhus, these are the three trainings; in these three trainings, all these training rules are included.

Bhikkhus, in this teaching, a bhikkhu is one who fulfills virtue, fulfills concentration, and fulfills wisdom. He may commit those minor and lesser training rules and rise from them. Why is that? Because, bhikkhus, I have not declared him incapable of progress in this regard. But as for those training rules that are fundamental to the holy life and suitable for the holy life, he is firm in virtue and steady in virtue, training himself in the training rules he has undertaken. With the destruction of the taints, he enters and dwells in the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, having realized it for himself in this very life through direct knowledge.

If he does not reach that Arahantship, if he does not penetrate it, then with the total destruction of the five lower fetters, he becomes an 'Antarāparinibbāyī' Anāgāmī, one who attains Nibbāna in the interval. If he does not reach that Arahantship... he becomes an 'Upahaccaparinibbāyī' Anāgāmī, one who attains Nibbāna after more than half the lifespan. If he does not reach that Arahantship... he becomes an 'Asaṅkhāraparinibbāyī' Anāgāmī, one who attains Nibbāna without exertion. If he does not reach that Arahantship... he becomes a 'Sasaṅkhāraparinibbāyī' Anāgāmī, one who attains Nibbāna with exertion. If he does not reach that Arahantship... he becomes an 'Uddhaṃsoto Akaniṭṭhagāmī' Anāgāmī, one who goes upstream to the Akaniṭṭha realm.

If he does not reach that Arahantship, if he does not penetrate it, then with the total destruction of the three fetters and the attenuation of greed, hatred, and delusion, he becomes a Sakadāgāmī (Once-returner), returning to this world only once to make an end of suffering.

If he does not reach that Arahantship, if he does not penetrate it, then with the total destruction of the three fetters, he becomes an 'Ekabījī' Sotāpanna (one-seeder), being reborn only once more in the human state to make an end of suffering. If he does not reach that Arahantship... he becomes a 'Kolaṃkola' Sotāpanna (going from family to family), wandering through two or three families to make an end of suffering. If he does not reach that Arahantship... he becomes a 'Sattakkhattuparama' Sotāpanna (seven times at most), wandering through gods and humans seven times at most to make an end of suffering.

Thus, bhikkhus, one who practices fully achieves fully; one who practices partially achieves partially. Bhikkhus, I say that the training rules are not fruitless.
237:
The Eighth Sutta.

## 9. Paṭhamasikkhattaya Sutta

90. Bhikkhus, there are these three trainings. What three? The training in higher virtue, the training in higher mind, and the training in higher wisdom.

And what, bhikkhus, is the training in higher virtue? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is virtuous... [...]... training himself in the training rules he has undertaken. Bhikkhus, this restraint of the Pātimokkha is called the training in higher virtue.

And what, bhikkhus, is the training in higher mind? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu, secluded from sensual pleasures... [...]... enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna. Bhikkhus, this entering and dwelling in the fourth jhāna is called the training in higher mind.

And what, bhikkhus, is the training in higher wisdom? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu understands as it really is: "This is suffering"... [...]... "This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering." Bhikkhus, this understanding of the Four Noble Truths is called the training in higher wisdom. Bhikkhus, these are the three trainings.

The Ninth Sutta.

## 10. Dutiyasikkhattaya Sutta

91. Bhikkhus, there are these three trainings. What three? The training in higher virtue, the training in higher mind, and the training in higher wisdom.

And what, bhikkhus, is the training in higher virtue? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is virtuous... [...]... training himself in the training rules he has undertaken. Bhikkhus, this restraint of the Pātimokkha is called the training in higher virtue.

And what, bhikkhus, is the training in higher mind? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu, secluded from sensual pleasures... [...]... enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna. Bhikkhus, this entering and dwelling in the fourth jhāna is called the training in higher mind.

And what, bhikkhus, is the training in higher wisdom? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu, with the destruction of the taints, enters and dwells in the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, having realized it for himself in this very life through direct knowledge. Bhikkhus, this wisdom of Arahantship is called the training in higher wisdom. Bhikkhus, these are the three trainings.

One who is energetic, possessed of strength, steadfast, a meditator, mindful, and with guarded senses, should practice the training in higher virtue, the training in higher mind, and the training in higher wisdom.
238:
“One who is energetic, steadfast, and resolute, possessing higher virtue, higher mind, and higher wisdom, should dwell meditative, mindful, and with guarded faculties.

“As before, so after; as after, so before;
As below, so above; as above, so below;
As by day, so by night; as by night, so by day;
Overcoming all directions with immeasurable concentration (of the path of Arahantship).

“One who is accomplished in practice and of pure conduct is called a trainee (sekha). One who is firm in concentration and has reached the end of the path through practice is called a Buddha in the world.

“With the cessation of consciousness, for one liberated by the destruction of craving, the liberation of the mind occurs just like the extinguishing of a lamp.”

Tenth Sutta.

## 11. Saṅkavā Sutta

92. On one occasion, the Blessed One was wandering in the Kosalan country with a large Saṅgha of monks and arrived at a Kosalan market town named Saṅkavā. There the Blessed One stayed at Saṅkavā. At that time, a monk named Kassapagotta was the resident monk at Saṅkavā. There the Blessed One was instructing, urging, rousing, and gladdening the monks with a Dhamma talk concerning the training rules (sikkhāpada). While the Blessed One was instructing, urging, rousing, and gladdening the monks with a Dhamma talk concerning the training rules, the monk Kassapagotta felt dissatisfied and resentful, thinking: “This ascetic Gotama is indeed too exacting.”

Then the Blessed One, having stayed at Saṅkavā as long as he liked, set out on a wandering tour toward Rājagaha. Wandering by stages, he arrived at Rājagaha and stayed there.

Not long after the Blessed One had departed, the monk Kassapagotta felt remorse and regret: “It is a loss for me, not a gain; it is poorly gained by me, not well gained, that I felt dissatisfaction and resentment when the Blessed One was instructing, urging, rousing, and gladdening the monks with a Dhamma talk concerning the training rules, thinking: ‘This ascetic Gotama is indeed too exacting.’
239:
“While the Blessed One was instructing, urging, rousing, and gladdening the monks with a Dhamma talk concerning the training rules, I felt dissatisfied and resentful, thinking: ‘This ascetic Gotama is indeed too exacting.’ What if I were to approach the Blessed One and confess my transgression as a transgression in his presence?”

Then the monk Kassapagotta set his lodgings in order, took his bowl and robes, and set out for Rājagaha. In due course, he arrived at Mount Vulture Peak in Rājagaha where the Blessed One was. Having approached the Blessed One and paid homage to him, he sat down at one side. Sitting there, the monk Kassapagotta said to the Blessed One:

“Venerable Sir, on one occasion the Blessed One was staying at Saṅkavā, a market town of the Kosalans. There, Venerable Sir, the Blessed One was instructing, urging, rousing, and gladdening the monks with a Dhamma talk concerning the training rules. While the Blessed One was instructing, urging, rousing, and gladdening the monks with a Dhamma talk concerning the training rules, I felt dissatisfied and resentful, thinking: ‘This ascetic Gotama is indeed too exacting.’ Then the Blessed One, having stayed at Saṅkavā as long as he liked, set out on a wandering tour toward Rājagaha.

“Not long after the Blessed One had departed, I felt remorse and regret: ‘It is a loss for me, not a gain; it is poorly gained by me, not well gained, that I felt dissatisfaction and resentment when the Blessed One was instructing, urging, rousing, and gladdening the monks with a Dhamma talk concerning the training rules, thinking: ‘This ascetic Gotama is indeed too exacting.’ Then I thought: ‘What if I were to approach the Blessed One and confess my transgression as a transgression in his presence?’

“Venerable Sir, a transgression (accaya) overcame me, in that I was foolish, confused, and unskilled, since I felt dissatisfied and resentful when the Blessed One was instructing, urging, rousing, and gladdening the monks with a Dhamma talk concerning the training rules, thinking: ‘This ascetic Gotama is indeed too exacting.’ Venerable Sir, may the Blessed One accept my confession of transgression as such for the sake of future restraint.”

“Indeed, Kassapa, a transgression overcame you, in that you were foolish, confused, and unskilled...”
240:
“Kassapa, when I was inspiring, inciting, rousing, and gladdening the bhikkhus with a Dhamma talk connected with the training rules, you felt intolerance and displeasure, thinking: ‘This ascetic Gotama is being excessively scrupulous.’ Kassapa, since you see your fault as a fault and make amends in accordance with the Dhamma, we accept it from you. For this is growth in the Discipline of the Noble One: when one sees one's fault as a fault, makes amends in accordance with the Dhamma, and practices restraint in the future.

Kassapa, even if a bhikkhu is an elder (thera), if he does not desire the three trainings, does not speak in praise of undertaking the three trainings, does not encourage other bhikkhus who do not desire the three trainings to undertake them, and does not speak in praise of other bhikkhus who do desire the three trainings at the proper time, truthfully and correctly—Kassapa, I do not praise such an elder bhikkhu. Why is that? Because if the Teacher were to praise him, other bhikkhus might associate with him. Those who associate with him might follow his example. For those who follow his example, it would lead to their harm and suffering for a long time. Therefore, Kassapa, I do not praise such an elder bhikkhu.

Kassapa, even if a bhikkhu is of middle standing... [pe]... Kassapa, even if a bhikkhu is a newly ordained one (nava), if he does not desire the three trainings, does not speak in praise of undertaking the three trainings, does not encourage other bhikkhus who do not desire the three trainings to undertake them, and does not speak in praise of other bhikkhus who do desire the three trainings at the proper time, truthfully and correctly—Kassapa, I do not praise such a newly ordained bhikkhu. Why is that? Because if the Teacher were to praise him, other bhikkhus might associate with him. Those who associate with him might follow his example. For those who follow his example, it would lead to their harm and suffering for a long time. Therefore, Kassapa, I do not praise such a newly ordained bhikkhu.”
241:
“Kassapa, if an elder bhikkhu desires the three trainings, speaks in praise of undertaking the three trainings, encourages other bhikkhus who do not desire the three trainings to undertake them, and speaks in praise of other bhikkhus who do desire the three trainings at the proper time, truthfully and correctly—Kassapa, I praise such an elder bhikkhu. Why is that? Because if the Teacher were to praise him, other bhikkhus might associate with him. Those who associate with him might follow his example. For those who follow his example, it would lead to their welfare and happiness for a long time. Therefore, Kassapa, I praise such an elder bhikkhu.

Kassapa, if a bhikkhu is of middle standing... [pe]... Kassapa, if a bhikkhu is a newly ordained one, if he desires the three trainings, speaks in praise of undertaking the three trainings, encourages other bhikkhus who do not desire the three trainings to undertake them, and speaks in praise of other bhikkhus who do desire the three trainings at the proper time, truthfully and correctly—Kassapa, I praise such a newly ordained bhikkhu. Why is that? Because if the Teacher were to praise him, other bhikkhus might associate with him. Those who associate with him might follow his example. For those who follow his example, it would lead to their welfare and happiness for a long time. Therefore, Kassapa, I praise such a newly ordained bhikkhu,” (the Buddha said).

The eleventh sutta [is finished].

The ninth chapter, the Samana Vagga, is finished.

## (10) 5. Loṇakapalla Vagga

## 1. Accāyika Sutta

93. Bhikkhus, there are these three urgent duties of a lay farmer. What three? Here, bhikkhus, a lay farmer quickly and well plows and levels his field.”
242:
Having quickly and thoroughly plowed the field and made the ground level and ready, he quickly sows the seeds. Having quickly sown the seeds, he quickly lets the water in and lets it out. Monks, these are the three urgent duties of a householder farmer. Monks, that householder farmer does not have the psychic power or authority to say: 'Let my crops sprout this very day, let them head tomorrow, and let them ripen the day after.' Rather, monks, there comes a time when those crops of that householder farmer, undergoing seasonal changes, sprout, head, and ripen.

In the same way, monks, there are these three urgent duties of a monk. What three? The undertaking of the training in higher virtue, the undertaking of the training in higher mind, and the undertaking of the training in higher wisdom. Monks, these are the three urgent duties of a monk. Monks, that monk does not have the psychic power or authority to say: 'Let my mind be liberated from the taints through non-clinging this very day, or tomorrow, or the day after.' Rather, monks, there comes a time when that monk training in higher virtue, training in higher mind, and training in higher wisdom, has his mind liberated from the taints through non-clinging.

Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus: 'Our desire shall be intense for the undertaking of the training in higher virtue; our desire shall be intense for the undertaking of the training in higher mind; our desire shall be intense for the undertaking of the training in higher wisdom.' Thus, monks, should you train yourselves.

First Sutta.

## 2. Paviveka Sutta

94. Monks, wanderers of other sects prescribe these three types of seclusion. What three? Seclusion in regard to robes, seclusion in regard to almsfood, and seclusion in regard to lodgings.

Therein, monks, wanderers of other sects prescribe seclusion in regard to robes in this way: they wear garments of hemp, they wear garments of mixed hemp, they wear garments of corpse-shrouds, they wear garments of rags from a dust heap, they wear garments of bark, they wear antelope skins, they wear garments of strips of antelope skin,
243:
they wear garments of kusa-grass, they wear garments of bark-fiber, they wear garments of wood-shavings, they wear blankets of human hair, they wear blankets of horsehair, they wear garments of owl wings. Monks, wanderers of other sects prescribe seclusion in regard to robes in this way.

Therein, monks, wanderers of other sects prescribe seclusion in regard to almsfood in this way: they eat green vegetables, they eat millet, they eat wild rice, they eat leather parings, they eat water plants, they eat rice bran, they eat the scum of boiling rice, they eat sesame flour, they eat grass, they eat cow dung, they subsist on forest roots and fruits, eating windfalls. Monks, wanderers of other sects prescribe seclusion in regard to almsfood in this way.

Therein, monks, wanderers of other sects prescribe seclusion in regard to lodgings in this way: they prescribe a forest, the foot of a tree, a cemetery, a woodland, the open air, a straw heap, or a threshing floor. Monks, wanderers of other sects prescribe seclusion in regard to lodgings in this way. Monks, wanderers of other sects prescribe these three types of seclusion.

But, monks, in this Dhamma-Vinaya, there are three types of seclusion for a monk. What three? Here, monks, a monk is virtuous, and his immorality is abandoned; he is secluded from that. He has right view, and his wrong view is abandoned; he is secluded from that. He is one whose taints are destroyed, and his taints are abandoned; he is secluded from them.

Monks, because a monk is virtuous, and his immorality is abandoned, and he is secluded from that; because he has right view, and his wrong view is abandoned, and he is secluded from that; because he is one whose taints are destroyed, and his taints are abandoned, and he is secluded from them; therefore, monks, this monk is called 'one who has reached the summit, one who has reached the core, one who is pure, one who is established in the core.'

Suppose, monks, a householder farmer has a ripe field of rice. That householder farmer would have it reaped quickly. Having had it reaped quickly, he would have it gathered quickly. Having had it gathered quickly,
244:
One is said to be established in the essence (of virtue, concentration, and wisdom).

Monks, the rice field of a householder farmer is complete. That householder farmer would have that rice field harvested quickly; having had it harvested quickly, he would have it gathered quickly; having had it gathered quickly, he would have it hauled quickly; having had it hauled quickly, he would have it stacked quickly; having had it stacked quickly, he would have it threshed quickly; having had it threshed quickly, he would have it winnowed quickly; having had it winnowed quickly, he would have it pounded quickly; having had it pounded quickly, he would have the husks removed quickly. Monks, when this is done, the grain of that householder farmer reaches the pinnacle (of rice), reaches the essence, becomes pure, and is established in the essence.

Monks, in the same way, for whatever reason a monk is virtuous, immorality is abandoned in him, and he is secluded from that immorality. He has right view, wrong view is abandoned in him, and he is secluded from that wrong view. He has destroyed the taints, the taints are abandoned in him, and he is secluded from those taints. Monks, therefore, this monk is called one who has reached the pinnacle, reached the essence, is pure, and is established in the essence (of virtue, concentration, and wisdom).

The Second Sutta.

## 3. Sarada Sutta

95. Monks, just as in the autumn season (Sarada), when the sky is clear and free of clouds, the sun rising into the sky dispels all darkness in the heavens, shining, glowing, and radiant; in the same way, monks, when the dustless, stainless Dhamma-eye (the knowledge of the path of stream-entry) arises in a noble disciple, simultaneously with the arising of that vision, monks, three fetters are abandoned in the noble disciple: self-identity view (sakkāya-diṭṭhi), doubt (vicikicchā), and attachment to rites and rituals (sīlabbata-parāmāsa).

Thereafter, he is liberated from two further states: covetousness (abhijjhā) and ill-will (byāpāda). Secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, he enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by thought (vitakka) and examination (vicāra), with rapture (pīti) and happiness (sukha) born of seclusion.
245:
Monks, if at that time the noble disciple should pass away, there is no fetter that could bring that disciple back to this world again.

The Third Sutta.

## 4. Parisā Sutta

96. Monks, there are these three types of assemblies. Which three? The foremost assembly (aggavatī), the discordant assembly (vaggā), and the harmonious assembly (samaggā).

And what, monks, is the foremost assembly? Here, monks, in an assembly where the elder monks are not luxurious, not lax, have given up the effort toward what leads downwards, and are leaders in seclusion; they arouse energy for the sake of reaching the unreached, attaining the unattained, and realizing the unrealized. The later generations of people follow the example of those elder monks; they too are not luxurious, not lax, have given up the effort toward what leads downwards, and are leaders in seclusion; they arouse energy for the sake of reaching the unreached, attaining the unattained, and realizing the unrealized. Monks, this is called the foremost assembly.

And what, monks, is the discordant assembly? Here, monks, in an assembly where the monks live quarrelsome, contentious, and disputatious, piercing each other with verbal daggers. Monks, this is called the discordant assembly.

And what, monks, is the harmonious assembly? Here, monks, in an assembly where the monks live in harmony, friendly, without dispute, mixing like milk and water, looking at each other with eyes of affection. Monks, this is called the harmonious assembly.

Monks, at the time when monks live in harmony, friendly, without dispute, mixing like milk and water, looking at each other with eyes of affection; at that time, monks, the monks generate much merit. At that time, monks, the monks dwell in the sublime dwelling (brahmavihāra) through appreciative joy (muditā) which is the liberation of the mind. In one who is joyful, rapture (pīti) arises; for one with a rapturous mind, the body becomes tranquil; one with a tranquil body experiences happiness (sukha); the mind of one who is happy becomes concentrated (samādhi).

Monks, just as when it rains heavily on a mountain top, the water flows down to the lowlands and fills the mountain clefts, rifts, and gullies...
246:
When the mountain clefts, rifts, and gullies are full, they fill the small pools. When the small pools are full, they fill the large pools. When the large pools are full, they fill the small rivers. When the small rivers are full, they fill the large rivers. When the large rivers are full, they fill the great ocean.

In the same way, bhikkhus, at whatever time bhikkhus dwell in harmony, friendly and without contention, like milk mixed with water, looking at each other with eyes of affection, at that time, bhikkhus, they generate much merit. At that time, bhikkhus, those bhikkhus dwell in the sublime abode, that is, the liberation of mind through altruistic joy (muditā). In one who is joyful, rapture (pīti) arises. For one whose mind is rapturous, the body becomes tranquil. One whose body is tranquil experiences happiness. The mind of one who is happy becomes concentrated. These, bhikkhus, are the three assemblies."

The Fourth Sutta.

## 5. Pathama Ājānīya Sutta

97. "Bhikkhus, a king's fine thoroughbred horse endowed with three qualities is worthy of a king, an asset to a king, and is counted as a limb of the king. With which three? Here, bhikkhus, a king's fine thoroughbred horse is endowed with beauty, endowed with strength, and endowed with speed. Bhikkhus, a king's fine thoroughbred horse endowed with these three qualities is worthy of a king, an asset to a king, and is counted as a limb of the king. In the same way, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu endowed with three qualities is worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, an unsurpassed field of merit for the world. With which three? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is endowed with beauty, endowed with strength, and endowed with speed.

And how, bhikkhus, is a bhikkhu endowed with beauty? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is virtuous; he dwells restrained by the Pātimokkha restraint, possessed of good conduct and resort, seeing danger in the slightest faults; having undertaken the rules of training, he trains in them. In this way, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is endowed with beauty.

And how, bhikkhus, is a bhikkhu endowed with strength? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu dwells with aroused energy for the abandoning of unwholesome states and for the acquisition of wholesome states...
247:
...is vigorous, firm in exertion, not shirking the responsibility of wholesome states. In this way, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is endowed with strength.

And how, bhikkhus, is a bhikkhu endowed with speed? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu understands as it really is: 'This is suffering'; he understands as it really is: 'This is the origin of suffering'; he understands as it really is: 'This is the cessation of suffering'; he understands as it really is: 'This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering.' In this way, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is endowed with speed. Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu endowed with these three qualities is worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, an unsurpassed field of merit for the world."

The Fifth Sutta.

## 6. Dutiya Ājānīya Sutta

98. "Bhikkhus, a king's fine thoroughbred horse endowed with three qualities is worthy of a king, an asset to a king, and is counted as a limb of the king. With which three? Here, bhikkhus, a king's fine thoroughbred horse is endowed with beauty, endowed with strength, and endowed with speed. Bhikkhus, a king's fine thoroughbred horse endowed with these three qualities is worthy of a king, an asset to a king, and is counted as a limb of the king. In the same way, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu endowed with three qualities is worthy of gifts... [as before] ...an unsurpassed field of merit for the world. With which three? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is endowed with beauty, endowed with strength, and endowed with speed.

And how, bhikkhus, is a bhikkhu endowed with beauty? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is virtuous... [as before] ...having undertaken the rules of training, he trains in them. In this way, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is endowed with beauty.

And how, bhikkhus, is a bhikkhu endowed with strength? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu dwells with aroused energy for the abandoning of unwholesome states and for the acquisition of wholesome states, is vigorous, firm in exertion, not shirking the responsibility of wholesome states. In this way, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is endowed with strength.

And how, bhikkhus, is a bhikkhu endowed with speed? Here, bhikkhus, with the utter destruction of the five lower fetters, a bhikkhu is one of spontaneous rebirth, due to attain Parinibbāna there, not subject to return from that world. [An Anāgāmī]."
248:
He is reborn spontaneously and attains Parinibbāna right there in that Brahma realm, not being subject to return from that world. In this way, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is possessed of speed. Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu possessed of these three qualities is worthy of gifts, [worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation], an unsurpassed field of merit for the world.

Sixth Sutta.

## 7. Third Ājānīya Sutta

99. Bhikkhus, a king's fine thoroughbred horse possessed of three factors is worthy of a king, is an asset to a king, and is counted as a very limb of the king. What are the three? Here, bhikkhus, a king's fine thoroughbred horse is possessed of beauty, possessed of strength, and possessed of speed. Bhikkhus, a king's fine thoroughbred horse possessed of these three factors is worthy of a king, is an asset to a king, and is counted as a very limb of the king.

In the same way, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu possessed of three qualities is worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, an unsurpassed field of merit for the world. What are the three? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is possessed of beauty, possessed of strength, and possessed of speed.

And how, bhikkhus, is a bhikkhu possessed of beauty? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is virtuous; he dwells restrained by the restraint of the Pātimokkha, possessed of proper conduct and resort (ācāra-gocara); seeing danger in the slightest faults, he trains himself by undertaking the rules of training. In this way, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is possessed of beauty.

And how, bhikkhus, is a bhikkhu possessed of strength? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu dwells with aroused energy for the abandoning of unwholesome states and the undertaking of wholesome states; he is steadfast, firm in effort, and does not neglect the duty of cultivating wholesome states. In this way, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is possessed of strength.

And how, bhikkhus, is a bhikkhu possessed of speed? Here, bhikkhus, with the destruction of the taints, a bhikkhu enters and dwells in the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, having realized it for himself with direct knowledge in this very life. In this way, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is possessed of speed. Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu possessed of these three qualities is worthy of gifts... an unsurpassed field of merit for the world.

Seventh Sutta.
249:
Seventh Sutta.

## 8. Potthaka Sutta

100. Bhikkhus, a new piece of coarse cloth is ugly in color, rough to the touch, and of little value. Bhikkhus, a middle-aged piece of coarse cloth is also ugly in color, rough to the touch, and of little value. Bhikkhus, an old piece of coarse cloth is also ugly in color, rough to the touch, and of little value. Bhikkhus, they use an old piece of coarse cloth as a cleaning rag or throw it away on a rubbish heap.

In the same way, bhikkhus, if a newly ordained bhikkhu is immoral and of evil nature, I say this is his ugliness in color. Bhikkhus, just as that new coarse cloth is ugly in color, I say this person is like that. To those who associate with, attend upon, serve, and follow the example of that immoral bhikkhu, it leads to their harm and suffering for a long time. I say this is his roughness to the touch. Bhikkhus, just as that new coarse cloth is rough to the touch, I say this person is like that. When he receives robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick, the gift given to him does not have great fruit or great benefit. I say this is his being of little value. Bhikkhus, just as that new coarse cloth is of little value, I say this person is like that.

If a bhikkhu of middle standing... [is immoral and of evil nature...]. If an elder bhikkhu is immoral and of evil nature, I say this is his ugliness in color. Bhikkhus, just as that new coarse cloth is ugly in color, I say this person is like that. To those who associate with, attend upon, serve, and follow the example of that immoral bhikkhu, it leads to their harm and suffering for a long time. I say this is his roughness to the touch. Bhikkhus, just as that new coarse cloth is rough to the touch, I say this person is like that. When he receives robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick, the gift given to him does not have great fruit or great benefit. I say this is his being of little value. Bhikkhus, just as that new coarse cloth is of little value, I say this person is like that.

Bhikkhus, if such an elder bhikkhu speaks in the midst of the Saṅgha, the bhikkhus say to him: 'What is the use of the speech of a fool and incompetent person like you? Do you even think you should speak?' Being angry and displeased, he [speaks such words...]
250:
That immoral elder monk, being angry and displeased, utters words of such a nature that the Saṅgha expels him, just as one would discard that coarse hempen cloth on a rubbish heap.

“Monks, new Kāsī cloth is beautiful in color, pleasant to the touch, and of great value. Monks, Kāsī cloth of middle age is also beautiful in color, pleasant to the touch, and of great value. Monks, even old and worn-out Kāsī cloth is beautiful in color, pleasant to the touch, and of great value. Monks, even worn-out Kāsī cloth is used for wrapping jewels or is placed in a perfume casket.

“In the same way, monks, if a new monk is virtuous and of good character, I say this is his beauty of color. Monks, just as that Kāsī cloth is beautiful in color, I say this person is comparable to it. To those who associate with, attend upon, serve, and follow the example of that virtuous monk, it will be for their long-term welfare and happiness; I say this is his pleasantness of touch. Monks, just as that Kāsī cloth is pleasant to the touch, I say this person is comparable to it. For those who give robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick to that monk, their gift will be of great fruit and great benefit; I say this is his great value. Monks, just as that Kāsī cloth is of great value, I say this person is comparable to it. Monks, if a monk of middle standing... [as above]... Monks, if an elder monk... [as above]... I say this person is comparable to it.

“Monks, when such an elder monk speaks in the midst of the Saṅgha, the monks say: ‘Venerables, be quiet; the elder monk is reciting the Dhamma and the Vinaya.’ Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus: ‘We shall be like Kāsī cloth, not like coarse hempen cloth.’ Thus, monks, should you train yourselves.”

The eighth sutta.

## 9. Loṇakapalla Sutta

101. “Monks, if anyone were to say: ‘In whatever way this person performs an action (kamma), in that same way he experiences its result,’ if this were so, monks, there would be no living of the holy life, and no opportunity would be seen for the complete ending of suffering. Monks, if anyone were to say: ‘In whatever way this person performs an action that is to be experienced, in that same way he experiences its result,’
251:
if this were so, monks, the living of the holy life is possible, and the opportunity is seen for the complete ending of suffering. Monks, here, a certain person performs even a slight bad deed, and it leads him to hell. But here, monks, another person performs the same kind of slight bad deed, and it is to be experienced in this very life; not even a small bit of it appears [in the next life], let alone much.

“Monks, what kind of person is it whose slight bad deed leads him to hell? Here, monks, a certain person is undeveloped in body, undeveloped in virtue, undeveloped in mind, and undeveloped in wisdom; he is insignificant, of small character, and lives in misery. Monks, it is for such a person that a slight bad deed leads him to hell.

“Monks, what kind of person is it for whom the same kind of slight bad deed is to be experienced in this very life, and not even a small bit of it appears [in the next life], let alone much? Here, monks, a certain person is developed in body, developed in virtue, developed in mind, and developed in wisdom; he is not insignificant, is of great character, and lives immeasurably. Monks, it is for such a person that the same kind of slight bad deed is to be experienced in this very life, and not even a small bit of it appears [in the next life], let alone much.

“Suppose, monks, a man were to drop a salt crystal into a small cup of water. What do you think, monks? Would that small amount of water become salty and undrinkable because of that salt crystal?” “Yes, Bhante.” “Why is that?” “Because, Bhante, there is only a small amount of water in the cup, it would become salty and undrinkable by that salt crystal.” “Suppose, monks, a man were to drop a salt crystal into the Ganges River. What do you think, monks? Would the Ganges River become salty and undrinkable because of that salt crystal?” “No, Bhante.” “Why is that?” “Because, Bhante, the mass of water in the Ganges River is vast; that vast mass of water would not become salty or undrinkable by that salt crystal.”

“In the same way, monks, here, a certain person performs even a slight bad deed, and it leads him to hell. Monks, here, another person performs the same kind of slight bad deed, and it is to be experienced in this very life; not even a small bit of it appears [in the next life], let alone much.”
252:
Monks, what kind of person is it whose small evil deed leads him to hell? Here, monks, a certain person has not developed the body, has not developed virtue, has not developed the mind, and has not developed wisdom; he is limited, insignificant, and dwells in suffering. Monks, for such a person, a small evil deed leads him to hell.

Monks, what kind of person is it for whom a similar small evil deed is to be experienced in this very life, and not even a tiny bit of it appears in the next life, let alone much? Here, monks, a certain person has developed the body, has developed virtue, has developed the mind, and has developed wisdom; he is not limited, he is a great soul, and dwells in the immeasurable. Monks, for such a person, a similar small evil deed is to be experienced in this very life, and not even a tiny bit of it appears in the next life, let alone much. (1)

Monks, in this world, a certain person is imprisoned for even half a kahāpana, or for one kahāpana, or for a hundred kahāpanas. Monks, in this world, a certain person is not imprisoned for half a kahāpana, or for one kahāpana, or for a hundred kahāpanas.

Monks, what kind of person is imprisoned for half a kahāpana, for one kahāpana, or for a hundred kahāpanas? Here, monks, a certain person is poor, with little property and little wealth. Monks, such a poor person is imprisoned for half a kahāpana, for one kahāpana, or for a hundred kahāpanas.

Monks, what kind of person is not imprisoned for half a kahāpana, for one kahāpana, or for a hundred kahāpanas? Here, monks, a certain person is rich, with great wealth and great property. Monks, such a wealthy person is not imprisoned for half a kahāpana, for one kahāpana, or for a hundred kahāpanas. In the same way, monks, for a certain person, a small evil deed leads him to hell. Monks, for a certain person, a similar small evil deed is to be experienced in this very life, and not even a tiny bit of it appears in the next life, let alone much.

Monks, what kind of person is it whose small evil deed leads him to hell? Here, monks, a certain person has not developed the body, has not developed virtue, has not developed the mind...
253:
...has not developed wisdom; he is limited, insignificant, and dwells in suffering. Monks, for such a person, a small evil deed leads him to hell.

Monks, what kind of person is it for whom a similar small evil deed is to be experienced in this very life, and not even a tiny bit of it appears in the next life, let alone much? Here, monks, a certain person has developed the body, has developed virtue, has developed the mind, and has developed wisdom; he is not limited, he is a great soul, and dwells in the immeasurable. Monks, for such a person, a similar small evil deed is to be experienced in this very life, and not even a tiny bit of it appears in the next life, let alone much. (2)

Monks, in this world, a certain person has developed the body, has developed virtue, has developed the mind, and has developed wisdom; he is not limited, he is a great soul, and dwells in the immeasurable. Monks, for such a person, a similar small evil deed is to be experienced in this very life, and not even a tiny bit of it appears in the next life, let alone much.

Monks, in this world, a certain goat-owner or goat-slaughterer is able to kill, bind, fine, or deal with as he sees fit, someone who takes a goat that was not given. But he is not able to kill, bind, fine, or deal with as he sees fit, someone else who takes a goat that was not given. Monks, what kind of person can a goat-owner or goat-slaughterer kill, bind, fine, or deal with as he sees fit, for taking a goat that was not given? Here, monks, a certain person is poor, with little property and little wealth. Monks, a goat-owner or goat-slaughterer is able to kill, bind, fine, or deal with as he sees fit, such a person who takes a goat that was not given.

Monks, what kind of person can a goat-owner or goat-slaughterer not kill, bind, fine, or deal with as he sees fit, for taking a goat that was not given?
254:
Monks, in this world, a certain person is rich, with great wealth and great possessions. He is either a king or a great royal minister. Monks, a sheep-owner or a sheep-slayer is not able to kill, bind, fine, or deal with as he pleases such a person who takes a sheep without it being given. On the contrary, he begs him with joined palms: 'Give me, sir, the sheep or the price of the sheep.'

In the same way, monks, a certain person performs even a minor evil deed, and it leads him to hell. But here, monks, a certain person performs even a minor evil deed, and it is to be experienced in this very life; not even a tiny bit [of the result] appears [in the next life], let alone much.

Monks, what kind of person is it whose minor evil deed leads him to hell? Here, monks, a certain person has not cultivated the body, has not cultivated virtue, has not cultivated the mind, and has not cultivated wisdom; he is limited, small-souled, and lives in misery with even a small amount of evil. Monks, it is such a person whose minor evil deed leads him to hell.

Monks, what kind of person is it whose minor evil deed is to be experienced in this very life, where not even a tiny bit [of the result] appears [in the next life], let alone much? Here, monks, a certain person has cultivated the body, has cultivated virtue, has cultivated the mind, and has cultivated wisdom; he is not limited, he is great-souled, and he lives immeasurably. Monks, it is such a person whose minor evil deed is to be experienced in this very life, where not even a tiny bit [of the result] appears [in the next life], let alone much. (3)

Monks, if anyone should say: 'In whatever way a man performs a deed, in that same way he experiences its result,' if this were so, monks, there would be no living of the holy life, no opportunity would be seen for the complete ending of suffering. But if anyone should say: 'In whatever way a man performs a deed that is to be experienced, in that same way he experiences its result,' if this were so, monks, there would be the living of the holy life, and an opportunity would be seen for the complete ending of suffering.
255:
Ninth Sutta.

## 10. Paṃsudhovaka Sutta

102. Monks, there are coarse impurities of gold: soil, sand, gravel, and pebbles. A dirt-washer or his apprentice pours it into a trough and washes it, rinses it, and cleanses it. When those are abandoned and eliminated, there remain middle-sized impurities: fine pebbles and coarse sand. The dirt-washer or his apprentice washes it, rinses it, and cleanses it. When those are abandoned and eliminated, there remain fine impurities: fine sand and black dust. The dirt-washer or his apprentice washes it, rinses it, and cleanses it.

After those are abandoned and cleansed, only the gold grains remain. A goldsmith or his apprentice puts that gold into a crucible and blows on it, blows on it repeatedly, blows on it thoroughly. That gold, though blown, repeatedly blown, and thoroughly blown, is not yet free of defects, is not supple, is not wieldy, and is not radiant; it is brittle and not yet ready for workmanship. Monks, there comes a time when the goldsmith or his apprentice blows on that gold, blows on it repeatedly, and blows on it thoroughly. Then that gold is free of defects, supple, wieldy, and radiant; it is no longer brittle and is ready for workmanship. Whatever ornament he desires—whether a gold plate, earrings, a necklace, or a gold garland—it serves that purpose.

In the same way, monks, for a monk devoted to the higher mind, there are coarse defilements: bodily misconduct, verbal misconduct, and mental misconduct. A wise monk, possessed of a [developed] mind, abandons them, dispels them, eliminates them, and brings them to non-existence. When those are abandoned and eliminated, for a monk devoted to the higher mind, there remain middle-sized defilements: thoughts of sensuality, thoughts of ill-will, and thoughts of harming. A wise monk, possessed of a [developed] mind, abandons them, dispels them, eliminates them, and brings them to non-existence. When those are abandoned and eliminated, for a monk devoted to the higher mind, there remain fine defilements: thoughts of relatives, thoughts of country, and thoughts of reputation...
256:
When that [gross impurity] is abandoned and eliminated, there remain in the monk devoted to the higher mind subtle impurities: thoughts of kin, thoughts of country, and thoughts concerning reputation. A wise and capable monk abandons, dispels, eliminates, and brings them to non-existence. When these are abandoned and eliminated, there remain thoughts of the Dhamma. That concentration is not yet peaceful, not sublime, not attained by tranquility, and not reached through unification of mind; it is attained by the suppression of defilements with effort.

Monks, there comes a time when the mind stands firm internally, settles down, becomes unified, and concentrated. That concentration is peaceful, sublime, attained by tranquility, and reached through unification of mind; it is not attained by the suppression of defilements with effort. To whatever state realizable by higher knowledge he directs his mind for realization, he achieves the capacity to witness it in each case, given the presence of the necessary conditions.

"If he wishes: 'May I experience manifold psychic powers—having been one, may I become many; having been many, may I become one; may I become visible or invisible; may I go unhindered through walls, enclosures, and mountains as if through space; may I dive in and out of the earth as if in water; may I walk on water without sinking as if on earth; may I travel through the sky cross-legged like a winged bird; may I touch and stroke with my hand these sun and moon, so mighty and powerful; may I exercise mastery with my body as far as the Brahma-world'—he achieves the capacity to witness it in each case, given the presence of the necessary conditions.

"If he wishes: 'With the divine ear-element, purified and surpassing that of humans, may I hear both kinds of sounds, the divine and the human, whether far or near'—he achieves the capacity to witness it in each case, given the presence of the necessary conditions.

"If he wishes: 'May I know the minds of other beings and other individuals, having encompassed them with my own mind. May I know a mind with lust as a mind with lust, and a mind without lust as a mind without lust.'"
257:
"May I know a mind with hatred as a mind with hatred, and a mind without hatred as a mind without hatred; a mind with delusion as a mind with delusion, and a mind without delusion as a mind without delusion; a contracted mind as a contracted mind, and a distracted mind as a distracted mind; an exalted mind as an exalted mind, and an unexalted mind as an unexalted mind; a surpassable mind as a surpassable mind, and an unsurpassable mind as an unsurpassable mind; a concentrated mind as a concentrated mind, and an unconcentrated mind as an unconcentrated mind; a liberated mind as a liberated mind, and an unliberated mind as an unliberated mind'—he achieves the capacity to witness it in each case, given the presence of the necessary conditions.

"If he wishes: 'May I recollect my manifold past lives, that is, one birth, two births, three births, four births, five births, ten births, twenty births, thirty births, forty births, fifty births, a hundred births, a thousand births, a hundred thousand births, many aeons of world-contraction, many aeons of world-expansion, many aeons of world-contraction and expansion: "There I had such a name, belonged to such a clan, had such an appearance, such food, such experience of pleasure and pain, and such a lifespan; passing away from there, I reappeared elsewhere; there too I had such a name, belonged to such a clan, had such an appearance, such food, such experience of pleasure and pain, and such a lifespan; passing away from there, I reappeared here." Thus may I recollect my manifold past lives with their modes and details'—he achieves the capacity to witness it in each case, given the presence of the necessary conditions.

"If he wishes: 'With the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans, may I see beings passing away and reappearing—lowly and exalted, beautiful and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate—and may I understand how beings pass on according to their kamma: "These worthy beings who were ill-conducted in body, speech, and mind, who reviled the noble ones, held wrong views, and undertook kamma based on wrong views, with the breakup of the body, after death, have reappeared in a state of misery, a bad destination, a state of ruin, even in hell. But these worthy beings who were well-conducted in body, speech, and mind, who did not revile the noble ones..."'"
258:
'...they have right view and undertake actions based on right view. These beings, with the breaking up of the body after death, have reappeared in a happy destination, in a heavenly world.' Thus, with the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans, I would see beings passing away and reappearing—inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate—and I would understand how beings pass on according to their kamma.' If that person so desires, and the necessary conditions are present, he attains the capacity to be a witness in each of those respective areas (the direct knowledge of the divine eye).

'By the destruction of the taints, may I enter and dwell in the taintless liberation of mind, liberation by wisdom, having realized it for myself with direct knowledge in this very life.' If that person so desires, and the necessary conditions are present, he attains the capacity to be a witness in each of those respective areas (the attainment of the fruition of arahantship).

The Tenth Sutta.

## 11. Nimitta Sutta

103. "Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu who is devoted to the higher mind (samatha and vipassanā) should from time to time give attention to three signs. He should from time to time give attention to the sign of concentration; he should from time to time give attention to the sign of exertion; he should from time to time give attention to the sign of equanimity. Bhikkhus, if a bhikkhu devoted to the higher mind were to give attention only to the sign of concentration, it is possible that his mind would lead to laziness. Bhikkhus, if a bhikkhu devoted to the higher mind were to give attention only to the sign of exertion, it is possible that his mind would lead to restlessness. Bhikkhus, if a bhikkhu devoted to the higher mind were to give attention only to the sign of equanimity, it is possible that his mind would not be properly concentrated for the destruction of the taints. But, bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu devoted to the higher mind from time to time gives attention to the sign of concentration, from time to time gives attention to the sign of exertion, and from time to time gives attention to the sign of equanimity, then his mind becomes malleable, wieldy, and radiant; it is not brittle and is properly concentrated for the destruction of the taints.

Bhikkhus, just as a goldsmith or a goldsmith's apprentice might prepare a furnace, and having prepared the furnace, light the opening of the furnace, and having lit the opening of the furnace, take the gold with tongs and place it in the opening of the furnace (in a crucible), and from time to time blow on it..."
259: "...from time to time he sprinkles it with water, and from time to time he looks on with equanimity. Monks, if the goldsmith or his apprentice were to blow on that gold exclusively, it would likely burn. If he were to sprinkle it with water exclusively, it would likely cool down. If he were to look on with equanimity exclusively, it would likely not reach full refinement. But, monks, when the goldsmith or his apprentice blows on that gold from time to time, sprinkles it with water from time to time, and looks on with equanimity from time to time, that gold becomes malleable, wieldy, and radiant; it is not brittle and it is properly fit for work. Then, whatever kind of ornament he wishes to create—whether a gold plate, earrings, a necklace, or a golden garland—it serves his purpose. In the same way, monks, a bhikkhu who is devoted to the higher mind (adhicitta) should attend to three signs from time to time. From time to time, he should attend to the sign of concentration; from time to time, he should attend to the sign of exertion; from time to time, he should attend to the sign of equanimity. Monks, if a bhikkhu devoted to the higher mind were to attend exclusively to the sign of concentration, it is possible that his mind would lead to laziness. Monks, if a bhikkhu devoted to the higher mind were to attend exclusively to the sign of exertion, it is possible that his mind would lead to restlessness. Monks, if a bhikkhu devoted to the higher mind were to attend exclusively to the sign of equanimity, it is possible that his mind would not be properly concentrated for the destruction of the taints. But, monks, when a bhikkhu devoted to the higher mind attends from time to time to the sign of concentration, from time to time to the sign of exertion, and from time to time to the sign of equanimity, then his mind becomes malleable, wieldy, and radiant; it is not brittle and it is properly concentrated for the destruction of the taints. He then directs his mind toward the realization by direct knowledge of whatever state is to be realized by direct knowledge..."
260: "...when the basis exists (such as the causes from previous lives and the concentration that is the basis for direct knowledge in this life), he attains the capacity to realize by direct knowledge (such as the various psychic powers) in each and every case. If he wishes: 'May I exercise the various kinds of psychic power...' [The six direct knowledges are to be expanded in detail] ... 'May I, by the destruction of the taints... realize and dwell in it,' if he so wishes, when the basis exists, he attains the capacity to realize it by direct knowledge in each and every case." The Eleventh Discourse. The Chapter on the Grain of Salt (Loṇakapalla-vagga), the fifth. The Summary: Urgent, Seclusion, Autumn, Assemblies (three), Thoroughbreds, and the Bark-cloth, Salt, Washing, and the Signs. The Second Fifty (Discourses) is complete.
261:
Eleventh Sutta.
The fifth, Loṇakapalla Vagga, is finished.
The second fifty suttas are finished.

## 3. Tatiya Paṇṇāsaka
3. The Third Fifty

## (11) 1. Sambodha Vagga

## 1. Pubbeva Sambodha Sutta

104. "Bhikkhus, before my enlightenment, while I was still an unenlightened Bodhisatta, the thought occurred to me: 'What is the gratification in the world, what is the danger, and what is the escape?' Then, bhikkhus, the thought occurred to me: 'The pleasure and joy that arise dependent on the world—this is the gratification in the world. That the world is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change—this is the danger in the world. The removal and abandoning of desire and lust for the world—this is the escape from the world.'

Bhikkhus, as long as I did not fully and truly understand the gratification as gratification, the danger as danger, and the escape as escape in this world, I did not claim to have realized the peerless supreme enlightenment in this world with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās, in this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its princes and people. But, bhikkhus, when I fully and truly understood the gratification as gratification, the danger as danger, and the escape as escape in this world, then I claimed to have realized the peerless supreme enlightenment in this world with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās, in this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its princes and people. The knowledge and vision arose in me: 'Unshakeable is my liberation; this is my last birth; now there is no more rebirth.'"

The First Sutta.

## 2. Paṭhama Assāda Sutta

105. "Bhikkhus, I wandered seeking the gratification of the world. I found that gratification in the world. Whatever gratification there is in the world, I have seen it clearly with wisdom (of insight and the path). Bhikkhus, I wandered seeking the danger of the world.
262:
I found that danger in the world. Whatever danger there is in the world, I have seen it clearly with wisdom (of insight and the path). Bhikkhus, I wandered seeking the escape from the world. I found that escape from the world. Whatever escape there is from the world, I have seen it clearly with wisdom (of insight and the path).

Bhikkhus, as long as I did not fully and truly understand the gratification as gratification, the danger as danger, and the escape as escape in this world, I did not claim to have realized the peerless supreme enlightenment in this world with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās, in this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its princes and people. But, bhikkhus, when I fully and truly understood the gratification as gratification, the danger as danger, and the escape as escape in this world, then I claimed to have realized the peerless supreme enlightenment in this world with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās, in this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its princes and people. The knowledge and vision arose in me: 'Unshakeable is my liberation; this is my last birth; now there is no more rebirth.'"

The Second Sutta.

## 3. Dutiya Assāda Sutta

106. "Bhikkhus, if there were no gratification in the world, beings would not be enamored with it. But because there is gratification in the world, beings are enamored with it. Bhikkhus, if there were no danger in the world, beings would not be disenchanted with it. But because there is danger in the world, beings are disenchanted with it. Bhikkhus, if there were no escape from the world, beings would not escape from the world. But because there is an escape from the world, beings escape from the world.

Bhikkhus, as long as beings do not fully and truly understand the gratification as gratification, the danger as danger, and the escape as escape in this world, they do not dwell detached, released, and liberated from this world with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās, from this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its princes and people, with a mind that has transcended boundaries (free from defilements and the cycle of existence)."
263:
Monks, when one understands as they really are the gratification of the world as gratification, its danger as danger, and the escape from it as escape, then beings—including the world of devas, Māras, and Brahmās, and this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its princes and people—dwell having escaped, detached, and released from the world, with a mind that has made boundaries non-existent.

The Third Sutta.

## 4. Samaṇabrāhmaṇa Sutta
107. Monks, whatever ascetics or brahmins do not understand as they really are the gratification of the world as gratification, its danger as danger, and the escape from it as escape; monks, these ascetics or brahmins are not considered by me to be true ascetics among ascetics, nor true brahmins among brahmins. Furthermore, these venerable ones do not, in this very life, realize for themselves through direct knowledge the goal of asceticism (the Noble Path) or the goal of brahminhood (the Noble Fruit), and having attained it, dwell therein.

Monks, whatever ascetics or brahmins understand as they really are the gratification of the world as gratification, its danger as danger, and the escape from it as escape; monks, these ascetics or brahmins are considered by me to be true ascetics among ascetics, and true brahmins among brahmins. Furthermore, these venerable ones, in this very life, realize for themselves through direct knowledge the goal of asceticism (the Noble Path) and the goal of brahminhood (the Noble Fruit), and having attained it, dwell therein.

The Fourth Sutta.

## 5. Ruṇṇa Sutta
108. Monks, in the Discipline of the Noble One, singing is wailing. Monks, in the Discipline of the Noble One, dancing is madness. Monks, in the Discipline of the Noble One, excessive laughing that shows the teeth is childish. Therefore, monks, in this Dispensation, the bridge to singing should be destroyed, the bridge to dancing should be destroyed. For you who are virtuous and delighted in the Dhamma, a mere smile is appropriate.

The Fifth Sutta.

## 6. Atitti Sutta
109. Monks, there is no satiety in the indulgence of three things. What three? Monks, there is no satiety in the indulgence of sleep.
264:
Monks, there is no satiety in the indulgence of drinking fermented and distilled liquors. Monks, there is no satiety in the indulgence of sexual intercourse. Monks, there is no satiety in the indulgence of these three things.

The Sixth Sutta.

## 7. Arakk hita Sutta
110. Then the householder Anāthapiṇḍika approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, and sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, the Blessed One said to him:

"Householder, when the mind is unprotected, bodily actions are also not considered protected, verbal actions are also not considered protected, and mental actions are also not considered protected. For one who does not protect bodily, verbal, and mental actions, the bodily action becomes wet (with defilements), the verbal action becomes wet, and the mental action becomes wet. For one whose bodily, verbal, and mental actions are wet, the bodily action becomes rotten, the verbal action becomes rotten, and the mental action becomes rotten. For one whose bodily, verbal, and mental actions are rotten, there is no auspicious death, no auspicious passing away.

Householder, just as when a peaked house is poorly roofed, the peak is not considered protected, the rafters are not considered protected, and the walls are not considered protected; the peak becomes wet (with rain), the rafters become wet, and the walls become wet; the peak becomes rotten, the rafters become rotten, and the walls become rotten;

Householder, in the same way, when the mind is unprotected, bodily actions are also not considered protected, verbal actions are also not considered protected, and mental actions are also not considered protected. For one who does not protect bodily, verbal, and mental actions, the bodily action becomes wet (with defilements), the verbal action becomes wet, and the mental action becomes wet. For one whose bodily, verbal, and mental actions are wet, the bodily action becomes rotten, the verbal action becomes rotten, and the mental action becomes rotten. For one whose bodily, verbal, and mental actions are rotten, there is no auspicious death, no auspicious passing away."
265:
“Householder, when the mind is protected, bodily action is also protected, verbal action is also protected, and mental action is also protected. For one whose bodily, verbal, and mental actions are protected, the bodily action is not soaked (by defilements), the verbal action is not soaked, and the mental action is not soaked. For one whose bodily, verbal, and mental actions are not soaked, the bodily action does not rot, the verbal action does not rot, and the mental action does not rot. For one whose bodily, verbal, and mental actions do not rot, there can be a good death, there can be a good passing away.

Householder, just as when a peaked house is well-roofed, the peak is protected, the rafters are protected, and the walls are protected. The peak is not soaked (by rainwater), the rafters are not soaked, and the walls are not soaked. The peak does not rot, the rafters do not rot, and the walls do not rot.

In the same way, householder, when the mind is protected, bodily action is also protected, verbal action is also protected, and mental action is also protected. For one whose bodily, verbal, and mental actions are protected, the bodily action is not soaked (by defilements), the verbal action is not soaked, and the mental action is not soaked. For one whose bodily, verbal, and mental actions are not soaked, the bodily action does not rot, the verbal action does not rot, and the mental action does not rot. For one whose bodily, verbal, and mental actions do not rot, there can be a good death, there can be a good passing away,” (the Buddha said).

The Seventh Sutta.

## 8. Byāpanna Sutta

111. While the householder Anāthapiṇḍika was sitting to one side, the Blessed One said this to him: “Householder, when the mind is corrupted, bodily action is also corrupted, verbal action is also corrupted, and mental action is also corrupted. For one whose bodily, verbal, and mental actions are corrupted, there cannot be a good death, there cannot be a good passing away. Householder, just as when a peaked house is poorly roofed, the peak is corrupted, the rafters are corrupted, the wall is corrupted,”
266:
“the wall is also corrupted. In the same way, householder, when the mind is corrupted, bodily action is also corrupted, verbal action is also corrupted, and mental action is also corrupted. For one whose bodily, verbal, and mental actions are corrupted, there cannot be a good death, there cannot be a good passing away.

Householder, when the mind is not corrupted, bodily action is also not corrupted, verbal action is also not corrupted, and mental action is also not corrupted. For one whose bodily, verbal, and mental actions are not corrupted, there can be a good death, there can be a good passing away. Householder, just as when a peaked house is well-roofed, the peak is not corrupted, the rafters are not corrupted, and the walls are not corrupted. In the same way, householder, when the mind is not corrupted, bodily action is also not corrupted, verbal action is also not corrupted, and mental action is also not corrupted. For one whose bodily, verbal, and mental actions are not corrupted, there can be a good death, there can be a good passing away,” (the Buddha said).

The Eighth Sutta.

## 9. Paṭhama Nidāna Sutta

112. Monks, there are these three causes for the origination of kamma (that causes the suffering of the round of rebirths). Which three? Greed is a cause for the origination of kamma, hatred is a cause for the origination of kamma, and delusion is a cause for the origination of kamma. Monks, whatever kamma is performed through greed, born of greed, having greed as its cause (nidāna), having greed as its source (samudaya), that kamma is unwholesome. That kamma is blameworthy. That kamma has suffering as its result. That kamma leads to the origination of (further) kamma (that causes the suffering of the round of rebirths); that kamma does not lead to the cessation of kamma. Monks, whatever kamma is performed through hatred, born of hatred, having hatred as its cause (nidāna), having hatred as its source (samudaya), that kamma is unwholesome. That kamma is blameworthy. That kamma has suffering as its result. That kamma leads to the origination of (further) kamma; that kamma does not lead to the cessation of kamma. Monks, whatever kamma is performed through delusion, born of delusion, having delusion as its cause (nidāna), having delusion as its source (samudaya), that kamma is unwholesome. That kamma is blameworthy. That kamma has suffering as its result. That kamma leads to the origination of (further) kamma; that kamma does not lead to the cessation of kamma. Monks, these are the three causes for the origination of kamma.

Monks, there are these three causes for the origination of kamma (that leads to Nibbāna, the end of the round of rebirths). Which three? Non-greed is a cause for the origination of kamma, non-hatred is a cause for the origination of kamma, and non-delusion is a cause for the origination of kamma. Monks, whatever kamma is performed through non-greed, born of non-greed, having non-greed as its cause (nidāna),”
267:
Kamma that has non-greed as its origin (samudaya) is wholesome; that kamma is blameless; that kamma has happiness as its result; that kamma leads to the cessation of kamma; that kamma does not lead to the arising of kamma (which causes the suffering of the round).

Monks, kamma that is performed through non-hatred, born of non-hatred, with non-hatred as its source (nidāna), and non-hatred as its origin (samudaya), is wholesome; that kamma is blameless; that kamma has happiness as its result; that kamma leads to the cessation of kamma; that kamma does not lead to the arising of kamma.

Monks, kamma that is performed through non-delusion, born of non-delusion, with non-delusion as its source (nidāna), and non-delusion as its origin (samudaya), is wholesome; that kamma is blameless; that kamma has happiness as its result; that kamma leads to the cessation of kamma; that kamma does not lead to the arising of kamma. Monks, these are the three sources for the arising of kamma (that leads to Nibbāna, where the round of suffering is absent).

The Ninth Sutta.

## 10. Dutiya Nidāna Sutta

113. Monks, there are these three sources for the arising of kamma (that causes the suffering of the round). What are the three? Monks, desire (chanda) arises based on past things that are grounds for desire and lust (chandarāga). Monks, desire arises based on future things that are grounds for desire and lust. Monks, desire arises based on present things that are grounds for desire and lust.

And how, monks, does desire arise based on past things that are grounds for desire and lust? Monks, one repeatedly thinks and repeatedly ponders with the mind on past things that are grounds for desire and lust. For one who repeatedly thinks and ponders with the mind on past things that are grounds for desire and lust, desire arises. One in whom desire has arisen is fettered to those things. Monks, I call this intense lust of the mind a 'fetter' (saṃyojana). Thus, monks, desire arises based on past things that are grounds for desire and lust.

And how, monks, does desire arise based on future things that are grounds for desire and lust? Monks, one repeatedly thinks and repeatedly ponders with the mind on future things that are grounds for desire and lust. For one who repeatedly thinks and ponders with the mind on future things that are grounds for desire and lust, desire arises. One in whom desire has arisen is fettered to those things. Monks, I call this intense lust of the mind a 'fetter' (saṃyojana). Thus, monks, desire arises based on future things that are grounds for desire and lust.

And how, monks, does desire arise based on present things that are grounds for desire and lust? Monks, one repeatedly thinks and repeatedly ponders with the mind on present things that are grounds for desire and lust...
268:
...repeatedly thinks and repeatedly ponders. For one who repeatedly thinks and ponders with the mind on present things that are grounds for desire and lust, desire arises. One in whom desire has arisen is fettered to those things. Monks, I call this intense lust of the mind a 'fetter' (saṃyojana). Thus, monks, desire arises based on present things that are grounds for desire and lust. Monks, these are the three sources for the arising of kamma (that causes the suffering of the round).

Monks, there are these three sources for the arising of kamma (that leads to Nibbāna, where the round of suffering is absent). What are the three? Monks, desire does not arise based on past things that are grounds for desire and lust. Monks, desire does not arise based on future things that are grounds for desire and lust. Monks, desire does not arise based on present things that are grounds for desire and lust.

And how, monks, does desire not arise based on past things that are grounds for desire and lust? Monks, one understands the future result of past things that are grounds for desire and lust. Having understood the future result, one turns away from that result; having turned away from that result, one penetrates it with the mind and sees it clearly with wisdom (paññā). Thus, monks, desire does not arise based on past things that are grounds for desire and lust.

And how, monks, does desire not arise based on future things that are grounds for desire and lust? Monks, one understands the future result of future things that are grounds for desire and lust. Having understood the future result, one turns away from that result; having turned away from that result, one penetrates it with the mind and sees it clearly with wisdom. Thus, monks, desire does not arise based on future things that are grounds for desire and lust.

And how, monks, does desire not arise based on present things that are grounds for desire and lust? Monks, one understands the future result of present things that are grounds for desire and lust. Having understood the future result, one turns away from that result; having turned away from that result, one penetrates it with the mind and sees it clearly with wisdom. Thus, monks, desire does not arise based on present things that are grounds for desire and lust. Monks, these are the three sources for the arising of kamma.

The Tenth Sutta.

The First Chapter: The Chapter on Enlightenment (Sambodhavagga).
269:
Monks, these are the three causes for the arising of kamma (that leads to the cessation of the suffering of the round of rebirths).

Tenth Sutta.
The first chapter, the Sambodhi Vagga, is finished.

## (12) 2. Āpāyika Vagga
## 1. Āpāyika Sutta

114. Monks, because of not abandoning these low qualities, there are these three types of people who go to the plane of misery and are reborn in hell. What three? One who, while leading an unholy life, claims to lead the holy life; one who falsely accuses a pure person leading the holy life of an unholy life without grounds; and one who has such a speech and such a view: 'There is no fault in sensual pleasures,' and thus indulges in sensual pleasures through that view. Monks, because of not abandoning these low qualities, these are the three types of people who go to the plane of misery and are reborn in hell.

First Sutta.

## 2. Dullabha Sutta

115. Monks, the appearance of three persons is rare in the world. What three? The appearance of a Tathāgata, an Arahant, a Perfectly Self-Enlightened One is rare in the world. A person who teaches the Dhamma-Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata is rare in the world. A person who is grateful and thankful (kataññū katavedī) is rare in the world. Monks, the appearance of these three persons is rare in the world.

Second Sutta.

## 3. Appameyya Sutta

116. Monks, these three persons are found existing in the world. What three? The easily measurable person, the difficult-to-measure person, and the immeasurable person.

And what, monks, is the easily measurable person? Here, monks, a certain person is restless, puffed up, fickle, talkative, of loose speech, muddled in mindfulness, lacking clear comprehension, unconcentrated, with a wandering mind, and with uncontrolled faculties. This, monks, is called the easily measurable person.
270:
This, monks, is called the easily measurable person.

And what, monks, is the difficult-to-measure person? Here, monks, a certain person is not restless, not puffed up, not fickle, not talkative, not of loose speech, with established mindfulness, possessing clear comprehension, concentrated, with a one-pointed mind, and with restrained faculties. This, monks, is called the difficult-to-measure person.

And what, monks, is the immeasurable person? Here, monks, in this Dispensation, a bhikkhu is an Arahant, one whose taints are destroyed. This, monks, is called the immeasurable person. Monks, these three persons are found existing in the world.

Third Sutta.

## 4. Āneñja Sutta

117. Monks, these three persons are found existing in the world. What three? Here, monks, a certain person, by completely transcending perceptions of form, by the passing away of perceptions of sensory reaction, and by not attending to perceptions of diversity, thinking 'space is infinite,' enters and dwells in the sphere of infinite space. He finds enjoyment in that, desires that, and finds satisfaction in that. Established therein, focused on it, dwelling much in it, and not falling away from it, when he dies, he is reborn in the company of the devas of the sphere of infinite space. Monks, the lifespan of the devas of the sphere of infinite space is twenty thousand aeons.
