There, a worldling stays for the full lifespan, and having exhausted the entire lifespan of those devas, he goes to hell, to the animal realm, or to the realm of hungry ghosts. But a disciple of the Blessed One (one who has attained the lower fruits) stays there for the full lifespan, and having exhausted the entire lifespan of those devas, he attains final Nibbāna in that very sphere of infinite space. Monks, regarding the destination, the rebirth, and the worldling's going to a state of woe versus the noble one's attaining final Nibbāna, this is the distinction, this is the disparity, this is the difference between the learned noble disciple and the unlearned worldling; this is the superior effort, this is the distinction.

Furthermore, monks, here a certain person, by completely transcending the sphere of infinite space, thinking 'consciousness is infinite,' enters and dwells in the sphere of infinite consciousness. He finds enjoyment in that, desires that, and finds satisfaction in that. Established therein, focused on it, dwelling much in it, and not falling away from it, when he dies, he is reborn in the company of the devas of the sphere of infinite consciousness. Monks, the lifespan of the devas who have reached the sphere of infinite consciousness is forty thousand aeons.
271:
In that sphere of infinite consciousness, an ordinary person stays for the full life-span, and having exhausted the entire life-span of those devas, they go to hell, to the animal realm, or to the realm of hungry ghosts. However, a disciple of the Buddha (one established in the lower fruits) stays there for the full life-span, and having exhausted the entire life-span of those devas, they attain Parinibbāna in that very sphere of infinite consciousness. Bhikkhus, this is the distinction, this is the difference, this is the divergence between the well-instructed noble disciple and the uninstructed ordinary person, regarding the destination and rebirth.

Furthermore, bhikkhus, here a certain person, by completely transcending the sphere of infinite consciousness, thinking 'there is nothing', enters and dwells in the sphere of nothingness. He enjoys that, desires that, and finds satisfaction in that. Established therein, focused on it, dwelling much in it, and not falling away from it, when he dies, he is reborn in the company of the devas of the sphere of nothingness. Bhikkhus, the life-span of the devas who have reached the sphere of nothingness is sixty thousand mahākappas. There, an ordinary person stays for the full life-span, and having exhausted the entire life-span of those devas, they go to hell, to the animal realm, or to the realm of hungry ghosts. However, a disciple of the Buddha (one established in the lower fruits) stays there for the full life-span, and having exhausted the entire life-span of those devas, they attain Parinibbāna in that very sphere of nothingness. Bhikkhus, this is the distinction, this is the difference, this is the divergence between the well-instructed noble disciple and the uninstructed ordinary person, regarding the destination and rebirth. Bhikkhus, these three types of persons are found existing in the world.

The Fourth Sutta.

1. Rūpasaññā—perception occurring in the fine-material jhānas.
2. Paṭighasaññā—the five-fold consciousness that arises when the five sense objects such as forms strike the five sense bases such as the eye.
3. Various perceptions of the sense sphere other than paṭighasaññā.

## 5. Vipattisampadā Sutta
118. Bhikkhus, there are these three failures. What three? Failure in virtue, failure in mind, and failure in view. And what, bhikkhus, is failure in virtue? Here, bhikkhus, a certain person kills living beings, takes what is not given, engages in sexual misconduct, speaks falsehood, speaks malicious words, speaks harsh words, and engages in idle chatter. This, bhikkhus, is called failure in virtue.

And what, bhikkhus, is failure in mind? Here, bhikkhus, a certain person is covetous (abhijjhā) and has a mind of ill will. This, bhikkhus, is called failure in mind.

And what, bhikkhus, is failure in view?
272:
And what, bhikkhus, is failure in view? Here, bhikkhus, a certain person has wrong view and a distorted perspective: 'There is nothing given, there is nothing offered, there is no sacrifice, there is no fruit or result of good and bad actions, there is no this world, there is no other world, there is no mother, there is no father, there are no spontaneously reborn beings, there are no ascetics and brahmins in the world who have reached the right path and practiced rightly, who describe this world and the other world having realized it themselves through direct knowledge.' This, bhikkhus, is called failure in view. Bhikkhus, because of failure in virtue, beings, with the breakup of the body, after death, are reborn in the plane of misery, the bad destination, the lower world, in hell. Bhikkhus, because of failure in mind, beings, with the breakup of the body, after death, are reborn in the plane of misery, the bad destination, the lower world, in hell. Bhikkhus, because of failure in view, beings, with the breakup of the body, after death, are reborn in the plane of misery, the bad destination, the lower world, in hell. Bhikkhus, these are the three failures.

Bhikkhus, there are these three accomplishments. What three? Accomplishment in virtue, accomplishment in mind, and accomplishment in view. And what, bhikkhus, is accomplishment in virtue? Here, bhikkhus, a certain person abstains from killing living beings, abstains from taking what is not given, abstains from sexual misconduct, abstains from speaking falsehood, abstains from speaking malicious words, abstains from speaking harsh words, and abstains from idle chatter. This, bhikkhus, is called accomplishment in virtue.

And what, bhikkhus, is accomplishment in mind? Here, bhikkhus, a certain person is not covetous and has a mind without ill will. This, bhikkhus, is called accomplishment in mind.

And what, bhikkhus, is accomplishment in view? Here, bhikkhus, a certain person has right view and an undistorted perspective: 'There is what is given, there is what is offered, there is sacrifice, there is the fruit and result of good and bad actions, there is this world, there is the other world, there is mother, there is father, there are spontaneously reborn beings, there are ascetics and brahmins in the world who have reached the right path and practiced rightly, who describe this world and the other world having realized it themselves through direct knowledge.' This, bhikkhus, is called accomplishment in view. Bhikkhus, because of accomplishment in virtue, beings, with the breakup of the body, after death, are reborn in a good destination, in the heavenly world. Bhikkhus, because of accomplishment in mind, beings, with the breakup of the body, after death, are reborn in a good destination, in the heavenly world.
273:
"Monks, because of accomplishment in view, beings, with the breaking up of the body, after death, are reborn in a good destination, a heavenly world. Monks, these are the three accomplishments." (The Buddha said this).

The Fifth Sutta.

1. It means there is no fruit of giving.
2. It means there is no fruit of good or bad deeds done to one's mother.

## 6. Apaṇṇakasutta

119. "Monks, there are these three failures. Which three? Failure in virtue (sīlavipatti), failure in mind (cittavipatti), and failure in view (diṭṭhivipatti). And what, monks, is failure in virtue? Here, monks, someone is one who kills living beings... [pe]... is one who speaks frivolous speech. This, monks, is called failure in virtue.

And what, monks, is failure in mind? Here, monks, someone is full of covetousness (abhijjhā) and has a mind of ill-will. This, monks, is called failure in mind.

And what, monks, is failure in view? Here, monks, someone has wrong view and a distorted perspective: 'There is nothing given, there is nothing offered... [pe]... there are no ascetics and brahmins in the world who, having practiced rightly and conducted themselves well, proclaim this world and the next world after having realized it themselves through direct knowledge.' This, monks, is called failure in view. Monks, because of failure in virtue... [pe]... Monks, because of failure in view, beings, with the breaking up of the body, after death, are reborn in the plane of misery, the bad destination, the lower world, hell (niraya). Monks, just as a six-sided die, when thrown upwards, stands firmly on whichever side it lands; even so, monks, because of failure in virtue... [pe]... beings are reborn. Monks, these are the three failures.

Monks, there are these three accomplishments. Which three? Accomplishment in virtue (sīlasampadā), accomplishment in mind (cittasampadā), and accomplishment in view (diṭṭhisampadā). And what, monks, is accomplishment in virtue? Here, monks, someone abstains from killing living beings... [pe]... This, monks, is called accomplishment in virtue.

And what, monks, is accomplishment in mind? Here, monks, someone is not full of covetousness (abhijjhā) and does not have a mind of ill-will. This, monks, is called accomplishment in mind.

And what, monks, is accomplishment in view? Here, monks, someone has right view and an undistorted perspective: 'There is what is given, there is what is offered... [pe]... there are those in the world who, having realized it themselves through direct knowledge, proclaim this world and the next world.' This, monks, is called accomplishment in view. Monks, because of accomplishment in virtue, beings, with the breaking up of the body, after death, are reborn in a good destination, a heavenly world. Monks, because of accomplishment in mind... [pe]..."
274:
"...because of accomplishment in view, monks, beings, with the breaking up of the body, after death, are reborn in a good destination, a heavenly world. Monks, just as a six-sided die, when thrown upwards, stands firmly on whichever side it lands; even so, monks, because of accomplishment in virtue, beings, with the breaking up of the body, after death, are reborn in a good destination, a heavenly world. Because of accomplishment in mind... [pe]... because of accomplishment in view, beings, with the breaking up of the body, after death, are reborn in a good destination, a heavenly world. Monks, these are the three accomplishments." (The Buddha said this).

The Sixth Sutta.

## 7. Kammantasutta

120. "Monks, there are these three failures. Which three? Failure in action (kammantavipatti), failure in livelihood (ājīvavipatti), and failure in view (diṭṭhivipatti). And what, monks, is failure in action? Here, monks, someone kills living beings... [pe]... speaks frivolous speech. This, monks, is called failure in action.

And what, monks, is failure in livelihood? Here, monks, someone has wrong livelihood and makes a living through wrong livelihood. This, monks, is called failure in livelihood.

And what, monks, is failure in view? Here, monks, someone has wrong view and a distorted perspective: 'There is nothing given, there is nothing offered... [pe]... there are no ascetics and brahmins in the world who, having practiced rightly and conducted themselves well, proclaim this world and the next world after having realized it themselves through direct knowledge.' This, monks, is called failure in view. Monks, these are the three failures.

Monks, there are these three accomplishments. Which three? Accomplishment in action (kammantasampadā), accomplishment in livelihood (ājīvasampadā), and accomplishment in view (diṭṭhisampadā). And what, monks, is accomplishment in action? Here, monks, someone abstains from killing living beings... [pe]... abstains from frivolous speech. This, monks, is called accomplishment in action.

And what, monks, is accomplishment in livelihood? Here, monks, someone has right livelihood and makes a living through right livelihood. This, monks, is called accomplishment in livelihood.

And what, monks, is accomplishment in view? Here, monks, someone has right view and an undistorted perspective: 'There is what is given, there is what is offered... [pe]... there are ascetics and brahmins in the world who, having practiced rightly and conducted themselves well, proclaim this world and the next world after having realized it themselves through direct knowledge'—thus he has right view,"
275:
...has an undistorted view. Monks, this is called accomplishment in view. Monks, these are the three accomplishments.

The Seventh Sutta.

## 8. Pathama Soceyya Sutta

121. Monks, there are these three purities. Which three? Purity of body, purity of speech, and purity of mind. And what, monks, is purity of body? Here, monks, a certain person abstains from taking life, abstains from taking what is not given, and abstains from sexual misconduct. This, monks, is called purity of body.

And what, monks, is purity of speech? Here, monks, a certain person abstains from false speech, abstains from divisive speech, abstains from harsh speech, and abstains from idle chatter. This, monks, is called purity of speech.

And what, monks, is purity of mind? Here, monks, a certain person is not covetous (abhijjhā), has a mind without ill will, and has right view. This, monks, is called purity of mind. Monks, these are the three purities.

The Eighth Sutta.

## 9. Dutiya Soceyya Sutta

122. Monks, there are these three purities. Which three? Purity of body, purity of speech, and purity of mind. And what, monks, is purity of body? Here, monks, a bhikkhu abstains from taking life, abstains from taking what is not given, and abstains from unchastity (abrahmacariya). This, monks, is called purity of body.

And what, monks, is purity of speech? Here, monks, a bhikkhu abstains from false speech, abstains from divisive speech, abstains from harsh speech, and abstains from idle chatter. This, monks, is called purity of speech.

And what, monks, is purity of mind? Here, monks, when there is sensual desire (kāmacchanda) present within him, a bhikkhu understands clearly: 'There is sensual desire present within me.' When there is no sensual desire present within him, he understands clearly: 'There is no sensual desire present within me.' And how unarisen...
276:
...sensual desire arises, he understands that clearly; and how arisen sensual desire is abandoned, he understands that clearly; and how abandoned sensual desire does not arise again in the future, he understands that clearly. When there is ill will (byāpāda) present within him, he understands clearly: 'There is ill will present within me.' When there is no ill will present within him, he understands clearly: 'There is no ill will present within me.' And how unarisen ill will arises, he understands that clearly; and how arisen ill will is abandoned, he understands that clearly; and how abandoned ill will does not arise again in the future, he understands that clearly. When there is sloth and torpor (thīna-middha) present within him, he understands clearly: 'There is sloth and torpor present within me.' When there is no sloth and torpor present within him, he understands clearly: 'There is no sloth and torpor present within me.' And how unarisen sloth and torpor arises, he understands that clearly; and how arisen sloth and torpor is abandoned, he understands that clearly; and how abandoned sloth and torpor does not arise again in the future, he understands that clearly. When there is restlessness and remorse (uddhacca-kukkucca) present within him, he understands clearly: 'There is restlessness and remorse present within me.' When there is no restlessness and remorse present within him, he understands clearly: 'There is no restlessness and remorse present within me.' And how unarisen restlessness and remorse arises, he understands that clearly; and how arisen restlessness and remorse is abandoned, he understands that clearly; and how abandoned restlessness and remorse does not arise again in the future, he understands that clearly. When there is doubt (vicikicchā) present within him, he understands clearly: 'There is doubt present within me.' When there is no doubt present within him, he understands clearly: 'There is no doubt present within me.' And how unarisen doubt arises, he understands that clearly; and how arisen doubt is abandoned, he understands that clearly; and how abandoned doubt does not arise again in the future, he understands that clearly. Monks, this is called purity of mind. Monks, these are the three purities.

"Pure in body, pure in speech, pure in mind, without taints (āsavas), pure and endowed with purity—him they call one who has washed away evil."

The Ninth Sutta.

## 10. Moneyya Sutta

123. Monks, there are these three sagacities (moneyya). Which three? Sagacity of body, sagacity of speech, and sagacity of mind.
277:
...and the state of being a sage in the mind-door. Bhikkhus, what is bodily sagacity? Here, bhikkhus, in this Dispensation, a bhikkhu abstains from killing living beings, abstains from taking what is not given, and abstains from unchaste conduct. This, bhikkhus, is called bodily sagacity. 

Bhikkhus, what is verbal sagacity? Here, bhikkhus, in this Dispensation, a bhikkhu abstains from false speech, abstains from divisive speech, abstains from harsh speech, and abstains from idle chatter. This, bhikkhus, is called verbal sagacity. 

Bhikkhus, what is mental sagacity? Here, bhikkhus, in this Dispensation, with the destruction of the taints, a bhikkhu enters and dwells in the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, having realized them for himself in this very life through direct knowledge. This, bhikkhus, is called mental sagacity. (Thus He said). One who is a sage in body, a sage in speech, and a sage in mind, who is taintless and endowed with the quality of sagacity, is called one who has abandoned everything. 

The tenth sutta. 

The second, Apāyika Vagga, is finished. 

## (13) 3-Kusināra Vagga 
## 1-Kusināra Sutta 

124. On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Kusinārā in the Baliharaṇa wood. There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: "Bhikkhus!" "Venerable Sir," those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this: 

Bhikkhus, here in this Dispensation, a bhikkhu dwells depending on a certain village or town. A householder or a householder's son approaches him and invites him for the next day's meal.
278:
If he so desires, bhikkhus, the bhikkhu accepts. Then, when the night has passed, in the morning, he dresses, takes his bowl and outer robe, and goes to the house of that householder or householder's son. Having arrived, he sits on the prepared seat. Then the householder or householder's son serves and satisfies him with his own hands with choice food, both hard and soft, until he is full and refuses more. 

The thought occurs to him: "How good it is that this householder or householder's son serves and satisfies me with his own hands with choice food, both hard and soft!" And it also occurs to him: "Oh, may this householder or householder's son also in the future serve and satisfy me with his own hands with such choice food, both hard and soft!" He eats that almsfood tied to it, infatuated with it, obsessed by it, not seeing the danger, and not possessing the wisdom of escape. There in that village or town, he thinks sensual thoughts, thoughts of ill-will, and thoughts of cruelty. I say, bhikkhus, that a gift given to such a bhikkhu is not of great fruit. Why is that? Because, bhikkhus, the bhikkhu dwells negligently. 

But here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu dwells depending on a certain village or town. A householder or a householder's son approaches him and invites him for the next day's meal. If he so desires, bhikkhus, the bhikkhu accepts. Then, when the night has passed, in the morning, he dresses, takes his bowl and outer robe, and goes to the house of that householder or householder's son. Having arrived, he sits on the prepared seat. Then the householder or householder's son serves and satisfies him with his own hands with choice food, both hard and soft, until he is full and refuses more. 

The thought does not occur to him: "How good it is that this householder or householder's son serves and satisfies me with his own hands with choice food, both hard and soft!" And it also does not occur to him: "Oh, may this householder or householder's son also in the future serve and satisfy me with his own hands with such choice food, both hard and soft!" He eats that almsfood without being tied to it, not infatuated with it, not obsessed by it, seeing the danger, and possessing the wisdom of escape.
279:
"That bhikkhu, in that village or town, thinks thoughts of renunciation, thoughts of non-ill will, and thoughts of non-harming. Bhikkhus, I say that a gift given to such a bhikkhu is of great fruit. Why is that? Because, bhikkhus, that bhikkhu dwells diligent."

The First Sutta.

## 2. Bhandana Sutta

125. "Bhikkhus, in whatever direction bhikkhus dwell quarrelsome, contentious, and disputatious, stabbing each other with the weapons of the tongue, that direction is not pleasant for me even to think about, let alone to go to. I come to the conclusion: 'Surely those venerable ones have abandoned three things and have practiced three things much.' Which three things have they abandoned? Thoughts of renunciation, thoughts of non-ill will, and thoughts of non-harming—these three things they have abandoned. Which three things have they practiced much? Thoughts of sensual desire, thoughts of ill will, and thoughts of harming—these three things they have practiced much. Bhikkhus, in whatever direction bhikkhus dwell quarrelsome, contentious, and disputatious, stabbing each other with the weapons of the tongue, that direction is not pleasant for me even to think about, let alone to go to. I come to the conclusion: 'Surely those venerable ones have abandoned these three things and have practiced these three things much.'

But, bhikkhus, in whatever direction bhikkhus dwell in harmony, cordially, without disputes, blending like milk and water, looking at each other with eyes of affection, that direction is pleasant for me to go to, let alone to think about. I come to the conclusion: 'Surely those venerable ones have abandoned three things and have practiced three things much.' Which three things have they abandoned? Thoughts of sensual desire, thoughts of ill will, and thoughts of harming—these three things they have abandoned. Which three things have they practiced much? Thoughts of renunciation, thoughts of non-ill will, and thoughts of non-harming—these three things they have practiced much. Bhikkhus, in whatever direction bhikkhus dwell in harmony, cordially, without disputes, blending like milk and water, looking at each other with eyes of affection, that direction is pleasant for me to go to, let alone to think about. I come to the conclusion: 'Surely those venerable ones have abandoned these three things and have practiced these three things much.'"

The Second Sutta.
280:
The second sutta.

## 3. Gotamaka Cetiya Sutta
126. On one occasion, the Blessed One was staying at the Gotamaka Cetiya in Vesālī. There, the Blessed One addressed the monks: "Monks!" "Venerable Sir," those monks replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this:

"Monks, I teach the Dhamma with direct knowledge, not without direct knowledge. Monks, I teach the Dhamma with a cause, not without a cause. Monks, I teach the Dhamma with marvels, not without marvels. Since I, monks, teach the Dhamma with direct knowledge and not without direct knowledge, with a cause and not without a cause, with marvels and not without marvels, my exhortation is to be followed and my instruction is to be followed. And you, monks, have good reason to be satisfied, good reason to be glad, and good reason to be joyful: 'The Blessed One is perfectly enlightened, the Dhamma is well-expounded, the Saṅgha has practiced well.'"

The Blessed One said this. Those monks rejoiced in the Blessed One's words. And while this exposition was being spoken, the thousandfold world system shook.

The third sutta.

## 4. Bharandu Kālāma Sutta
127. On one occasion, the Blessed One was wandering on tour among the Kosalans and arrived at Kapilavatthu. Mahānāma the Sakyan heard: "The Blessed One, it is said, has arrived at Kapilavatthu." Then Mahānāma the Sakyan approached the Blessed One, paid homage, and sat down to one side. As Mahānāma the Sakyan was sitting to one side, the Blessed One said to him:

"Go, Mahānāma, into Kapilavatthu and find a suitable lodging where we may stay for one night." "Yes, Bhante," Mahānāma the Sakyan replied to the Blessed One, and after entering Kapilavatthu and wandering throughout the entire city, he did not see a suitable lodging in Kapilavatthu where the Blessed One might stay for one night.

Then Mahānāma the Sakyan approached the Blessed One and said to him: "Bhante, there is no suitable lodging in Kapilavatthu where the Blessed One might stay for one night."
281:
(However,) "Bhante, the ascetic Bharandu Kālāma was a former fellow-practitioner of the Blessed One. May the Blessed One stay for one night in his hermitage today," he said. "Go, Mahānāma, and prepare the bedding," (the Buddha said).

"Very well, Bhante," Mahānāma the Sakyan replied to the Blessed One and went to the hermitage of the ascetic Bharandu Kālāma. Having arrived, he prepared the bedding, set out water for washing the feet, and returned to the Blessed One. He said, "Bhante, the bedding is prepared, and the water for washing the feet is set out. Now is the time for the Blessed One to do as he sees fit (the Blessed One knows the time to go)."

Then the Blessed One went to the hermitage of the ascetic Bharandu Kālāma and sat on the prepared seat. Having sat down, the Blessed One washed his feet. Then Mahānāma the Sakyan thought, "It is not the right time to wait upon the Blessed One today. The Blessed One is tired. I will wait upon the Blessed One tomorrow." He paid homage to the Blessed One, performed a circumambulation, and departed.

When the night had passed, Mahānāma the Sakyan approached the Blessed One and sat to one side. As he was sitting there, the Blessed One said to him: "Mahānāma, there are these three types of teachers found in the world. What three? Here, Mahānāma, a certain teacher prescribes the full understanding of sensual pleasures (rūpāvacara jhāna), but not the full understanding of forms (arūpāvacara jhāna), nor the full understanding of feelings (Nibbāna). Here, Mahānāma, another teacher prescribes the full understanding of sensual pleasures and the full understanding of forms, but not the full understanding of feelings. Here, Mahānāma, another teacher prescribes the full understanding of sensual pleasures, the full understanding of forms, and the full understanding of feelings. These, Mahānāma, are the three types of teachers found in the world.

Mahānāma, is the goal (conclusion) of these three teachers the same, or is it different?" When this was said, the ascetic Bharandu Kālāma said to Mahānāma the Sakyan, "Mahānāma, say it is the same." When this was said, the Blessed One said to Mahānāma the Sakyan, "Mahānāma, say it is different." For a second time, the ascetic Bharandu Kālāma said to Mahānāma the Sakyan, "Mahānāma, say it is the same." For a second time, the Blessed One said to Mahānāma the Sakyan, "Mahānāma, say it is different."
282:
For a third time, the ascetic Bharandu Kālāma said to Mahānāma the Sakyan, "Mahānāma, say it is the same." For a third time, the Blessed One said to Mahānāma the Sakyan, "Mahānāma, say it is different."

Then the ascetic Bharandu Kālāma thought, "In the presence of the influential Mahānāma the Sakyan, the ascetic Gotama has rebuked me up to three times. It would be better if I were to leave Kapilavatthu." Then the ascetic Bharandu Kālāma left Kapilavatthu, departing never to return.

The Fourth Sutta.

## 5. Hatthaka Sutta

128. On one occasion, the Blessed One was staying at Sāvatthī in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇဍika's monastery. Then the young deva Hatthaka, when the night was far spent (at midnight), with a magnificent beauty that illuminated the entire Jeta's Grove, approached the Blessed One. Thinking, "I will stand before the Blessed One," (as he tried to stand) he sank down and foundered, unable to remain standing. Just as butter or oil poured onto sand sinks down and founders, unable to remain still, so too the young deva Hatthaka, thinking "I will stand before the Blessed One," sank down and foundered, unable to remain standing.

Then the Blessed One said to the young deva Hatthaka, "Hatthaka, create a coarse physical form."

"Very well, Bhante," the young deva Hatthaka replied to the Blessed One. He created a coarse physical form, paid homage to the Blessed One, and stood to one side. As he was standing there, the Blessed One said to him: "Hatthaka, are those teachings that you practiced before when you were a human being still practiced by you now that you are a deva?"

"Bhante, those teachings that I practiced before when I was a human being are still practiced by me now that I am a deva. And Bhante, those teachings that I had not yet practiced when I was a human being are also practiced by me now that I am a deva. Bhante, just as the Blessed One now stays surrounded by monks, nuns, male lay followers, female lay followers, kings, royal ministers, ascetics of other sects, and their disciples..."
283:
"In the same way, Bhante, I dwell crowded by the sons of devas. Bhante, even from afar, the sons of devas come to the presence of Hatthaka, the son of a deva, saying, 'We will listen to the Dhamma.' Bhante, I passed away without being satiated or weary of three things. Which three? Bhante, I passed away without being satiated or weary of seeing the Blessed One. Bhante, I passed away without being satiated or weary of hearing the True Dhamma. Bhante, I passed away without being satiated or weary of serving the Saṅgha. Bhante, I passed away without being satiated or weary of these three things."

"I never reached satiety in seeing the Blessed One, nor in serving the Saṅgha, nor in hearing the True Dhamma. Practicing the higher virtue (adhisīla), delighting in hearing the True Dhamma, Hatthaka, never satiated with these three things, has gone to the Aviha realm."

The Fifth Sutta.

## 6. Kaṭuviya Sutta

129. On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Vārāṇasī in the Deer Park at Isipatana. Then, in the morning, the Blessed One dressed, took his bowl and robe, and entered Vārāṇasī for alms. While walking for alms near the Goyoga-pilakkha tree, the Blessed One saw a certain bhikkhu who was empty of [spiritual] delight, seeking external delight, unmindful, lacking clear comprehension, unconcentrated, with a wandering mind and uncontrolled faculties. Seeing that bhikkhu, he said this:

"Bhikkhu, do not make yourself into refuse (kaṭuviya). Indeed, bhikkhu, it is impossible that flies would not descend upon and attack one who has made himself into refuse, who is moist with the stench of raw flesh."

Then that bhikkhu, being exhorted by this exhortation of the Blessed One, was struck with spiritual urgency (saṃvega). Then the Blessed One, having walked for alms in Vārāṇasī, after the meal, having returned from the alms round, addressed the bhikkhus: "Here, bhikkhus, in the morning, I dressed, took my bowl and robe, and entered Vārāṇasī for alms."
284:
"Bhikkhus, while walking for alms near the Goyoga-pilakkha tree, I saw a certain bhikkhu who was empty of delight, seeking external delight, unmindful, lacking clear comprehension, unconcentrated, with a wandering mind and uncontrolled faculties. Seeing that bhikkhu, I said this:

'Bhikkhu, do not make yourself into refuse. Indeed, bhikkhu, it is impossible that flies would not descend upon and attack one who has made himself into refuse, who is moist with the stench of raw flesh.'

Bhikkhus, then that bhikkhu, being exhorted by me with this exhortation, was struck with spiritual urgency (saṃvega)."

When this was said, a certain bhikkhu said to the Blessed One: "Bhante, what is refuse? What is the stench of raw flesh? What are the flies?"

"Bhikkhu, refuse is covetousness (abhijjhā). The stench of raw flesh is ill-will (byāpāda). The flies are evil unwholesome thoughts. Indeed, bhikkhu, it is impossible that flies would not descend upon and attack one who has made himself into refuse, who is moist with the stench of raw flesh."

"For one unguarded in the doors of the eye and ear, with uncontrolled faculties, the flies of wrong thoughts based on lust will descend. A bhikkhu who has become refuse, moist with the stench of raw flesh, is far from Nibbāna; he has only a share of distress. Whether in the village or the forest, a fool of poor wisdom, not having found peace for himself, wanders about surrounded by flies. But those endowed with virtue, delighting in the peace of wisdom, having destroyed the flies, dwell in peace and sleep happily."

The Sixth Sutta.

## 7. First Anuruddha Sutta

130. Then the Venerable Anuruddha approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, and sat down to one side. Sitting there, the Venerable Anuruddha said to the Blessed One: "Bhante, with the divine eye (dibba-cakkhu), which is purified and surpasses that of humans, I often see women, after the breakup of the body, after death, reborn in the plane of misery, the bad destination, the lower realm, in hell."
285:
"Venerable Sir, possessed of what qualities is a woman, after the breakup of the body, after death, reborn in a state of misery, a bad destination, a state of ruin, in hell?"

"Anuruddha, possessed of three qualities, a woman, after the breakup of the body, after death, is reborn in a state of misery, a bad destination, a state of ruin, in hell. Which three? Here, Anuruddha, a woman dwells at home in the morning with a heart obsessed by the stain of stinginess (macchariya); at midday she dwells at home with a heart obsessed by envy (issā); in the evening she dwells at home with a heart obsessed by sensual lust (kāmarāga). Anuruddha, possessed of these three qualities, a woman, after the breakup of the body, after death, is reborn in a state of misery, a bad destination, a state of ruin, in hell."

The Seventh Sutta.

## 8. Second Anuruddha Sutta

131. Then the Venerable Anuruddha approached the Venerable Sāriputta and exchanged greetings with him. When they had concluded their greetings and cordial talk, he sat down to one side. Sitting there, the Venerable Anuruddha said to the Venerable Sāriputta: "Friend Sāriputta, with the divine eye (dibba-cakkhu), purified and surpassing that of humans, I survey the thousandfold world system. My energy is aroused and unflagging, my mindfulness is established and unconfused, my body is tranquil and untroubled, and my mind is concentrated and one-pointed. Yet, despite this, my mind is not yet liberated from the taints (āsavas) through non-clinging."

"Friend Anuruddha, when you think, 'With the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans, I survey the thousandfold world system,' this is your conceit (māna). Friend Anuruddha, when you think, 'My energy is aroused and unflagging, my mindfulness is established and unconfused, my body is tranquil and untroubled, and my mind is concentrated and one-pointed,' this is your restlessness (uddhacca). Friend Anuruddha, when you think, 'Yet, despite this, my mind is not yet liberated from the taints through non-clinging,' this is your remorse (kukkucca). I urge you:"
286:
"It would be good if the Venerable Anuruddha, having abandoned these three things and not attending to them, would direct his mind to the Deathless element (nibbāna)."

After this was said, at a later time, the Venerable Anuruddha abandoned those three things, and without attending to them, directed his mind to the Deathless element. Then the Venerable Anuruddha, dwelling alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent, and resolute, soon realized for himself with direct knowledge, in this very life, that supreme goal of the holy life for the sake of which clansmen rightly go forth from the household life into homelessness, and having reached it, he remained in it. He knew through direct knowledge: "Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more for this state of being." And the Venerable Anuruddha became one of the Arahants.

The Eighth Sutta.

## 9. Paṭicchanna Sutta

132. "Monks, these three things carry prestige when they are hidden, not when they are open. Which three? A woman, monks, carries prestige when hidden, not when open. The mantras of the brahmins, monks, carry prestige when hidden, not when open. Wrong view, monks, carries prestige when hidden, not when open. Monks, these three things carry prestige when they are hidden, not when they are open.

Monks, these three things shine when they are open, not when they are hidden. Which three? The moon's disk, monks, shines when open, not when hidden. The sun's disk, monks, shines when open, not when hidden. The Dhamma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata, monks, shine when open, not when hidden. Monks, these three things shine when they are open, not when they are hidden."

The Ninth Sutta.

## 10. Lekha Sutta

133. "Monks, these three types of persons are found existing in the world. Which three? The person like an inscription in stone, the person like an inscription in the earth, and the person like an inscription in water. And what, monks, is the person like an inscription in stone? Here, monks, a certain person is frequently angry, and that anger of his..."
287:
Monks, in this world, a certain person is frequently angry, and that anger of his lingers for a long time. Monks, just as an inscription carved in rock is not quickly destroyed by wind or water and lasts for a long time, even so, monks, a certain person in this world is frequently angry, and that anger of his lingers for a long time. This person, monks, is called one like an inscription in rock.

Monks, what is the person like an inscription in the soil? Monks, in this world, a certain person is frequently angry, but that anger of his does not linger for a long time. Monks, just as an inscription scratched in the soil is quickly destroyed by wind or water and does not last for a long time, even so, monks, a certain person in this world is frequently angry, but that anger of his does not linger for a long time. This person, monks, is called one like an inscription in the soil.

Monks, what is the person like an inscription in water? Monks, in this world, a certain person, even when spoken to with harsh words, rough words, or unpleasant words, remains connected, friendly, and companionable. Monks, just as an inscription written in water quickly disappears and does not last for a long time, even so, monks, a certain person in this world, even when spoken to with harsh words, rough words, or unpleasant words, remains connected, friendly, and companionable. This person, monks, is called one like an inscription in water. Monks, these three types of persons are found existing in the world.

The Tenth Sutta.
The third, Kusināra Vagga, is finished.

## (14) 4. Yodhājīva Vagga
## 1. Yodhājīva Sutta
134. Monks, a warrior possessed of three qualities is worthy of a king, is an asset to a king, and is reckoned as a limb of the king. What are the three?
289:
“‘This is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering (Nibbāna),’ he understands as it really is. In this way, monks, a monk is one who pierces the target without fail.

And how, monks, is a monk one who pierces a great mass? Here, monks, a monk pierces the great mass of ignorance (avijjā). In this way, monks, a monk is one who pierces a great mass. Monks, a monk possessed of these three qualities is worthy of offerings, worthy of hospitality... an unsurpassed field of merit for the world,” (the Buddha said).

The First Sutta.

## 2. Pariṣā Sutta

135. “Monks, there are these three types of assemblies. Which three? The assembly disciplined without questioning because it is not difficult to discipline, the assembly disciplined by questioning because it is not easy to discipline, and the assembly disciplined by knowing the measure. Monks, these are the three types of assemblies,” (the Buddha said).

The Second Sutta.

## 3. Mitta Sutta

136. “Monks, a good friend possessed of three qualities should be associated with. Which three? He gives what is difficult to give, he does what is difficult to do, and he endures what is difficult to endure. Monks, a good friend possessed of these three qualities should be associated with,” (the Buddha said).

The Third Sutta.

## 4. Uppādā Sutta

137. “Monks, whether Tathāgatas arise or not, that element (dhātu) stands, the stability of the Dhamma (dhammaṭṭhitatā), the fixed course of the Dhamma (dhammaniyāmatā). All conditioned things are impermanent (anicca). The Tathāgata awakens to this and realizes it with wisdom. Having awakened to it and realized it with wisdom, he points it out, teaches it, describes it, establishes it, reveals it, analyzes it, and makes it clear: ‘All conditioned things are impermanent.’

Monks, whether Tathāgatas arise or not, that element (dhātu) stands, the stability of the Dhamma, the fixed course of the Dhamma. All conditioned things are suffering (dukkha). The Tathāgata awakens to this and realizes it with wisdom. Having awakened to it and realized it with wisdom,”
290:
“Having awakened to it and realized it with wisdom, he points it out, teaches it, describes it, establishes it, reveals it, analyzes it, and makes it clear: ‘All conditioned things are suffering.’

Monks, whether Tathāgatas arise or not, that element (dhātu) stands, the stability of the Dhamma, the fixed course of the Dhamma. All phenomena are non-self (anatta). The Tathāgata awakens to this and realizes it with wisdom. Having awakened to it and realized it with wisdom, he points it out, teaches it, describes it, establishes it, reveals it, analyzes it, and makes it clear: ‘All phenomena are non-self (anatta),’” (the Buddha said).

The Fourth Sutta.

## 5. Kesakambala Sutta

138. “Monks, of all garments woven with thread, a hair blanket (kesakambala) is said to be the worst. Monks, a hair blanket is cold in the cold season, hot in the hot season, of an ugly color, of a foul smell, and rough to the touch. Monks, just so, of all the many doctrines of recluses and brahmins, the doctrine of Makkhali is said to be the worst.

Monks, that fatuous man Makkhali Gosāla has such a view and such a doctrine as this: ‘There is no kamma, there is no action (kiriya), there is no effort (vīriya).’ Monks, those Arahants, the Perfectly Enlightened Ones who arose in the past, those Blessed Ones also taught that there is kamma, there is action, and there is effort. Monks, that fatuous man Makkhali opposes even those past Buddhas, saying: ‘There is no kamma, there is no action, there is no effort.’ Monks, those Arahants, the Perfectly Enlightened Ones who will arise in the future, those Blessed Ones will also teach that there is kamma, there is action, and there is effort. Monks, that fatuous man Makkhali opposes even those future Buddhas, saying: ‘There is no kamma, there is no action, there is no effort.’ Monks, I too, who am now an Arahant, a Perfectly Enlightened One, teach that there is kamma, there is action, and there is effort. Monks, that fatuous man Makkhali opposes me too, saying: ‘There is no kamma, there is no action, there is no effort.’

Monks, just as a fish trap (khippa) placed at a river mouth is for the harm, suffering, misfortune, and ruin of many fish; monks, just so, I think that fatuous man Makkhali Gosāla has appeared in the world as a ‘human-trap’ for the harm, suffering, misfortune, and ruin of many beings,” (the Buddha said).

The Fifth Sutta.
291:
Fifth Sutta.

## 6. Sampadā Sutta

139. "Monks, there are these three accomplishments. Which three? Accomplishment in faith, accomplishment in virtue, and accomplishment in wisdom. Monks, these are the three accomplishments," (He said).

Sixth Sutta.

## 7. Vuddhi Sutta

140. "Monks, there are these three growths. Which three? Growth in faith, growth in virtue, and growth in wisdom. Monks, these are the three growths," (He said).

Seventh Sutta.

## 8. Assakhaḷuṅka Sutta

141. "Monks, I will teach you three types of inferior horses and three types of inferior men. Listen to that teaching and pay close attention; I will speak." "Yes, Bhante," those monks replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this:

"Monks, what are the three types of inferior horses? Here, monks, a certain inferior horse is possessed of speed but not of beauty, nor of proportions. Here, monks, a certain inferior horse is possessed of speed and beauty, but not of proportions. Here, monks, a certain inferior horse is possessed of speed, beauty, and proportions. Monks, these are the three types of inferior horses.

Monks, what are the three types of inferior men? Here, monks, a certain inferior man is possessed of speed but not of beauty, nor of proportions. Here, monks, a certain inferior man is possessed of speed and beauty, but not of proportions. Here, monks, a certain inferior man is possessed of speed, beauty, and proportions.

Monks, how is an inferior man possessed of speed but not of beauty, nor of proportions? Here, monks, in this Dispensation, a monk understands as it really is, 'This is suffering.' ... [p] ... 'This is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering.' This understanding, I say, is the speed (of his knowledge). However, when asked a question regarding the Abhidhamma or the Abhivinaya, he falters and cannot answer."
292:
"This inability to answer, I say, is his lack of beauty (of quality). He does not receive robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick. This lack of receiving the four requisites, I say, is his lack of proportions. Thus, monks, an inferior man is possessed of speed but not of beauty, nor of proportions.

Monks, how is an inferior man possessed of speed and beauty, but not of proportions? Here, monks, in this Dispensation, a monk understands as it really is, 'This is suffering.' ... [p] ... 'This is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering.' ... [p] This understanding, I say, is the speed (of his knowledge). When asked a question regarding the Abhidhamma or the Abhivinaya, he can answer and does not falter. This ability to answer, I say, is his beauty (of quality). However, he does not receive robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick. This lack of receiving, I say, is his lack of proportions. Thus, monks, an inferior man is possessed of speed and beauty, but not of proportions.

Monks, how is an inferior man possessed of speed, beauty, and proportions? Here, monks, in this Dispensation, a monk understands as it really is, 'This is suffering.' ... [p] ... 'This is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering.' This understanding, I say, is the speed (of his knowledge). When asked a question regarding the Abhidhamma or the Abhivinaya, he can answer and does not falter. This ability to answer, I say, is his beauty (of quality). He receives robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick. This receiving, I say, is his proportions. Thus, monks, an inferior man is possessed of speed, beauty, and proportions. Monks, these are the three types of inferior men," (He said).

Eighth Sutta.

## 9. Assaparassa Sutta

142. "Monks, I will teach you three types of excellent horses and three types of excellent men. Listen to that teaching and pay close attention; I will speak." "Yes, Bhante," those monks replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this:
293:
What, bhikkhus, are the three excellent horses? Here, bhikkhus, a certain excellent horse is possessed of speed, but not of beauty, nor of proportions. Here, bhikkhus, a certain excellent horse is possessed of speed and beauty, but not of proportions. Here, bhikkhus, a certain excellent horse is possessed of speed, beauty, and proportions. These, bhikkhus, are the three excellent horses.

Bhikkhus, what are the three excellent men? Here, bhikkhus, a certain excellent man is possessed of speed, but not of beauty, nor of proportions. Here, bhikkhus, a certain excellent man is possessed of speed and beauty, but not of proportions. Here, bhikkhus, a certain excellent man is possessed of speed, beauty, and proportions.

And how, bhikkhus, is an excellent man possessed of speed, but not of beauty, nor of proportions? Here, bhikkhus, with the utter destruction of the five lower fetters, a bhikkhu is of spontaneous birth, attaining final Nibbāna there, not subject to return from that world. This, I say, is his speed. When asked a question concerning the Abhidhamma or the Abhivinaya, he falters and does not answer. This, I say, is his lack of beauty. He is not one who receives robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick. This, I say, is his lack of proportions. Thus, bhikkhus, an excellent man is possessed of speed, but not of beauty, nor of proportions.

And how, bhikkhus, is an excellent man possessed of speed and beauty, but not of proportions? Here, bhikkhus, with the utter destruction of the five lower fetters, a bhikkhu is of spontaneous birth, attaining final Nibbāna there, not subject to return from that world. This, I say, is his speed. When asked a question concerning the Abhidhamma or the Abhivinaya, he answers and does not falter. This, I say, is his beauty. He is not one who receives robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick. This, I say, is his lack of proportions. Thus, bhikkhus, an excellent man is possessed of speed and beauty, but not of proportions.

## 10. Assājānīya Sutta

143. "Bhikkhus, I will teach you the three noble thoroughbred horses and the three noble thoroughbred men. Listen and attend closely to it; I will speak." "Yes, Bhante," those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this:

Bhikkhus, what are the three noble thoroughbred horses? Here, bhikkhus... [as before] ...a certain noble thoroughbred horse is possessed of speed, beauty, and proportions. These, bhikkhus, are the three noble thoroughbred horses.

Bhikkhus, what are the three noble thoroughbred men? Here, bhikkhus... [as before] ...a certain noble thoroughbred man is possessed of speed, beauty, and proportions.

And how, bhikkhus, is a noble thoroughbred man... [as before] ...possessed of speed, beauty, and proportions? Here, bhikkhus, with the destruction of the taints, a bhikkhu enters and dwells in the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, having realized it for himself by direct knowledge in this very life. This, I say, is his speed. When asked a question concerning the Abhidhamma or the Abhivinaya, he answers and does not falter. This, I say, is his beauty. He is one who receives robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick. This, I say, is his proportions. Thus, bhikkhus, a noble thoroughbred man is possessed of speed...
295:
He is endowed with beauty and endowed with stature. Monks, these are the three noble thoroughbred men.

Tenth Sutta.

## 11. First Moranivāpa Sutta

144. At one time the Blessed One was staying at Rājagaha, in the Peacocks' Feeding Ground (Moranivāpa), the monastery of the wanderers. There the Blessed One addressed the monks: "Monks." "Venerable Sir," those monks replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this:

"Monks, a monk endowed with three qualities is one who has reached the absolute goal, the absolute security from bondage, the absolute holy life, the absolute end, and is the foremost among gods and humans. What three? The virtue of an adept (asekha), the concentration of an adept, and the wisdom of an adept. Monks, a monk endowed with these three qualities is one who has reached the absolute goal, the absolute security from bondage, the absolute holy life, the absolute end, and is the foremost among gods and humans."

## (16) 6. Acelakavagga
157-163. "Monks, there are these three practices. Which three? The indulgent practice, the scorching practice, and the middle practice. And what, monks, is the indulgent practice? Here, monks, someone has such a view and says: 'There is no fault in sensual pleasures.' He gives himself over to indulgence in sensual pleasures. This, monks, is called the indulgent practice.

And what, monks, is the scorching practice? Here, monks, someone goes naked, is of loose habits, licks his hands (after eating), does not come when asked, does not stop when asked. He does not accept food brought to him, or food specially prepared for him, or an invitation to a meal. He does not accept food from the mouth of a pot or a bowl. He does not accept food across a threshold, or across a stick, or across a pestle. He does not accept food from two people eating together, or from a pregnant woman, or from a woman giving suck, or from a woman in the company of a man. He does not accept food from collections (of food), or from where a dog is waiting, or where flies are swarming. He eats no fish or meat, drinks no liquor or wine or fermented gruel. He is a one-houser, taking one morsel; or a two-houser, taking two morsels... or a seven-houser, taking seven morsels. He subsists on one small saucer of food, or two... or seven. He takes food once a day, or once every two days... or once every seven days. Thus he dwells pursuing the practice of taking food at fixed intervals up to even half a month.

He is an eater of potherbs, or of millet, or of wild rice, or of hide-parings, or of water-moss, or of rice-bran, or of the scum of boiling rice, or of sesamum flour, or of grass, or of cow-dung. He subsists on forest roots and fruits, eating only what has fallen of itself.

He wears clothes of hemp, or of hemp-mixed cloth, or of shrouds, or of rags from a dust-heap, or of tree-bark, or of antelope skin, or of strips of antelope skin, or of kusa-grass fabric, or of bark fabric, or of wood-shavings fabric, or of a blanket of human hair, or of a blanket of horsehair, or of the wings of an owl. He is a plucker-out of hair and beard, addicted to the practice of plucking out hair and beard. He is one who stands continuously, rejecting seats. He is one who squats, addicted to the effort of squatting."
301:
He practices the plucking out of hair and beard; he rejects a seat and remains standing; he crouches and practices the exertion of crouching; he stays on a bed of thorns and sleeps on a bed of thorns; in the evening, for the third time, he practices descending into the water. In this way, he lives constantly practicing many such ways of scorching and tormenting the body. This, bhikkhus, is called the scorching practice.

And what, bhikkhus, is the middle way? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu dwells contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in the world. In feelings... [p]... in the mind... [p]... he dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in the world. This, bhikkhus, is called the middle way. These, bhikkhus, are the three practices. (1)

Bhikkhus, there are these three practices. Which three? The indulgent practice (taken firmly through the power of greed), the scorching practice, and the middle way. And what, bhikkhus, is the indulgent practice? [p] This, bhikkhus, is called the indulgent practice.

And what, bhikkhus, is the scorching practice? [p] This, bhikkhus, is called the scorching practice.

And what, bhikkhus, is the middle way? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu generates desire, makes an effort, arouses energy, exerts his mind, and strives for the non-arising of unarisen evil unwholesome states. He generates desire, makes an effort, arouses energy, exerts his mind, and strives for the abandoning of arisen evil unwholesome states. He generates desire, makes an effort, arouses energy, exerts his mind, and strives for the arising of unarisen wholesome states. He generates desire, makes an effort, arouses energy, exerts his mind, and strives for the maintenance, non-disappearance, increase, abundance, development, and fulfillment of arisen wholesome states. (2)

He develops the base of power that possesses concentration due to desire and volitional formations of striving. He develops the base of power that possesses concentration due to energy... [p]... concentration due to mind... [p]... concentration due to investigation... [p]...
302:
He develops the base of power that possesses concentration due to investigation and volitional formations of striving. [p] (3)

He develops the faculty of faith. He develops the faculty of energy. He develops the faculty of mindfulness. He develops the faculty of concentration. He develops the faculty of wisdom. [p] (4)

He develops the power of faith. He develops the power of energy. He develops the power of mindfulness. He develops the power of concentration. He develops the power of wisdom. [p] (5)

He develops the enlightenment factor of mindfulness. He develops the enlightenment factor of investigation of phenomena. He develops the enlightenment factor of energy. He develops the enlightenment factor of rapture. He develops the enlightenment factor of tranquility. He develops the enlightenment factor of concentration. He develops the enlightenment factor of equanimity. [p] (6)

He develops Right View. He develops Right Intention. He develops Right Speech. He develops Right Action. He develops Right Livelihood. He develops Right Effort. He develops Right Mindfulness. He develops Right Concentration. This, bhikkhus, is called the middle way. These, bhikkhus, are the three practices. (7)
